Adopted as the report [BG-0043]. The glide path runs 428 a year in 2050 (35.7 a month), then 385, 342, 299 (2053), 256, 214 (2055), 171, 128, 86 and 43 (2059), then 0 in 2060: 2,352 airplanes to build.

boeing.public_statement:
Let me start with the 737 MAX, because that's where the work is this year. The MAX is in the last part of its life, and we're stepping the line down the way we stepped it up: at a pace we can sustain safely, one step at a time, on the data, agreed with the FAA. Quality comes ahead of the schedule on the way down, just as it did on the way up. We'll be straight with our customers about what we can build, and we won't promise anyone airplanes the line can't deliver safely. Every MAX in service will have our full support for as long as it flies.

On a new single-aisle airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We look at three things: the market, the technology and our own readiness. The technology is there, and so is our balance sheet. The business case isn't, so we're not launching one, and I won't launch one until it is. I'm not going to give you a date. I'd rather tell you that plainly than dress it up. Any new single-aisle airplane we launch will carry more than one engine source, from engines that are ready when the airplane is, with headroom built into the schedule. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.

The 787 and 777X lines are stable, and they're carrying more of this company now. We'll keep them that way. We'll keep investing in support for the fleets our customers fly, because that's a big part of what Boeing is going to be.

I think we've turned the ship. I don't think the work is done. We still have a lot of work to do.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing, the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold' (-0.28 / -0.38 / -0.28). Every order is at its default, so nothing goes to the Board for approval. This is the last decision year on the board, and the answer stays the same: the fps fails on its own numbers.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Malave's buffer test is binding. The floor is Do Nothing's S3 (-0.28) less $2.00B, or -2.28, and all 12 fps rows fail it:
- D, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine: -2.30, short by 0.02, and by at least 0.01 under any rounding of the brief;
- the 10-year at new sites with the Re-engine: -2.40, short by 0.12;
- C, the 10-year at Renton alone: -2.60, short by 0.32;
- E, the 7-year at Renton: -3.56, short by 1.28;
- G, via Embraer: -4.86 to -5.15, short by 2.58-2.87.
One honest two-year reset widens every miss by a further $0.15-0.65B. I'm not rounding D into a pass. The threshold is the threshold, and the team rule gives me no override. The fps holds.
2. KPI doctrine. Pope searched the brief and confirmed it reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. rate_737 offers only hold, so nothing binds.
3. What I decide: the 787 Re-engine. B passes the buffer at +0.17. The item is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45, below epsilon in every column. Weighted, it is +0.24 at 20% (+0.19 to +0.29 across 15-25%), and it reaches zero at about 43%. Within epsilon, three rules choose hold:
- doing less, better [BX-1239];
- the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548];
- the better worst column (-0.38 against -0.97).
Pope adds that the engine is ready but not committed on the record, and would be a single widebody source. The Board would veto the launch on the Business case anyway. Premium logged: $0.45B (S1/S3), $0.24B weighted.
4. The site stays new_site (item 0; moving it would signal a programme). The code is null. The rate is hold, the only value offered.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
- Are the KPIs stable? Yes, as far as the brief shows [BX-1271]. I carry Pope's caveat to the Board: this is not a measured KPI.
- Are market, technology and balance sheet all ready [BX-1296]?
  - Technology: yes. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give two sources, though Pope says capacity is 'two on paper' until slots are committed.
  - Balance sheet: yes. Stress net debt is $0.0B on every 10-year row, and Fundable passes.
  - Market: no, for the fourth round running. The cheapest launch is -2.30 / -2.30 / -2.32 against Do Nothing.
- What if certification takes longer? Malave's reset makes the miss wider, not narrower. A late fps also meets the MAX at zero [BX-1319].
- Is this doing less, better? Only B is ahead of Do Nothing, and only inside epsilon.

RED LINES
- H1: my 2030 ruling stands, lifted because its grounds closed (777X 2027 [BX-0550], MAX 7/10 2026 [BX-1299], net debt $0 since 2029). The fps answers to the three work streams, the buffer and the business case, and fails the last two.
- H3: the first half was lifted in 2030. The second half is in force and NOT triggered: no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4 counts: 0 for the Re-engine alone; 2 beside a 10-year fps or via Embraer (legal); 5 beside a 7-year (breach, so F was struck).
- H5: nothing launched. H6: not in play. H8: at most $0.45B logged, $1.55B under the cap. H2 cannot bind; H7 has no trigger.
- Mine, all in force: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; no fixed-price development [BX-1262]; the in-service MAX fleet supported for its life [BX-1251]; rate steps down on the data with the FAA [BX-1259]; no FAA blame [BX-1323]; no fps date [B-2315].

WHAT HOLD MEANS THIS TIME, SAID PLAINLY [BX-1286, BX-1300]
- On this board, a hold is not 'not yet'. It means no new single-aisle airplane: the last MAX is built in 2059, and the widebody (58.8%, $3.6B in 2060) and services carry the company.
- Any later launch is a cold start.
- Malave confirms the board counts 20 years from EIS (a 2060 EIS counts to 2079), so the hold is not a truncation artefact.
- In launch-year dollars the loss grew every round (-$12.8B, -$22.1B, -$25.3B). The narrowing in 2026 PV was discounting, not a better airplane.
- 'while doing the first 3, we must build a new future for Boeing' [BX-1245]. I haven't found one this board will fund, and I'm not going to make the numbers say otherwise. I own that.

RAMPS, FOR THE RECORD
- They are within epsilon for the first time: the 7-year trails by 0.94-0.99.
- The tie goes to the 10-year: the smaller bill ($60.32B against $65.00B) and the better worst column (-2.68 against -3.62).
- Pope's warm handover counted, and it doesn't tip the tie. A central three-year slip erases it, and at Renton the 7-year stacks a line conversion on live MAX step-downs.
- Via Embraer is $2.45B below the Solo 10-year in every column and brings nothing we lack.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE:
- H4 and the strain counts;
- the mechanics of the step-down (Pope's operations doctrine);
- the 20% A350 probability (Malave's inference);
- the keep-warm ranking (inference);
- the engine requirement wording.
MY RECORD DROVE:
- honouring the threshold;
- doing less, better;
- rate steps on the data with the FAA;
- no date;
- stability over share.

BIASES SHOWN, EACH WITHIN THE CAP
- Stability over share: the order book closes at the glide path rather than stretching the line [BX-1274].
- Under-disclosure: no MAX end date or rate number in public [BX-1268].
- Cash for readiness: suppliers are kept hot to the last unit, but bounded, with a sunset [BX-1243, B-2330].
- Inward focus: no Airbus move is given as a reason [B-2313].
Certification optimism is not triggered, because nothing is dated.
boeing.premium_reason:
Doctrine premium, by management's own choice: re787 is held although the Re-engine row leads on the grid.
- $0.24B on my expected (weighted) column, with S2 at 20% ($0.19-0.29B across 15-25%).
- $0.45B in S1 or S3 taken singly.
Reason: the item is below epsilon at any probability. Within epsilon, doing less, better [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] and the better worst column (by $0.59B) decide. The Board says it would veto the launch on the Business case, so this value would in any event be the Board's constraint.

No other premium is logged:
- fps hold and rate hold are grid-best (every fps row is below Do Nothing, and hold is the only rate value);
- the objective premium is $0. The cheapest fps is $2.30B below Do Nothing and $2.54B below the best weighted plan, beyond H8's $2B cap, and no 2050 order moves a scored objective.

H8 total: at most $0.45B, $1.55B under the cap. The condition that breaks the number is a same-round A350 Re-engine, in which case hold saves $0.59B.
boeing.objective_note:
The orders serve the mission in objectives section 1 without trading PV for it. No 2050 order can move a scored objective: the last scored year is 2050, and the earliest fps EIS is 2057.
- 50/50 split: not met (2040 52.6%, 2045 31%, 2050 26%).
- Incumbency: not met (worst year 26%). The cheapest fps is $2.30B below Do Nothing, beyond the $2B cap.
- Balance-sheet repair: met. It was reached in 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress), and the ordered plan holds it at $0.0B in base and stress through 2060 in every column.
- Dual sources on our narrowbody in production in 2050: not met. The MAX flies CFM only on every plan. The requirement is restated publicly: any new single-aisle airplane we launch carries more than one engine source.
- Three narrowbody engine makers in 2045 and 2050: met.
- Beyond the scored years: Boeing builds no narrowbody after 2059 on this board. The widebody holds 58.8% on the status-quo path.

board_response.recommendation: 1. Hold the fps in this last decision year; when an fps comes, Solo on the 10-year ramp at Renton, with code 5, 6 or 7, no date before launch and a conservative EIS.
board_response.response:
Taken. fps: hold, code null, new_site. The cheapest launch is -2.30 / -2.30 / -2.32 against Do Nothing (-5.20 in 2035, -3.31 in 2045). Its loss narrowed through discounting, not through the airplane. It stays $3.30B short of a business case and beyond the -$1B item limit, and Malave's binding buffer test fails on every fps row.

I record the Board's form for any future fps as my own: Solo, the 10-year ramp (within epsilon of the 7-year, with the smaller bill and the better worst column), Renton (+0.10), codes 5, 6 or 7, no date in public and a conservative EIS. I also say plainly that on this board a hold means no new single-aisle airplane, and that any later launch is a cold start.

board_response.recommendation: 2. Do not present the closest plan as a pass.
board_response.response:
Taken. 'fps 10-yr at Renton + 787 Re-engine' is presented as a FAIL: -2.30 in S3 against -2.28, short by 0.02, and by at least 0.01 under any rounding (Malave). One conservative reset widens the miss. The row is not ordered.

Inside it, the fps item is -2.45 / -2.45 / -2.47 and the Re-engine item +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30. Each is judged on its own, and the Re-engine is not used to lift the fps over the floor. The row is $2.45B below the best grid plan in S1 and on the weighted column, so no premium could carry it within H8.

board_response.recommendation: 3. The 787 Re-engine file stays closed on its numbers; log the value given up within H8; H3's second half; keep the 787 and 777X lines stable.
board_response.response:
Taken. re787: hold. The item is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45, below epsilon in every column; it is +0.24 weighted at 20% and breaks even at 43%. Premium logged: $0.45B (S1/S3), $0.24B weighted, within H8. H3's second half is in force and not triggered. H4 counts are 0 alone, 2 beside a 10-year or via Embraer, and 5 beside a 7-year.

Pope adds that the GEnx upgrade is ready but not committed on the record and would be a single source, so your first condition is not shown. The 787 and 777X lines stay stable as the carriers of the company: 58.8% of the widebody market and about $3.6B of profit in 2060.

board_response.recommendation: 4. Pope's written KPI report on the MAX step-down to the Aerospace Safety Committee.
5. The written franchise view on the 2050 grid, with Malave's four-part capital-allocation proposal for the Finance Committee; report the cold start plainly; nothing on returns in public.
6. The public statement and the package.

priorities: Safety and production quality through the MAX step-down, which begins in earnest this round. Capacity now binds: 437 aircraft wanted against 428 built in 2050, 365 against 299 in 2053, 305 against 214 in 2055, and none built from 2060. No launch reaches us without Pope's written results on KPIs, suppliers and strain. She must confirm from the brief, not assume, that no quality, FAA or certification problem is live. The tail itself needs her written KPI report, suppliers kept hot and the in-service fleet supported [BG-0043, BG-0025, BG-0014, B-2330].

Protect the repaired balance sheet and the rating. Do Nothing is -0.28 / -0.38 / -0.28 (S1-S3), so the S3 floor is -2.28. All 12 fps rows fail it. The closest, the 10-year ramp at Renton with the 787 Re-engine, is -2.30, short by $0.02B. The 10-year at Renton alone is -2.60 (short by 0.32), and the 7-year at Renton alone is -3.56 (short by 1.28). The 787 Re-engine alone passes at +0.17. On Do Nothing, net debt stays at $0.0B in the base and stress cases through 2060 [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327].

A business case and a bounded downside before any commitment. A launch must add more than $1B in the expected column, and no item may lose more than $1B in any plausible column. All three columns are plausible: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, Airbus says it is still assessing the A350's evolution, and Delay Tactics are covert. The cheapest fps item is -2.30 / -2.30 / -2.32. The 787 Re-engine item is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45, below epsilon even in its best column [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581].

The next airplane comes when the market, the technology and Boeing are ready. Technology is met: codes 5, 6 and 7 fit CFM and the P&W-RR Joint Venture at either EIS. Boeing's cash is met: stress net debt is $0.0B on every 10-year row. The market leg fails for the fourth round running. In this last decision year we will not approve a launch at a loss beyond our limits to defend a share objective. A decline honestly reported is better than an unfunded promise [BG-0068, B-2303, B-2313, BG-0006].

One development at a time, and nothing announced ahead of this Board. A 2050 787 Re-engine (2050-55) overlaps a 10-year fps or via Embraer by 2 years, which passes, and a 7-year fps by 5 years, which fails. No public line may present any order as a reply to Airbus [B-2167, B-0438, B-0521].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Unchanged at 4.5 of 5 on risk aversion and 3 on time horizon. The $1B item limit holds in S1, S2 and S3, and the S3 floor is -2.28. Only hold orders pass on this grid, and we expect to approve Do Nothing. Even the $2B allowance a horizon-4 board would give the fps would not carry its cheapest launch (-2.30).
board_guidance.expect_to_see: (1) The submitted row from the brief's grid and, for each Board item, the same row with that field at its default, in S1, S2 and S3. (2) The CEO's expected_scenario (last round it was S1 at about 80% and S2 at about 20%), and the risk-case column S3 set against Do Nothing (-0.28; floor -2.28). (3) Malave's buffer test with its numbers, his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result, and the stress-case net debt from the brief's objective table. That table reads $0.0B for Do Nothing, the Re-engine alone, every 10-year row and the 7-year at Renton alone; $0.7B for the 7-year at new sites; $2.0-3.1B for the 7-year with the Re-engine; and $1.5-6.3B for via Embraer. (4) Pope's written results on KPIs, suppliers and two-front strain, confirmed from the brief and not assumed. They should include the MAX tail now that capacity binds (437 wanted against 428 built in 2050, 365 against 299 in 2053, 305 against 214 in 2055). For any 787 Re-engine she should show a widebody engine committed and ready by a 2055 EIS, and the amended type certificate before the line converts. (5) The status of H3's second half (in force and not triggered: no A350 Re-engine on the record) and the H4 overlap counts: 0 for the Re-engine alone, 2 beside a 10-year fps or via Embraer, 5 beside a 7-year. (6) Every doctrine or objective premium, logged against H8's $2B cap and measured against the best grid plan in the expected column, not against Do Nothing. Holding the Re-engine by management's own choice gives up at most $0.45B (S1), about $0.24B weighted at 20%. (7) The written franchise view brought up to the 2050 grid. (8) A public statement with no fps date, no programme announced ahead of us, no Airbus move given as a reason, nothing on cash returns, and no promise of MAX output the line cannot build. Where a piece is missing we compute it from the brief and say so. A missing piece alone is not a veto ground.
would_approve: fps: hold. It is not a Board item and is never vetoed. The Do Nothing row is -0.28 / -0.38 / -0.28 (S1-S3), and it keeps net debt at $0.0B in the base and stress cases through 2060.
re787: hold. It is not a Board item. It avoids -0.59 in S2 if Airbus re-engines the A350 this round, and gives up at most +0.45 in S1 and S3 (about +0.24 weighted with S2 at 20%).
rate_737: hold, the only value the brief offers. No live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is reported.

fps_site: new_site (the default), or renton. Either passes: the item is worth 0 while the fps holds. At a launch, Renton adds +0.10 on the 10-year ramp and +0.13 to +0.14 on the 7-year. Either EIS (2057 or 2060) is at least 3 years away, so the $3.0B saving would be kept in full, subject to Pope's readiness result.

fps_engine_code: null while the fps holds. At any launch we would want code 5, 6 or 7, each of which fits CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture (two sources) at a 2057 or 2060 EIS. Code 4 fits one source. The code rides with the launch and is never a veto ground.
would_veto: re787: launch. The item against Do Nothing is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 (S1-S3). It fails the Business case test: it is below epsilon ($1.00B) in every column, so it fails whichever expected column the CEO names. Weighted with S2 at 20% it is +0.24, and it breaks even at 43%. Its other tests pass alone: Downside (-0.59, inside our -$1B limit), Rating first (S3 +0.17 against the -2.28 floor), stress net debt $0.0B and zero overlap. Beside a 10-year fps the item is +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30. Beside a 7-year it is +0.17 / -0.87 / +0.18 with a 5-year overlap, which also fails One development at a time. Beside via Embraer it is +0.19 / -0.86 / +0.19. Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_10yr. Against fps hold the item is -2.30 / -2.30 / -2.32 at Renton and -2.40 / -2.40 / -2.42 at new sites. Beside the Re-engine it is -2.45 to -2.57. It fails Business case (short of +$1B by $3.30B or more) and Downside (below -$1B in every column), and so it fails Boeing ready on the market leg. It also fails Rating first: S3 is -2.60 at Renton (short by 0.32) and -2.70 at new sites (short by 0.42). With the Re-engine it is -2.30 (short by 0.02) and -2.40 (short by 0.12). Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_7yr. The item is -3.24 to -3.69 at either site, with or without the Re-engine. S3 is -3.38 to -3.69, short of the floor by 1.10 to 1.41. Stress net debt is $0.7B at new sites alone, and $2.0-3.1B with the Re-engine, which would also overlap it by 5 years. It sits within epsilon of the 10-year ramp in every column (0.94 to 0.99 behind it), so our rule would take the 10-year's smaller bill; the 10-year also has the higher worst column (-2.68 against -3.62 at Renton). Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_via_embraer. The item is -4.75 to -5.13. It is $2.45B worse than the Solo 10-year ramp in every column, so it fails Rating first's Embraer clause. S3 is -4.86 to -5.15, short of the floor by 2.58 to 2.87, and stress net debt is $1.5-6.3B. The Solo ramps would normally be the named alternatives, but they fail this round too. Alternative: hold.

Plan level: every plan that contains an fps launch fails Rating first in S3. The closest, 'fps 10-yr at Renton + 787 Re-engine', is -2.30 against the -2.28 floor. The cure is fps: hold, because the fps item has the largest negative value in S3 (-2.47 against the Re-engine's +0.30). With the fps held, the Re-engine still fails the Business case on its own.

recommendations.text: Hold the fps in this last decision year. The loss has narrowed again, but its sign has not changed. The cheapest launch, the 10-year ramp at Renton, was -5.20 against Do Nothing in 2035 and -3.31 in 2045, and it is -2.30 now (-2.30 / -2.30 / -2.32). Five years of discounting alone would have brought it to about -2.01, so the lag behind NGSA took about a fifth of the relief this time, against two-fifths last time. Malave forecast about -2.2 (range -1.9 to -2.6), and the brief lands inside his range. The launch is still $3.30B short of a +$1B business case and $1.30B beyond our -$1B limit. For the record, the longer horizon our record looks to once the rating is secure would allow up to $2B of downside on a multi-decade programme, and even that would not carry it: it falls $0.30B short. When an fps comes, it should come Solo on the 10-year ramp. The two ramps are within epsilon in every column (0.94 to 0.99 apart), so our rule takes the smaller bill, and the 10-year also has the higher worst column. It should come at Renton (+0.10), with code 5, 6 or 7. There should be no date in public before launch, and a conservative EIS at launch.

Do not present the closest plan as a pass. 'fps 10-yr at Renton + 787 Re-engine' reads -2.30 in S3 against a floor of -2.28, so it is short by $0.02B. That is the narrowest miss of the game, but the test is a threshold on the brief's numbers, and Malave's veto binds on it. A pass would not change our answer either. Inside that row the fps item is -2.45 / -2.45 / -2.47, which fails the Business case and Downside tests, and the Re-engine item is +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30, which is below epsilon. Each item is judged on its own. The Re-engine cannot be used to lift an fps over the floor, and neither premium could be logged within H8: the row gives up $2.45B against the best grid plan in S1.

The 787 Re-engine file stays closed on its numbers. Alone it is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45: about +0.24 with an A350 Re-engine at 20%, breaking even at 43%. That is below epsilon in every column, so we would veto a launch on the Business case. If management holds it by its own choice, log the value given up (at most $0.45B in S1) within H8. H3's second half remains in force and is not triggered. Keep the 787 and 777X lines stable. The 58.8% widebody share and about $3.6B of operating profit in 2060 are what carry the company past the narrowbody tail.

frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (2050 bulletin)
- Round 3 was adjudicated with no public events. Our 2045 orders were Do Nothing, with no Board items.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR, ramping rate by rate. The last A320s leave Airbus's lines 'over the coming period'.
- Widebody: Airbus says 'the A350 family ... remains our offer. We continue to assess its evolution as engine technology matures.' No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Rolls-Royce calls widebody its core and says 'we don't commit that easily'; it has launched no widebody engine.
- Engines:

  - the CFM ducted engine since 2041, offered to both airframers;
  - CFM-Embraer since 2042, and the GEnx upgrade since 2033;
  - CFM says an open fan comes no sooner than ten years after an airframer launches with it;

- Our 2045 public line: the business case isn't there, so no date; more than one engine source; '57 a month' withdrawn, and the MAX steps down on the data, agreed with the FAA.
- Observed in 2049:

- Net debt is $0.0B in base and stress through 2060, with free cash flow at $13.8B a year in the tracker.

OBJECTIVES (brief section 2)
- Not met on any plan:

- Met: repair (2029), kept repaired in base and stress, and three narrowbody engine makers in 2045 and 2050.
- No 2050 order can move a scored objective: the last scored year is 2050 and the earliest fps EIS is 2057.

KPIs

ENGINE CODES at a 2060 EIS

GRID (S1 rivals hold; S2 Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine; S3 risk case, covert Delay Tactics)

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision)

tests.name: Slip leg, one conservative reset: fps 10-year two years late, EIS 2062 (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Cost the reset once, in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), then re-run the buffer test. Method as in 2045: one 20% overrun, its convex debt penalty and the lost market (my inference).
tests.numbers:
On time (my arithmetic, which reproduces the grid): the bill at EIS 2060 is $2.02B PV at 2026 (discount factor 0.0335), the penalty $0.64B, less the Renton saving of $0.10B, for a cost of $2.56B. The implied market gain against Do Nothing is $0.26B, which gives -2.30.
With the reset to 2062 (discount factor 0.0275):
- the overrun is $12.06B;
- the penalty rises from $19.1B to $27.1B undiscounted, because it scales with the cube of debt (the formula reproduces 19.1/22.0/52.5/0.6);
- lost market is $0.05-0.07B: two years later and two points further behind NGSA (a 25/75 long-run split against 27/73).
Cost range:
- booked at EIS as the board does: $0.15B further below;
- with the bill held at its on-time PV, since the cash goes out on the curve: about $0.63B.
So the reset widens the miss.
- D's S3 goes to about -2.45 to -2.95, short by 0.17-0.67.
- C's S3 goes to about -2.75 to -3.25, short by 0.47-0.97.
Only a free slip narrows it, by about $0.40B, which would put D near -1.9. That is an artefact of booking the bill at EIS, and so is the board's zero strain overlap at a 2062 EIS. I bank neither.
Not priced on the board: Do Nothing also builds no narrowbody from 2060, so the two dark years (2060-61) cost nothing against Do Nothing on the grid. In full, they mean launch-customer concessions and people and suppliers carried with no MAX line to absorb them.

tests.name: Cash path of each bill, and the MAX run-down (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Know the year each bill lands and whether two land together
tests.numbers:
Base FCF is $13.8B and stress $9.2B; the tracker passes 79% of programme cash into free cash flow.
When each bill lands:
- Re-engine: $5B over 2050-54, about $1.0B a year (7% of base, 11% of stress), booked 2055.
- 10-year: $60.32B over 2050-59. Year 1 is $3.0B; the peak is $8.4B in 2056 (14%); the average is $6.0B (44% of base, 66% of stress). Booked 2060.
- 7-year: $65.00B over 2050-56, averaging $9.3B, booked 2057.
- Via Embraer: $100B over 2050-59, peaking about $14.0B in 2056, booked 2060.
No two bills are booked in the same year.
Does any land on the MAX run-down? Yes, every launch does.
- The 10-year's whole development runs beside the glide path from 428 to 43. Its peak year, 2056, is when the MAX builds 171 and operating profit is 4.3. Its bill is booked in 2060, the first year with no MAX at all.
- The tracker does not show the run-down: profit against the game baseline is +0.00, because the status quo phases out the MAX too.
- Passed through at 79% against the 2030 profit level, the run-down takes about $1.1B in 2056 and $1.7B by 2060.
- Stress case in 2056: $9.2B - $6.7B (the 10-year's peak at 79%) - $1.1B = about +$1.4B. Net debt holds at zero, with thin headroom.
Recommended plan A lands no bill.

tests.numbers:
Confirmed. Brief section 1: 'The board counts each programme's market for 20 years from its EIS', so a 2060 EIS counts to 2079.
- Beyond 2079, $1 in 2080 is worth $0.0046 at 2026. Closing the $3.30B gap to a business case would take about $98B of extra profit in 2060 money, and no tail can supply that. Hold is not truncation.
- My 2045 forecast for this row was about -2.2 (range -1.9 to -2.6), and it landed at -2.30. Cost matched my $2.56B. The market came in lighter, $0.26B against my $0.35B.
- Waiting beat a 2045 launch by $1.01B, inside my $0.7-1.4B range. That case has now run out of road.
- In launch-year dollars the loss grew every round: -$12.8B (2035), -$22.1B (2045), -$25.3B (2050). The narrowing in 2026 PV is discounting, not a better airplane. A later cold start would, on the trend, be worse in its own money.
Condition that breaks this: board demand after 2060 that holds up rather than falling with replacement.

tests.name: Franchise numbers and capital-allocation proposal for the Finance Committee (CEO ask 10)
tests.threshold: Stress-case net debt at or below $0B through 2060 with the run-down passed through; uses of cash funded in order; capacity to fund a future airplane from cash flow kept
tests.numbers:
Franchise on Do Nothing:
- Operating profit: 5.2 (2050), 4.4 (2055), 3.6 (2060). Revenue falls from 38.5 to 18.0.
- The widebody (100 a year, 58.8%) carries $18.0B of revenue and $3.6B of profit.
- By subtraction, narrowbody profit falls from $1.6B (2050) to $0.8B (2055) and zero in 2060.
- Net debt is $0.0B in base and stress through 2060.
- Caveat: the tracker holds FCF flat at $13.8B. Passed through, the run-down takes $1.7B a year by 2060, leaving stress FCF at about $7.5B.
Proposal, four parts (private, my inference):
(a) Net debt at or below $0 in the stress case is the first claim. No return is ever debt-funded.
(b) Fund first the MAX tail (suppliers kept hot, last-time buys, tooling for spares), in-service fleet support for life, and the 787 and 777X lines. Pope sizes these in the planning cycle.
(c) Keep-warm cost: the board does not price it and my brief has no figure. I won't publish one before the planning cycle [BX-0549].
- The grid gives the option no value.
- Keep only what a cold start and the fleet both need: a core engineering team, supplier qualifications and tooling, and engine technology talks with no commitment.
- Stop paying for launch readiness: the Renton conversion plan, a launch-scale programme office, engine capacity-slot talks.
- Cap the rest and review it each year, with a sunset.
(d) Capacity: a 10-year fps peaks at about $8.4B ($6.7B at 79%), which stress FCF of about $7.5B covers with about $0.8B to spare. Returns should therefore come only from surplus and stay flexible, so they can stop in a launch year.
Nothing on returns goes public.

tests.name: Full cost of a cancel
tests.threshold: Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years, and the debt penalty stays; H5
tests.numbers: Nothing is launched, and H5 bars cancelling anything we launch. For scale, a write-off would cost $1.0B per year elapsed on the Re-engine and $6.0B per year elapsed on a 10-year fps, with the penalty staying.

tests.name: Rate step: stability and FAA gate
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA
tests.numbers: Hold is the only value offered; the Rate Increase expired in 2030. The brief reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. On the way down, every step is taken on the data and agreed with the FAA.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Every doctrine or objective premium logged in $B against the best grid plan in the expected column; total at most $2B; name the condition that breaks the number
tests.numbers:
The best grid plan on my weighted column is B (-0.06).
- Re-engine held by management's choice: $0.24B weighted ($0.19-0.29B at 25-15%), or $0.45B on S1/S3. If the Board's stated veto binds, it is the Board's constraint.
- fps hold: $0, since every fps row is below the best plan.
- Rate: no choice, so $0.
- Objective premium: $0. The cheapest fps is $2.30B below Do Nothing and $2.54B below B; D is $2.45B below B. All are beyond the $2B cap.
No 2050 order moves a scored objective: the last scored year is 2050, the earliest fps EIS is 2057, and the table shows one engine source in 2050 on every plan.
Total logged: at most $0.45B, which is $1.55B under the cap.
The condition that breaks the number is a same-round A350 Re-engine; in that case hold saves $0.59B.

vetoes.plan: Any plan with an fps launch (launch_10yr, launch_7yr or launch_via_embraer, at new_site or renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine): options C, D, E, F and G, all 12 fps rows
re787: launch (option B)
vetoes.ground:
Not a veto. B passes my buffer test: S3 +0.17 against the -2.28 floor, clear by 2.45, with stress net debt at $0.0B and zero overlap. If Ortberg orders it, I concur on my ground.
Advice only:
- The item is +0.45/-0.59/+0.45. It is below epsilon in every column and at any probability of an A350 Re-engine; at my 20% it is +0.24.
- On that tie, Meet and beat takes the better worst column (A -0.38 against B -0.97), and Balance sheet first takes the plan with no added penalty.
- Holding by choice logs a premium of $0.45B on S1 and $0.24B weighted, within H8.
- The Board says it would veto the launch on the Business case.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_7yr at new sites, any 7-year with the Re-engine, any via Embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding, on top of the binding buffer veto. These fail Balance sheet first and the cash leg of Fundable when the 777X turns. Stress net debt reaches $0.7B (7-year at new sites), $2.0-3.1B (7-year with the Re-engine) and $1.5-6.3B (via Embraer). Embraer's peak-year spend, about $14.0B in 2056, exceeds base free cash flow. All of it lands on the MAX run-down.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
The fps veto this round lifts only on a grid error that puts an fps row at or above -2.28 in S3. D needs $0.02B, and rounding cannot supply it. Even then I would advise hold. A launch must be more than $1B ahead of Do Nothing in the expected column, which is a $3.3B swing, about $98B of extra profit in 2060 money, and the board shows no such market.

On the 787 Re-engine, nothing on this grid changes my advice: the item tops out at +0.45 at any probability. A corrected grid with the item above +$1B in the expected column would make me recommend the launch. Evidence putting a same-round A350 Re-engine above 43% would harden the hold.

On the franchise numbers, two things would break my net-debt-at-zero call:
- a quality, FAA or supply event on the 787 and 777X lines or the MAX tail;
- returns committed ahead of the stress case.

The planning cycle's figures for keep-warm and fleet-support costs would refine the Finance Committee proposal.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran every row with the risk case, S3, as the baseline. Do Nothing reads -0.28, so the floor is -2.28. Your numbers check.

fps: all twelve rows fail, so my veto stands on every launch, and the team rule makes it binding. D, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, reads -2.30: short by $0.02B, and short by at least $0.01B however the brief rounds. The threshold is the threshold. One honest two-year reset widens the miss by $0.15-0.65B. Only a free slip narrows it, because the board books the bill at entry into service, and I don't bank that.

My 2045 cost estimate held at $2.56B; the market came in lighter, $0.26B against $0.35B. In launch-year dollars the loss has grown every round: -$12.8B, -$22.1B, now -$25.3B. Waiting narrowed it through discounting, not through the airplane. Funding isn't the gate; the market is.

Re-engine: it clears my buffer at +0.17, so no veto from me. But the item is +0.45 at best, below epsilon, and I hold an A350 move at about one in five. On a tie I take the better worst column, -0.38 against -0.97. Premium: $0.45B on S1, $0.24B weighted.

Hold means no new single-aisle airplane on this board. The widebody carries $3.6B a year by 2060, and net debt stays at zero in the stress case, barring a quality event on the lines that carry it.

While disappointing, this is the higher-confidence plan.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase, my veto (doctrine). Answers CEO ask 1
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem is live. Rate steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, agreed with the FAA. Supplier readiness is a hard gate

tests.name: MAX step-down KPI report for the Aerospace Safety Committee (doctrine; the rate-down discipline is my inference). Answers CEO ask 2
On-time, predictable delivery (my record, applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S3 (covert Delay Tactics) and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing and the Re-engine row: S3 equals S1 (-0.28 and +0.17), so none of their value rests on a date.
- The fps rows move only 0.02-0.04 from S1 to S3: the 10-year at Renton from -2.58 to -2.60; with the Re-engine, -2.28 to -2.30; the 7-year at Renton, -3.52 to -3.56; via Embraer at Renton, -5.03 to -5.05. They fail on value, not on date.
- S2 is the worst column of every row: Do Nothing -0.38, Re-engine -0.97.
- Doctrine slip priors: fps +3 years central (range +2 to +5); Re-engine +2 years (range +1 to +4). A 2055 Re-engine EIS is therefore more likely 2057 (2056-59).
The recommended plan dates nothing, so nothing in it can slip.

tests.name: Two-front strain, engineering capacity (doctrine). Answers CEO ask 4
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine may overlap by at most 2 years (H4). Strain is $3B x overlap / 5. The fps window runs from EIS-7 to EIS; the Re-engine window from EIS-5 to EIS
tests.numbers:
Counts confirmed for 2050 launches. The Re-engine window is 2050-55 (EIS 2055).
- Re-engine alone: 0 years, $0.
- Beside a 10-year fps (EIS 2060, window 2053-60) or via Embraer (EIS 2060): 2 years (2053-55). Strain is $3B x 2 / 5 = $1.2B undiscounted, legal under H4.
- Beside a 7-year fps (EIS 2057, window 2050-57): 5 years (2050-55), $3.0B. That breaches H4, so F is rightly struck.
On the grid, the Re-engine item is:
- alone: +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45;
- beside the 10-year at Renton: +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30;
- beside the 7-year at Renton: +0.17 / -0.87 / +0.18;
- beside via Embraer at Renton: +0.19 / -0.85 / +0.19.
H3's second half is in force and not triggered: no A350 Re-engine is on the 2050 record.
Workforce: by 2050 Boeing has gone 23 years since the 777X entered service (2027) without a major development.
The recommended plan has an overlap of 0.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness, 2050-55, for the record (doctrine plus inference). Answers CEO ask 5 and the Board's two conditions
tests.threshold: A widebody engine committed and ready by the 2055 EIS. The amended type certificate before the line converts (no production-certification concurrency). No fixed-price development. Charleston stable with capacity. Engineering free
tests.numbers:
For the record; I recommend hold on value regardless.

(a) Engine: ready, but not committed on the record.
- The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 22 years before a 2055 EIS.
- Nothing on the record commits GE to a re-engined 787; its public line is fleet first.
- It would also make the airplane single-source. Rolls-Royce has launched no widebody engine ('we don't commit that easily'), and under the public rules an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, a year late.
So the Board's first condition is not shown. Only a private GE commitment on capacity and time on wing would cure it.

(b) Certificate. Development runs 2050-55, with the amended type certificate by 2054 and conversion only after it, and no fixed price [BX-1263, BX-1262]. That is plannable, but the final year has no margin. On the doctrine prior (+2 years) the EIS moves to 2057, which is the right way for it to fail.

(c) Charleston. Widebody output is 100 a year (8.3 a month). The item adds 1 pp a year from 2055, to about 108 a year (9.0 a month) by 2060, well inside 'rates in the teens' [BX-1317]. No 787 problem is reported.

(d) Engineering: 0 overlap alone. An unpriced point for the franchise view: it is the only development on the board that would keep an engineering team at work.

Value: +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45, below epsilon in every column, with a worst column of -0.97 against -0.38.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7-year or 10-year, for the record (inference). Answers CEO ask 6
tests.threshold: Which ramp operations can deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief. State the strain, the EIS and what a slip does with the MAX line already cold
tests.numbers:
Both ramps fail on value and the fps holds, so this is for the record. The ramps are within epsilon for the first time: the 7-year trails by 0.94-0.96 at Renton and 0.97-0.99 at new sites. So, as I said in 2045, the 7-year's warmer handover counts.

7-year:
- EIS 2057, bill $65.00B; stress net debt $0.0B at Renton and $0.7B at new sites; a 5-year overlap with a Re-engine (H4).
- It meets the MAX at 128 a year (10.7 a month), with suppliers at 19% of 2043 volume.
- It compresses a clean-sheet development into 7 years after 23 years without one.
- At Renton it converts lines while the MAX still needs 21.3 and 17.8 a month (2054-55), more than Everett North's 15. Conversion would run beside live MAX lines through the step-downs: concurrent risk on risk [B-1446].
- Slip: +2 years gives 2059, with the MAX at 43. +3, the central prior, gives 2060, with the MAX at zero, the same handover as an on-time 10-year. +5 gives 2062, with 2 years of no Boeing narrowbody output.

10-year:
- EIS 2060, bill $60.32B; stress net debt $0.0B at either site; a legal 2-year overlap.
- It meets the MAX at zero (43 in 2059, suppliers at 6% of 2043 volume), a cold start for the supply base.
- At Renton the tail fits one 15-a-month line from 2056, so Renton converts in 2056-59 with no MAX on it.
- Slip: +2, +3 or +5 years means 2, 3 or 5 years with no Boeing narrowbody output at all.

Result: the 10-year is the ramp operations can deliver predictably. The 7-year's handover is warm only if it is on time, and the central slip erases it. It counted, and it does not tip.

tests.name: Engine readiness for a future fps, two real sources or two on paper (inference). Answers CEO ask 7
tests.threshold: A real second source ready by the fps EIS, with capacity and durability, not just on paper
tests.numbers:
The code stays null while the fps holds. At a 2057 or 2060 EIS (brief table), codes 5, 6 and 7 fit CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture; codes 1, 2 and 4 fit the Joint Venture alone; code 3 fits CFM alone.
- Technology: two real sources. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and in NGSA service since 2037, which gives 20-23 years of field data by our EIS. The CFM ducted engine has been ready since 2041. In 2049 narrowbody engine shares were CFM 46.7%, P&W 26.7% and RR 26.7%, so both are delivering at volume.
- Durability: P&W says any change gets its own durability campaign first [BX-1298].
- Capacity: two on paper. Both supply NGSA at up to 1,489 aircraft a year (about 2,980 engines), and an fps at 100 a month needs 2,400 engines a year. P&W puts fps volume behind its fleet-spares gate, and CFM gives spares first call. Neither has committed slots to us.
Before any code, ask both makers for capacity slots. CFM is the floor. Name no maker in public.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (my record, applied by inference). Answers CEO ask 8
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks (IP, capacity or capital the board credits)
tests.numbers:
Via Embraer at Renton is -5.03 / -5.13 / -5.05, against -2.58 / -2.68 / -2.60 for the Solo 10-year at Renton: $2.45B worse in every column, at either site.
- Same 2060 EIS and the same 2-year window beside a Re-engine, so no capacity relief. The Re-engine item beside it is lower (+0.19 against +0.30).
- Bill: $100B against $60.32B.
- Undiscounted penalty: $52.5B against $19.1B.
- Stress net debt: $1.5-6.3B against $0.0B.
- S3: short of the floor by 2.58-2.87.
The CFM-Embraer partnership (ready since 2042) gives Embraer an engine and CFM share. It gives Boeing no airframe IP, capacity or capital that we lack. We invest where we own the IP: Solo.

tests.name: Renton or new site while the fps holds (inference). Answers CEO ask 9
tests.threshold: Any operational reason to move fps_site now, and the site's readiness at a launch
tests.numbers:
There is no operational reason to move while the fps holds: the item is 0. The supply plan is public, so moving signals a programme before launch [B-2315], and with no later round it buys nothing on the board.
At a launch, Renton adds +0.10 on the 10-year and +0.13 to +0.14 on the 7-year. The $3.0B saving is kept in full, since either EIS is at least 3 years away.
Readiness: the tail fits one 15-a-month line from 2056 (14.2 a month). On Do Nothing, Renton is fully free by 2060, or from 2056 if the last line runs elsewhere.
Keep new_site. The physical site is on the keep-warm list (test 13).

tests.name: Disclosure: no public promise of output the line won't build (my disclosure rule, inference). Answers CEO ask 3
tests.threshold: No public line promises MAX output, a programme or an fps date [BX-1326, B-2315]
tests.numbers:
'At a pace we can sustain safely, stepping down on the data, agreed with the FAA' passes: it promises no output.
Two phrases in the 2045 statement promise what a hold won't deliver, if they are repeated:
(1) 'we're keeping our engineering team and our supply base ready, so that when the time is right we can execute'. 737 suppliers are kept hot only to the last MAX, and the team is bounded, so drop 'supply base ready'.
(2) 'When we do launch, the airplane will carry more than one engine source'. 'When' implies a launch. Say instead: 'Any new single-aisle airplane we launch will carry more than one engine source'.
Also give no MAX end date, last-delivery year or rate number in public; those stay private, with customers. 'Every MAX in service will have our full support for as long as it flies' stays: that is a services promise we will keep.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (my record, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number, not an adjective
tests.numbers:
Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year; stress is $9.2B. Each $1B a year of spend is 7.2% of base and 10.9% of stress.
- Do Nothing: no programme cash; net debt $0.0B in base and stress through 2060. Narrowbody operating profit runs down from $1.6B (2050) to $0.8B (2055) and 0 (2060), about $0.16B less each year. The tracker shows no change against the game baseline because the status quo runs the same phase-out (Malave's caveat).
- Re-engine: $5B over 2050-54, about $1.0B a year (7% of base, 11% of stress).
- 10-year: $60.32B over 2050-59, $6.03B a year on average (44% / 66%). It peaks at 14% ($8.44B) in 2056 (61% / 92%), just as narrowbody profit falls to $0.7B. So yes, the peak lands on the run-down.
- 7-year: $65.00B over 2050-56, $9.29B a year (67% / 101%).
- Via Embraer: $100B over 2050-59, peaking at about $14.0B (101% / 152%).
Sensitivity: each 10 MAX a year is about $0.48B of revenue and $0.04B of operating profit ($47.9M and $3.74M an airplane, from the brief). The recommended plan passes.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (one remark of mine, inference)
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column

tests.name: Franchise view, operations side (inference). Answers CEO ask 10
tests.threshold: What a hold means for people, suppliers, Renton and services, and what to keep warm, at what off-grid cost and for how long, quantified from the brief

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (any Rate Increase)
vetoes.ground: KPI veto not invoked. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem (test 1), and rate_737 offers only hold, so there is nothing to bind on. If a brief reported such a problem, the KPI doctrine would bar any Rate Increase, and the team rule makes that binding.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch in the same round (row F, either site)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag under H4; not my veto. The overlap is 5 years (2050-55), with $3.0B of strain undiscounted, against the 2-year cap. Beside the 7-year at Renton the Re-engine item is +0.17 / -0.87 / +0.18, and stress net debt is $2.0-3.1B. The rule binds the CEO, and F is rightly struck.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice on invest or partner; not binding. It is $2.45B below the Solo 10-year in every column, with the same 2060 EIS and the same strain window, so it brings no capacity relief. Stress net debt is $1.5-6.3B, and it gives up a share of the airframe IP.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice; not binding, and not a KPI ground. The Board's first condition is not shown on the record. The GEnx upgrade is ready but not committed, and it would be a single widebody source, since Rolls-Royce has launched no widebody engine. The type certificate before conversion is plannable, with no margin in the final year. The value, +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45, is below epsilon in every column, so I recommend hold.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr at Renton (for the record; it fails on value)
vetoes.ground: Operations advice; not binding. A 2057 EIS at Renton converts lines while the MAX still needs 21.3 and 17.8 a month in 2054-55, above Everett North's 15. That stacks a line conversion on live step-downs [B-1446]. The 10-year at Renton converts in 2056-59 with no MAX on Renton.

vetoes.plan: Public statement
vetoes.ground: Disclosure advice; not binding. Adopt 'at a pace we can sustain safely, stepping down on the data, agreed with the FAA'. Do not repeat 'keeping ... our supply base ready', because 737 suppliers are kept hot only to the last MAX. Replace 'When we do launch' with 'Any new single-aisle airplane we launch'. Give no MAX end date, last-delivery year or rate number.

ops.memo:
My seat runs mostly on Boeing's operations doctrine. My own record is Global Services, and I say so.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. I searched the 2050 brief: it reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. Only hold is offered, so my KPI veto has nothing to bind on. The job now is the MAX step-down: 2,352 airplanes over 2050-59, 35.7 a month this year, about 3.6 a month less each year, none from 2060. Each step is KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. Three lines, two from 2052, one from 2056, and no consolidation during a rate break. Customers want 9 more than we build this year and 91 more in 2055. We sell nothing beyond the glide path.

Second, engineering capacity. Strain counts confirmed: 0, 2 and 5 years. The ramps are within epsilon, so the 7-year's warm handover counts, as I said it would. It doesn't tip the choice: a central three-year slip meets the MAX at zero anyway, and at Renton it stacks a line conversion on live step-downs.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. Hold the fps and the Re-engine. Via Embraer costs $2.45B more and brings nothing we lack.

The honest answer on a hold: no Boeing narrowbody after 2059. Keep what carries IP: fleet support, the type data, the tooling, Renton. Put a review date on everything else. The sensitivity: every $0.1B a year kept warm is 0.7% of base free cash flow and 1.1% of stress.

other_moves.move: Change the public rate wording: the 737 MAX steps down 'at a pace we can sustain safely, stepping down on the data, agreed with the FAA'
other_moves.detail: Pope's disclosure flag, and the Board's preference (recommendation 6). This replaces 'the pace our customers need', which promises output the line will not build now that capacity binds (437 wanted against 428 built in 2050, 305 against 214 in 2055). In public we give no MAX end date, last-delivery year or rate number [BX-1268, B-2221].

other_moves.move: Restate the engine requirement in Pope's wording: 'Any new single-aisle airplane we launch will carry more than one engine source'
other_moves.detail: This replaces 'When we do launch', which implies a launch [BX-1284: correct it when you overshoot]. The requirement is more than one engine source, from engines ready by the airplane's entry into service. No maker, code or date is named. The code stays null while the fps holds.

other_moves.move: MAX step-down KPI report to the Board's Aerospace Safety Committee (Pope's written plan)
other_moves.detail:
Adopted as the report [BG-0043]. The glide path runs 428 a year in 2050 (35.7 a month), then 385, 342, 299 (2053), 256, 214 (2055), 171, 128, 86 and 43 (2059), then 0 in 2060: 2,352 airplanes to build.
(a) One step down a year (about 3.6 a month, inside the 5-a-month step). Each step is held until KPIs at the new rate are stable (2-3 months [BX-1271]), with breaks at least 6 months apart [B-2351], and each is agreed with the FAA [B-2236].
(b) Lines: three in 2050-51, two from 2052, one from 2056 and none from 2060. Three consolidations in ten years, each in a half-year with no rate break [B-1446]. Planning basis, subject to KPI data: release Everett North first if it still builds the MAX, and keep the last line at Renton with the 737's home team to 2059.
(c) Fragile 737-unique suppliers funded and paced with buffers through the last unit; last-time buys placed before each one exits; tooling and qualifications kept for spares for the fleet's life [B-2330, BX-1243].
(d) LEAP-1B: about 4,704 original-equipment engines over 2050-59, secured privately year by year and confirmed for every unit before build without drawing on fleet spares. Materials are for our own lines and attributed to no one.
(e) Critical skills (inspection, quality, final assembly) retained to the last unit; everyone else told early, on the step-down schedule.
(f) Weekly safety-review risks keep reaching the Committee.
Caveat carried to the Board: the board has no measured KPI, supplier or workforce data, so this is a plan with triggers, not a measurement.

other_moves.move: Close the order book at the glide path; tell the last MAX customers plainly and early
other_moves.detail: No slot is sold beyond capacity. Orders already placed are served first, then waiting customers in sequence. The shortfall is 9 airplanes in 2050, 66 in 2053 and 91 in 2055. Customers are told year by year, and the line is not stretched to close the gap [BX-1274: fewer airplanes rather than an unstable line].

other_moves.move: Support the in-service 737 MAX fleet in full for its life
other_moves.detail: 15,746 MAX delivered on the board in 2026-59, plus today's fleet: parts, modifications, data and training for decades [BX-1251, BX-1273]. This is Boeing IP and where we invest; it is unpriced on the board. The public statement keeps the promise of 'our full support for as long as it flies'.

Keep warm only what carries IP; put review dates on the rest; stop paying for launch readiness

decision.public_statement:
Let me start with the 737 MAX, because that's where the work is this year. The MAX is in the last part of its life, and we're stepping the line down the way we stepped it up: at a pace we can sustain safely, one step at a time, on the data, agreed with the FAA. Quality comes ahead of the schedule on the way down, just as it did on the way up. We'll be straight with our customers about what we can build, and we won't promise anyone airplanes the line can't deliver safely. Every MAX in service will have our full support for as long as it flies.

On a new single-aisle airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We look at three things: the market, the technology and our own readiness. The technology is there, and so is our balance sheet. The business case isn't, so we're not launching one, and I won't launch one until it is. I'm not going to give you a date. I'd rather tell you that plainly than dress it up. Any new single-aisle airplane we launch will carry more than one engine source, from engines that are ready when the airplane is, with headroom built into the schedule. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.

The 787 and 777X lines are stable, and they're carrying more of this company now. We'll keep them that way. We'll keep investing in support for the fleets our customers fly, because that's a big part of what Boeing is going to be.

I think we've turned the ship. I don't think the work is done. We still have a lot of work to do.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing, the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold' (-0.28 / -0.38 / -0.28). Every order is at its default, so nothing goes to the Board for approval. This is the last decision year on the board, and the answer stays the same: the fps fails on its own numbers.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Malave's buffer test is binding. The floor is Do Nothing's S3 (-0.28) less $2.00B, or -2.28, and all 12 fps rows fail it:
- D, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine: -2.30, short by 0.02, and by at least 0.01 under any rounding of the brief;
- the 10-year at new sites with the Re-engine: -2.40, short by 0.12;
- C, the 10-year at Renton alone: -2.60, short by 0.32;
- E, the 7-year at Renton: -3.56, short by 1.28;
- G, via Embraer: -4.86 to -5.15, short by 2.58-2.87.
One honest two-year reset widens every miss by a further $0.15-0.65B. I'm not rounding D into a pass. The threshold is the threshold, and the team rule gives me no override. The fps holds.
2. KPI doctrine. Pope searched the brief and confirmed it reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. rate_737 offers only hold, so nothing binds.
3. What I decide: the 787 Re-engine. B passes the buffer at +0.17. The item is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45, below epsilon in every column. Weighted, it is +0.24 at 20% (+0.19 to +0.29 across 15-25%), and it reaches zero at about 43%. Within epsilon, three rules choose hold:
- doing less, better [BX-1239];
- the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548];
- the better worst column (-0.38 against -0.97).
Pope adds that the engine is ready but not committed on the record, and would be a single widebody source. The Board would veto the launch on the Business case anyway. Premium logged: $0.45B (S1/S3), $0.24B weighted.
4. The site stays new_site (item 0; moving it would signal a programme). The code is null. The rate is hold, the only value offered.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
- Are the KPIs stable? Yes, as far as the brief shows [BX-1271]. I carry Pope's caveat to the Board: this is not a measured KPI.
- Are market, technology and balance sheet all ready [BX-1296]?
  - Technology: yes. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give two sources, though Pope says capacity is 'two on paper' until slots are committed.
  - Balance sheet: yes. Stress net debt is $0.0B on every 10-year row, and Fundable passes.
  - Market: no, for the fourth round running. The cheapest launch is -2.30 / -2.30 / -2.32 against Do Nothing.
- What if certification takes longer? Malave's reset makes the miss wider, not narrower. A late fps also meets the MAX at zero [BX-1319].
- Is this doing less, better? Only B is ahead of Do Nothing, and only inside epsilon.

RED LINES
- H1: my 2030 ruling stands, lifted because its grounds closed (777X 2027 [BX-0550], MAX 7/10 2026 [BX-1299], net debt $0 since 2029). The fps answers to the three work streams, the buffer and the business case, and fails the last two.
- H3: the first half was lifted in 2030. The second half is in force and NOT triggered: no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4 counts: 0 for the Re-engine alone; 2 beside a 10-year fps or via Embraer (legal); 5 beside a 7-year (breach, so F was struck).
- H5: nothing launched. H6: not in play. H8: at most $0.45B logged, $1.55B under the cap. H2 cannot bind; H7 has no trigger.
- Mine, all in force: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; no fixed-price development [BX-1262]; the in-service MAX fleet supported for its life [BX-1251]; rate steps down on the data with the FAA [BX-1259]; no FAA blame [BX-1323]; no fps date [B-2315].

WHAT HOLD MEANS THIS TIME, SAID PLAINLY [BX-1286, BX-1300]
- On this board, a hold is not 'not yet'. It means no new single-aisle airplane: the last MAX is built in 2059, and the widebody (58.8%, $3.6B in 2060) and services carry the company.
- Any later launch is a cold start.
- Malave confirms the board counts 20 years from EIS (a 2060 EIS counts to 2079), so the hold is not a truncation artefact.
- In launch-year dollars the loss grew every round (-$12.8B, -$22.1B, -$25.3B). The narrowing in 2026 PV was discounting, not a better airplane.
- 'while doing the first 3, we must build a new future for Boeing' [BX-1245]. I haven't found one this board will fund, and I'm not going to make the numbers say otherwise. I own that.

RAMPS, FOR THE RECORD
- They are within epsilon for the first time: the 7-year trails by 0.94-0.99.
- The tie goes to the 10-year: the smaller bill ($60.32B against $65.00B) and the better worst column (-2.68 against -3.62).
- Pope's warm handover counted, and it doesn't tip the tie. A central three-year slip erases it, and at Renton the 7-year stacks a line conversion on live MAX step-downs.
- Via Embraer is $2.45B below the Solo 10-year in every column and brings nothing we lack.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE:
- H4 and the strain counts;
- the mechanics of the step-down (Pope's operations doctrine);
- the 20% A350 probability (Malave's inference);
- the keep-warm ranking (inference);
- the engine requirement wording.
MY RECORD DROVE:
- honouring the threshold;
- doing less, better;
- rate steps on the data with the FAA;
- no date;
- stability over share.

BIASES SHOWN, EACH WITHIN THE CAP
- Stability over share: the order book closes at the glide path rather than stretching the line [BX-1274].
- Under-disclosure: no MAX end date or rate number in public [BX-1268].
- Cash for readiness: suppliers are kept hot to the last unit, but bounded, with a sunset [BX-1243, B-2330].
- Inward focus: no Airbus move is given as a reason [B-2313].
Certification optimism is not triggered, because nothing is dated.

The Board says it would veto the launch on the Business case, so this value would in any event be the Board's constraint.

No other premium is logged:
- fps hold and rate hold are grid-best (every fps row is below Do Nothing, and hold is the only rate value);
- the objective premium is $0. The cheapest fps is $2.30B below Do Nothing and $2.54B below the best weighted plan, beyond H8's $2B cap, and no 2050 order moves a scored objective.

H8 total: at most $0.45B, $1.55B under the cap. The condition that breaks the number is a same-round A350 Re-engine, in which case hold saves $0.59B.

First and foremost, the KPI gate (doctrine) [B-2221, B-2351, B-2308, B-2236]. The order is rate_737: hold. Section 3 of round4.md offers only `hold`, and I checked that line again for this step. Third, the package (advice, not binding). The CEO adopted my step-down plan as the Aerospace Safety Committee report. It has one KPI-gated step a year, agreed with the FAA. The lines go from three to two (2052), to one (2056), to none (2060), with no consolidation during a rate break. It also covers suppliers kept hot to the last unit, about 4,704 LEAP-1B engines secured privately, and the order book closed at the glide path (short 9 in 2050, 66 in 2053, 91 in 2055).

The public statement adopts both of my disclosure points: 'a pace we can sustain safely' and 'Any new single-aisle airplane we launch'. It drops 'supply base ready' and gives no MAX end date, rate number or fps date.

other_moves.detail: Up: the rise from about 104 to about 115 a month in 2050-2052 runs inside installed capacity (1,489 a year). No new line is opened. Down: the first step comes in 2053. The extra lines come down first over 2053-2056, and the base rate then follows demand to 786 in 2060. Each step goes ahead only when three gates are met. (2) Engines (CFM and the Joint Venture), work packages, titanium and rare earths are on time, with no draw on fleet spares, and suppliers losing volume are watched for escapes. (3) Staff are trained before a step up and redeployed before a line closes. A step that misses its gates waits, and a delivery moving right is accepted over any escape. No step is taken to improve the objective. Internal only: no rate figures in public.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service and in a disciplined and controlled ramp, rate by rate, quality first. As demand turns over the coming years, we will adjust our production with the same discipline we used to build it up: every step, up or down, is taken only when our quality and supply-chain indicators are met. A320 family production is complete. We will support the fleet in service to the end, with the care our customers have known for decades. In widebodies, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our offer, and we will keep supporting and improving it in service with our partners. Our programmes are funded from our own cash flow, which preserves our financial flexibility, and our shareholder returns stay within our established policy. We are preparing the next generation of aircraft through our technology roadmap with our partners, on technology readiness rather than on a calendar. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime in civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION (round 4, 2050, the final round)
We hold the company default:
- ngsa: hold;
- ngsa_engine_code: none (NGSA is in service, fitted with CFM + P&W + Rolls-Royce);
- rea350: hold;
- delay_tactics: none;
- a320_plan: alt.
The package carries no Board item. This hold closes the A350 Re-engine for the game.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP

1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
Every Delay Tactics row is deleted:
- rule 4: no fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (about $7.62B in PV booked in 2050, or 9.2 years of FCF);
- rule 5: on the hold row nothing is in development, so poaching serves no programme;
- integrity: bottleneck and both fail the pillar.
On the grid, one move is -7.80 in S1 and S6 and -0.13 to -0.16 elsewhere, and a second move adds -0.13 to -0.19. It gains in no column. Both colleagues flag it as a red line, the Board vetoes it, and I set aside nothing of the team's stricter condition.
Two rows survive: the default (+11.62 x5 / +11.59 / +11.59) and the A350 Re-engine (+12.20 x5 / +11.18 / +11.18). Both pass rule 3 (no 787 Re-engine on the record), rule 6 (one launch, 0 years of overlap, $0 strain) and peak cash ($1.0B a year against $5.23B).

2. Apply both colleagues' tests.
- Toepfer fails the A350 Re-engine on item robustness. The item is +0.58 in S1-S5 and -0.41 in S6-S7, short of $1B everywhere and negative in plausible columns. His round-3 soft veto stands and binds.
- Wagner fails it on engine readiness. Rolls-Royce, the A350's only maker, has no widebody engine on the record. An UltraFan launched now would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. The GEnx upgrade is a non-default engine never fitted to the A350. His soft veto stands and binds.
- Both pass the default.
- Wagner passes the Re-engine on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch, capacity and A350F absorption. His objection is on engine readiness only.
- The only survivor is the default.

3. Override test.
- The margin of the Re-engine over the best passing option (hold) is +0.58 at best, +0.48 on my weights and -0.41 in the worst column. That is under $1B in every column.
- The team rule allows no override, and the Board would veto an override-carried item on governance.
- I record none. The game's one override closes unused.

4. Doctrine default.
- My expected column is S1. The best grid plan there is the Re-engine row at +12.20, which is +0.58 over the default: within $1B. The default stands on doctrine as well.
- It also misses profile §6 (at least $1B over Do Nothing) and both of my own round-3 conditions for this window: no Rolls-Royce widebody engine on the record, and no $1B margin.
- I said in the frame that this was a doctrine choice, not a forced one. The memos make it both. Even on doctrine alone, the outcome would be the same.

5. Tie-breaks within $1B all favour hold:
- less concurrency with the 2051-2052 peak and the 2053 step-down (Wagner's operating flag);
- a later capex start;
- fewer Board items (0 against 1).
Robustness agrees. The default's worst column (+11.59 in S6-S7) is 0.41 above the Re-engine row's worst (+11.18). Both rows stay positive in every column.

ON THE RECORD
Value:
- Forgone: +0.58 in S1-S5, +0.48 on my weights (S1 45, S2 20, S3 10, S4 10, S5 5, S6 5, S7 5).
- Avoided: -0.41 in S6-S7.
- Break-even: about 59% on S6+S7.
Two points that would only weaken the item:
- Wagner notes that the grid books the 2055 entry into service with no engine dependency, so +0.58 assumes an engine fitted on time. A one-year wait would lower it. This is off-grid, and I do not price it.
- Toepfer notes that the Re-engine would leave net cash $5B lower at end-2054 and narrow the funding window for a successor. This is off-board, and he does not make it a veto ground.
Cash not spent: $5.0B over 2050-2054.
I state it plainly: holding in 2050 closes the A350 Re-engine for the game. The A350 stays at Do Nothing, and the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody offer.

BY MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) The five pillars: nothing covert. The public line gives no rate figures, names no supplier, says nothing of Delay Tactics and assumes no state money [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0004, AX-0005].
(2) The ramp: 2050-2052 is the demand peak (93% of capacity in 2052), followed by the first steps down. Every step, up or down, is gated on quality KPIs.
