- The default package carries none: ngsa hold, rea350 hold and delay_tactics none are defaults, and a320_plan alt was approved in round 1.
- rea350 launch would be the only item: $5B / 1.10 = EUR 4.55bn, above EUR 800m, so Qualified Majority [AG-0049].
- Each Delay Tactics move ($1B, about EUR 0.91bn, an abnormal level of risk [A-0299]) would also be one.
- The payout and buyback proposals are reserved to the Board in any case [AG-0058].
Confirmed: 0 items against 1. The tie-break favours hold.

tests.name: Capex timing (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: The Re-engine is within $1B of hold in every column (+0.58 in S1-S5, -0.41 in S6-S7). Hold starts no capex; the Re-engine starts $1.0B a year in 2050. The tie-break favours hold, as does the Board-item count. Confirmed.

tests.name: Cancel
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA (rule 7). Cancel an A350 Re-engine only if Boeing's 787 Re-engine enters service first and its remaining spend loses at least $1B. Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years.
tests.numbers:
- NGSA is in service, so there is nothing to cancel.
- No Re-engine has been launched.
- If one were launched now, a 787 Re-engine launched in the same round would also enter service in 2055. That is not 'first', so it would not qualify for a cancel, and there is no later round in any case.

tests.name: Five pillars, internal control and disclosure
tests.threshold: No order or statement whose integrity or compliance I could not defend to the Audit Committee. The Board vets all market disclosures. No internal targets.
tests.numbers:
- Nothing in the default package is covert, and every spend is on the record.
- 'Funded from our own cash flow' holds: $0 against $5.23B on hold, $1.0B on the Re-engine path.
- The public statement goes to the Board [AX-0004]. It carries no internal targets [AX-0005], no rate figures, no state money and no word of Delay Tactics, and it gives windows, not dates.
- Supply security and talent remain first claims on our own needs, not bottleneck or poaching.

tests.name: Engine code
tests.threshold: No financial test; defer to Mr Wagner on supply
tests.numbers: NGSA is in service, so the code is final and has no payoff effect. It is null in my orders, and I defer to Mr Wagner. The objective counts two sources and three makers in 2050 on every row.

vetoes.plan: NGSA hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 (rea350: launch), alone or with Delay Tactics
vetoes.ground:
Soft veto: the added item fails the robustness test. My round-3 soft veto stands on these numbers.

THE ITEM against the same plan without it: +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / -0.41 / -0.41.
- It is negative in S6-S7, which the bulletin does not rule out.
- It is short of $1B in every column (profile §6; the drafter's reading).

MARGIN against the best passing option (hold, the default): +0.58 at best, +0.48 on the CEO's weights, -0.41 in the worst column. That is under $1B in every column, so the team rule offers no override route, and the Board would veto an override-carried item on governance.

It is not a red line: peak cash ($1.0B against $5.228B), rule 3 (open) and rule 6 (one launch, 0 years of overlap) all pass. Whether to override is the CEO's call, not mine to pre-clear; on these numbers the rule does not allow it. With Delay Tactics added, the row also breaks rule 4 (see below).

vetoes.plan: Every Delay Tactics row: bottleneck, poaching or both, on hold or with an A350 Re-engine
vetoes.ground:
Company red lines, not overridable.

RULE 4: no fps is on the record, so every move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine, booked in 2050. That is $7.62B in PV, 9.2 years of FCF, and 1.4-2.5 times stress net cash.
- One move is -7.80 in S1 and S6 (-7.81 with the Re-engine) and -0.13 to -0.16 in every other column.
- It falls short of $1B everywhere and breaks the Board's $2B limit in S1 and S6.
- `both` is a second move that buys nothing (a further -0.13 to -0.19).

RULE 5: on the hold row nothing is in development, so poaching has no programme to serve.

INTEGRITY: bottleneck and both also fail the pillar.

The Board vetoes all three this round. The team's stricter condition stands, and nothing is to be set aside.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view if any of the following is shown:

(1) The record rules out S6-S7, so that no 787 Re-engine is plausible this round. The item would then be +0.58 in every plausible column, my robustness test would pass, and I would lift the soft veto. Cash already passes. Whether +0.58 is enough under the company's $1B doctrine would then be the CEO's call, not a CFO veto. In a simultaneous final round I do not expect this.

(2) A grid shows the A350 Re-engine at least $1B over hold in the expected column.

(3) The Board decides otherwise.

(4) Audited net cash entering 2050 comes in below my stress low case ($19.2B after share-plan cover), or FCF falls well below the 2025 base. I would then recalibrate the payout toward the 30% floor and hold any discretionary buyback. The orders would not change.

(5) Audited net cash comes in at or above my central path ($28.8B after cover). I would then put a discretionary buyback on the 2026 precedent's scale to the Board, still sized so that an NGSA-sized successor stays fundable at any payout inside policy.
cfo.memo:
Round 4 (2050), the final round. I concur with the lean: ngsa hold, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. Engine code: none, as NGSA is in service; I defer to Mr Wagner. No Board item.

Peak cash. Hold: programme cash nil; no Alt-plan tail remains. A350 Re-engine: $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year in 2050-2054, no strain, against one year's free cash flow, EUR 4,753m x 1.10 = $5.23B [AX-0104]. Both pass.

Balance sheet. The brief has no audited figures. My stress, carried forward, puts net cash entering 2050 at $24.3-33.8B, or $19.2-28.8B after share-plan buybacks; it counts none of NGSA's margin. Payout 48%. Renew the 18-month, 10% authority for share-plan cover; a discretionary programme only on audited figures. An NGSA-sized successor stays fundable without equity, with the payout nearer the floor on the low path. No equity raise, dividend cut or state money on either path.

Robustness. Both rows stay positive; worst columns S6-S7: hold +11.59, Re-engine +11.18. The item is +0.58 in S1-S5 and -0.41 in S6-S7, +0.48 weighted, break-even 59%. It turns negative in a plausible column and misses $1B everywhere. My round-3 soft veto stands and binds; no override can carry +0.58. Not a red line.

Hold forgoes +0.58 (+0.48 weighted), avoids -0.41, and closes the A350 Re-engine for the game.

Delay Tactics: red line. Naked; the $48.32B fine is $7.62B in PV, 9.2 years of free cash flow.

A prudent risk approach [AX-0022].

tests.name: Safety, quality and the five pillars: the package and the public line (asks 1 and 7)
tests.threshold: No order, and no public explanation, that contradicts safety and quality. No rate step goes ahead of its quality KPIs, and no quality is traded for the 60/40 objective.
tests.numbers:
- The round-4 brief reports no safety, quality or supply event on NGSA (in service since 2037), the A350 and A350F, or the in-service A320 fleet.
- Every order in the default package is a default, and none is covert. Nothing fails the five pillars.

Public line (ask 7), confirmed:
- NGSA 'in service', with the ramp 'rate by rate, quality first' through the peak and the turn in demand.
- A320 production complete, with the fleet supported.
- No rate figure (not 1,489, 1,384 or 786), no extra-line figure, no supplier named, no past reset.
- If the A350 is held, no engine maker is named as the reason.
- Windows, not dates, for any Re-engine. No word of Delay Tactics.

tests.name: NGSA rate plan through the 2052 peak and the step-down to 2060, each step gated on quality KPIs (ask 2)
tests.threshold: Each rate step, up or down, and each line consolidation goes ahead only once its quality KPIs are met. No line kept or opened that demand will not need. No step taken to improve the objective.
tests.numbers:
Capacity 1,489 a year (about 124 a month) from 2050. Deliveries (brief), a month:
- 2050: 1,250 (about 104), slack 239, 84% used.
- 2051: 1,352 (about 113), slack 137.
- 2052 peak: 1,384 (about 115), slack 105, 93% used.
- 2053: 1,255 (about 105); 2055: 1,191 (about 99); 2056: 1,148 (about 96); 2060: 786 (about 66), 53% used.

Lines, on my reading of the public plan (inference): about rate 100 (1,200 a year) plus up to 20 a month of extra lines (240), plus the board's top-ups. Without the extra lines, capacity would be about 1,200-1,250, below 2051-2052 demand. So:
- Up: the rise from about 104 to 115 a month in 2050-2052 runs inside installed capacity. No new line is needed or opened.
- Down: the first step is 2053 (-129 aircraft, about -11 a month). The extra lines come down first in 2053-2056 as deliveries fall to 1,255-1,148. The base rate then follows demand: -120 in 2057, -105 in 2058, -69 and -68 to 786 in 2060.

Gates for every step (inference; the brief gives no thresholds):
1. Conformance and concessions flat or improving at the current configuration, with zero safety-related escapes. A consolidation goes ahead only when the receiving line's KPIs hold.
2. Engines (CFM and the Joint Venture) and work packages on time, with no draw on fleet spares; titanium and rare earths covered. Suppliers losing volume are watched for escapes.
3. Staff trained before a step up, and redeployed before a line closes, keeping the skills the remaining lines need (recruitment and redeployment).

No step is held back today, because no event is reported. A step that misses its gates waits; I accept a delivery moving right over an escape.

tests.name: The A320 tail and in-service fleet support (ask 3)
tests.threshold: Production closed without drawing on fleet spares; any 2046 unit had engines confirmed before build or the tail stopped at what was covered; the in-service fleet supported to the end with no draw on fleet spares.
tests.numbers:
- A320 capacity: 26 in 2045, 0 from 2047 (brief: 0 + 1,429). Production is complete.
- The brief does not show 2046, so I claim no 2046 figure. The round-3 rule applied: engines for any 2046 unit confirmed before build without fleet spares, or the tail stops at what is covered. The brief reports no supply event and no draw on fleet spares.
- I report it to the Board's safety review as 'no safety, quality or supply event recorded', claiming no figure.
- In-service fleet: CFM ('spares never crowd out the new engines') and P&W ('new production never crowds out its spares'; GTF Advantage kit at shop visits) both put the fleet first. That supports A320 fleet support to the end, with no draw on fleet spares from our side.

tests.name: Supply crunch, on the default and with an A350 Re-engine (asks 4 and 5d)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency.
tests.numbers:
- None reported: nothing on engines, work packages, titanium or rare earths.
- NGSA engines: 2,500 (2050), 2,704 (2051), 2,768 at the 2052 peak, against 2,534 in 2049 (1,267 x 2): about +9% at the peak, then falling (2,510 in 2053, 1,572 in 2060).
- Rival capacity falls from 428 (2050) to 299 (2053) and 214 (2055), so MAX LEAP-1B volume falls as NGSA rises. CFM's total narrowbody volume is roughly flat (inference).
- Watch item, as attribution: P&W puts GTF spares ahead of new production. If Joint Venture new engines ever compete with GTF spares at the peak, spares come first, so the engine gate applies. No maker publishes a capacity figure.
- Work packages, titanium and rare earths: a first claim on our own needs only (renewed on the record).
- An A350 Re-engine would add about 140 widebody engines a year (70 aircraft), a different engine family. On the brief's numbers that creates no crunch.

tests.name: Engine supply on NGSA (code recommendation, not a veto ground; ask 4)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker. New engine standards certified in sequence, never dropping CFM.
tests.numbers:
- The code is final because NGSA is in service. Fitted: CFM + P&W + RR, giving 2 sources (CFM and the Joint Venture) and 3 makers in 2050 in every cell of the objective table.
- Joint Venture engine: ready since 2036, on NGSA since 2037. P&W and RR each at 26.7% of narrowbody engines in 2049.
- CFM ducted engine: ready since 2041. Any new standard is certified on NGSA in sequence and cut in only at a step whose KPIs are met. The current CFM standard stays until the new one passes.
- No maturity slip is reported.

tests.name: Engineering capacity: A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 (ask 5a; rule 6)
tests.threshold: NGSA and A350 Re-engine development may overlap by 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round.
tests.numbers:
- NGSA development ran 2030-2036 and has ended. A350 Re-engine development would run 2050-2054.
- Overlap: 0 years. Strain: $3B x 0/5 = $0. It would be the only launch this round.
- Staffing would come from recruitment and redeployment, not from the NGSA lines.

Operating flag, not a failed test: those development years run beside the 2051-2052 peak and the 2053 step-down. The same production-engineering, quality and supplier-development people serve both. The step-down from 2053 frees people for redeployment, and 105-239 aircraft of slack keeps the load manageable.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption; A350 line readiness (ask 5c)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: round 2 at the earliest.
tests.numbers:
- 2050 is round 4.
- The A350F entered its industrial phase in 2025, and the Spirit packages date from 2025-26. The brief reports nothing on either, so treating both as absorbed is an inference.
- The A350 line runs steady at 70 widebody deliveries a year (41.2%) in every year of the brief. Cutting in a new engine at 70 a year is a manageable industrial change, if an engine exists.

tests.name: A350 Re-engine: engine readiness for entry into service in 2055 (ask 5b; teams.md Step 3 engine test, inference)
tests.threshold: Step 3 passes the default engine (Rolls-Royce on the A350) when it adds no years. Any other engine, or one that adds years, needs at least $1B on the grid. Faury's own round-3 condition for this window: a Rolls-Royce widebody engine on the public record.
tests.numbers:
The default maker:
- The A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB only.
- The public record shows no UltraFan widebody launch and no other new widebody engine for the A350. Rolls-Royce: 'Widebody is our core, and we defend it through time on wing'; 'we don't commit that easily'.
- Under rules.md the UltraFan widebody is ready 6 years after launch. Ready by 2055 needed a launch by 2049, and none was. Launched this round, it is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. There is no later round, so nothing this round can clear it.
- The Trent 1000 upgrade is a 787 engine.

The only mature alternative:
- The GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033, is GE's 787 engine. It has never been fitted to the A350, and no GE offer for the A350 is on the record. It would be a non-default engine, a new integration.

Against the grid:
- Item: +0.58 in S1-S5 (12.20 - 11.62), -0.41 in S6-S7 (11.18 - 11.59), +0.48 on Faury's weights.
- Below $1B in every column, so it fails. My round-3 engine-readiness soft veto stands for this window and binds.

Caveat: the board books the 2055 entry into service with no engine dependency, so +0.58 assumes an engine is fitted. A one-year wait to 2056 would lower it, and that case is not on the grid.

Scope: this is an engine readiness and supply result, not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result.

tests.name: Ramp shield (A320 commitment and the NGSA ramp)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open ramp commitment. It passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.
tests.numbers:
- The end-2027 A320 commitment is long past, and A320 production is complete (0 from 2047).
- No ramp problem is reported on NGSA.
- Hold adds no spend. A Re-engine adds $1.0B a year in 2050-2054 with $0 strain. It is flagged against the 2052 peak (see capacity) but does not fail the shield.

tests.name: Delay Tactics (rules 4 and 5, five pillars; option 4)
tests.threshold: At most one move, only after an fps launch and before its entry into service. 'Both' counts as two. Bottleneck only as a first claim on our own capacity. Poaching only while an Airbus programme is in development.
tests.numbers:
This fails for any move. The default, at none, passes.
- No fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine.
- One move on hold: -7.80 / -0.13 / -0.13 / -0.15 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13 (S1-S7).
- One move with a Re-engine: -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.16 / -0.14 / -7.81 / -0.14.
- A second move adds -0.13 to -0.19. It loses in every column and gains in none.
- On the hold row nothing is in development, because NGSA is in service, so poaching also breaks rule 5.
- Bottleneck and both breach the integrity pillar.

tests.name: Production readiness, rule 1 and engine maturity slip (NGSA)
tests.threshold: No NGSA entry into service before 2035. On a reported engine slip, re-time NGSA; never cancel it.
tests.numbers:
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, so rule 1 was met.
- No slip is reported, and there is nothing to re-time or cancel.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: we keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers:
- None is on the record. Boeing withdrew its '57 a month' line, and the MAX steps down (rival capacity 428 in 2050, 0 by 2060).
- That changes none of our programmes.

tests.name: Next generation: read only, for the Board's strategy off-site (ask 6; no order on this board)
tests.threshold: The gates I would apply: a wing buildable at rate, a mature production system, and two engine sources with CFM in the set. No programme commitment.
tests.numbers:
- CFM: an open fan comes 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer', so 2060 at the earliest for a 2050 launch.
- The board counts NGSA's market to 2056.
- No second maker has an open-fan line on the record. The Joint Venture's development spend is 'behind us', and Rolls-Royce does not 'commit that easily'.
- An open-fan successor would not meet the two-source gate today.
- Read: a 2060+ technology question for the off-site, with no commitment.

vetoes.plan: A350 Re-engine launched in 2050, entry into service 2055 (option 2)
vetoes.ground:
Failed engine-readiness test (teams.md Step 3 engine test, applied to the public record; inference).

The engine:
- Rolls-Royce, the A350's only maker, has no widebody engine on the record. An UltraFan widebody launched this round is ready in 2056 (6 years under rules.md), a year after the 2055 entry into service. No later round exists to close the gap.
- The only mature widebody upgrade is GE's GEnx (ready 2033), a 787 engine never fitted to the A350. A non-default engine, or one that adds a year, needs at least $1B on the grid.

Grid margin against the best passing option (hold):
- +0.58 in S1-S5, -0.41 in S6-S7, +0.48 weighted.
- That is under $1B in every column, so no override can carry it. The Board's override review would fail it too.

Scope:
- It is a soft veto, binding under the team rule.
- The ground is engine readiness and supply. It is not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result: the Re-engine passes those.
- The board books the 2055 entry into service with no engine dependency, so this constraint is off-grid.
- If launched, it would carry an unresolved ExCo objection.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics (bottleneck, poaching or both), on the hold row or the Re-engine row (option 4)
vetoes.ground:
Company red lines and the integrity pillar:
- Rule 4: no fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. 'Both' counts as two moves.
- Rule 5: poaching with nothing in development on the hold row.
- Integrity pillar: bottleneck and both.

Grid:
- One move: -7.80 in S1 and S6, -0.13 to -0.16 elsewhere.
- A second move adds -0.13 to -0.19.
- It gains in no column.

Not overridable.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
A350 Re-engine:
- I would pass the engine test only if a widebody engine for the A350 were on the public record and ready by the 2055 entry into service. Under rules.md, a Rolls-Royce UltraFan widebody would have had to launch by 2049, and none did. A launch this round is ready in 2056, so nothing on this board can clear the test in the last round.
- A non-default engine (the GEnx upgrade) passes only if the grid shows at least $1B over hold. It shows +0.58.
- A reported supply crunch or quality event would also fail it on concurrency.
- If the CEO's expected scenario moved to S6-S7, the item would lose 0.41. That strengthens hold.

Ramp:
- A reported quality escape on NGSA, or a supply event on CFM or Joint Venture engines, work packages, titanium or rare earths, would hold the next step (a rate rise to the 2052 peak, or a line consolidation on the way down) until its KPIs recover.

A320 fleet:
- Any draw on fleet spares would go to the Board's safety review at once.

Delay Tactics:
- Nothing on this board changes them.
ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived; none of my record is in my own words (Very low confidence).

I recommend the default: ngsa hold, no engine code (in service, CFM + P&W + RR), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt.

Safety and quality: the brief reports no event on NGSA, the A350 and A350F, or the A320 fleet. Nothing in the package or the public line fails the pillars.

The ramp, up and down: capacity 1,489 against 1,384 at the 2052 peak (105 slack), then 1,255 in 2053 and 786 by 2060. The extra lines carry the peak and come down first; the base rate then follows demand. Every step, up or down, on the same gates: zero safety-related escapes; engines and work packages on time, no draw on fleet spares; staff trained or redeployed before the step. I hold no step back today.

A320: production complete; fleet supported to the end without fleet spares.

Engines: about 2,768 at the peak from CFM and the Joint Venture, while the MAX steps down. No crunch reported. Two sources, three makers.

A350 Re-engine: capacity passes, 0 years overlap, $0 strain. It fails on the engine. Rolls-Royce, our A350 maker, has no widebody engine on the record; launched now, an UltraFan is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. The GEnx upgrade is GE's 787 engine. A non-default engine needs $1B; the grid shows +0.58. Soft veto, binding; no override can carry it.

Delay Tactics: red line, binding.

other_moves.move: NGSA rate plan through the 2052 peak and the step-down to 2060, every step gated on quality KPIs (Wagner's plan, adopted)
other_moves.detail: Up: the rise from about 104 to about 115 a month in 2050-2052 runs inside installed capacity (1,489 a year). No new line is opened. Down: the first step comes in 2053. The extra lines come down first over 2053-2056, and the base rate then follows demand to 786 in 2060. Each step goes ahead only when three gates are met. (1) Conformance and concessions are flat or improving, with zero safety-related escapes; a line consolidation goes ahead only when the receiving line's KPIs hold. (2) Engines (CFM and the Joint Venture), work packages, titanium and rare earths are on time, with no draw on fleet spares, and suppliers losing volume are watched for escapes. (3) Staff are trained before a step up and redeployed before a line closes. A step that misses its gates waits, and a delivery moving right is accepted over any escape. No step is taken to improve the objective. Internal only: no rate figures in public.

other_moves.move: Safety oversight through the turn in demand, reported to the Board's twice-yearly safety review
other_moves.detail: Mr Wagner reports on three things: NGSA in-service safety and quality, the step-down plan against its gates, and in-service A320 fleet support with no draw on fleet spares. Any draw on fleet spares, and any quality escape, goes to the Board at once.

other_moves.move: Talent: recruitment and redeployment (renewed)
other_moves.detail: The workforce through the peak and the decline is planned through hiring, internal development and redeployment between lines, keeping the skills the remaining lines need [A-0366, A-0485]. It covers our own people only and takes nothing from any rival's workforce.

other_moves.move: Supply security for our own lines and A320 fleet support (renewed)
other_moves.detail: We keep securing our own work packages, titanium and rare earths for the NGSA lines [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. This is a first claim on our own needs only. A320 production is complete. The in-service fleet is supported to the end, with no draw on fleet spares. The public line names no engine supplier and refers to no past reset.

other_moves.move: Engine standards on NGSA certified in sequence
other_moves.detail: Any new standard (for example CFM's ducted engine, ready since 2041) is certified on NGSA in sequence and cut in only at a step whose KPIs are met. The current CFM standard stays until the new one passes, and CFM is never dropped. We keep two sources (CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture) and three makers.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy (renewed)
other_moves.detail: Through industry coalitions, with Boeing an ally on trade, for a tariff-free regime on civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation proposal to the Board (CFO), reserved to the Board
other_moves.detail: Mr Toepfer reports net cash on audited figures. Where audited figures are absent, his stated stress applies: $24.3-33.8B entering 2050 before share-plan cover and $19.2-28.8B after it, with no NGSA margin counted. The proposal has three parts: (1) a payout of 48%, inside the 30-50% policy and recalibrated at each Yearly Budget; (2) renewal of the standard AGM authority (18 months, 10%) for share-plan cover; (3) a discretionary buyback brought to the Board only on audited net cash at or above the central path, sized so that a successor of NGSA's order of magnitude stays fundable from our own cash. No equity raise, no dividend cut and no state money in the case [AG-0058, AG-0035, AG-0062].

other_moves.move: A350 kept at Do Nothing; the Re-engine path closed for the game, on the record
other_moves.detail: Forgone: +0.58 in S1-S5, +0.48 on my weights. Avoided: -0.41 in S6-S7. Cash not spent: $5.0B over 2050-2054. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody offer, supported in service.

other_moves.move: NGSA successor at the Board's strategy off-site
other_moves.detail: A roadmap and technology-gate review with no programme commitment. The gates are technology and production readiness and at least two engine sources with CFM in the set. CFM's open fan comes no sooner than ten years from an airframer launch, and no second maker has an open-fan line on the record, so this is a 2060+ question [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0243, A-0360].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service and in a disciplined and controlled ramp, rate by rate, quality first. As demand turns over the coming years, we will adjust our production with the same discipline we used to build it up: every step, up or down, is taken only when our quality and supply-chain indicators are met. A320 family production is complete. We will support the fleet in service to the end, with the care our customers have known for decades. In widebodies, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our offer, and we will keep supporting and improving it in service with our partners. Our programmes are funded from our own cash flow, which preserves our financial flexibility, and our shareholder returns stay within our established policy. We are preparing the next generation of aircraft through our technology roadmap with our partners, on technology readiness rather than on a calendar. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION (round 4, 2050, the final round)
We hold the company default:
- ngsa: hold;
- ngsa_engine_code: none (NGSA is in service, fitted with CFM + P&W + Rolls-Royce);
- rea350: hold;
- delay_tactics: none;
- a320_plan: alt.
The package carries no Board item. This hold closes the A350 Re-engine for the game.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP

1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
Every Delay Tactics row is deleted:
- rule 4: no fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (about $7.62B in PV booked in 2050, or 9.2 years of FCF);
- rule 5: on the hold row nothing is in development, so poaching serves no programme;
- integrity: bottleneck and both fail the pillar.
On the grid, one move is -7.80 in S1 and S6 and -0.13 to -0.16 elsewhere, and a second move adds -0.13 to -0.19. It gains in no column. Both colleagues flag it as a red line, the Board vetoes it, and I set aside nothing of the team's stricter condition.
Two rows survive: the default (+11.62 x5 / +11.59 / +11.59) and the A350 Re-engine (+12.20 x5 / +11.18 / +11.18). Both pass rule 3 (no 787 Re-engine on the record), rule 6 (one launch, 0 years of overlap, $0 strain) and peak cash ($1.0B a year against $5.23B).

2. Apply both colleagues' tests.
- Toepfer fails the A350 Re-engine on item robustness. The item is +0.58 in S1-S5 and -0.41 in S6-S7, short of $1B everywhere and negative in plausible columns. His round-3 soft veto stands and binds.
- Wagner fails it on engine readiness. Rolls-Royce, the A350's only maker, has no widebody engine on the record. An UltraFan launched now would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. The GEnx upgrade is a non-default engine never fitted to the A350. His soft veto stands and binds.
- Both pass the default.
- Wagner passes the Re-engine on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch, capacity and A350F absorption. His objection is on engine readiness only.
- The only survivor is the default.

3. Override test.
- The margin of the Re-engine over the best passing option (hold) is +0.58 at best, +0.48 on my weights and -0.41 in the worst column. That is under $1B in every column.
- The team rule allows no override, and the Board would veto an override-carried item on governance.
- I record none. The game's one override closes unused.

4. Doctrine default.
- My expected column is S1. The best grid plan there is the Re-engine row at +12.20, which is +0.58 over the default: within $1B. The default stands on doctrine as well.
- It also misses profile §6 (at least $1B over Do Nothing) and both of my own round-3 conditions for this window: no Rolls-Royce widebody engine on the record, and no $1B margin.
- I said in the frame that this was a doctrine choice, not a forced one. The memos make it both. Even on doctrine alone, the outcome would be the same.

5. Tie-breaks within $1B all favour hold:
- less concurrency with the 2051-2052 peak and the 2053 step-down (Wagner's operating flag);
- a later capex start;
- fewer Board items (0 against 1).
Robustness agrees. The default's worst column (+11.59 in S6-S7) is 0.41 above the Re-engine row's worst (+11.18). Both rows stay positive in every column.

ON THE RECORD
Value:
- Forgone: +0.58 in S1-S5, +0.48 on my weights (S1 45, S2 20, S3 10, S4 10, S5 5, S6 5, S7 5).
- Avoided: -0.41 in S6-S7.
- Break-even: about 59% on S6+S7.
Two points that would only weaken the item:
- Wagner notes that the grid books the 2055 entry into service with no engine dependency, so +0.58 assumes an engine fitted on time. A one-year wait would lower it. This is off-grid, and I do not price it.
- Toepfer notes that the Re-engine would leave net cash $5B lower at end-2054 and narrow the funding window for a successor. This is off-board, and he does not make it a veto ground.
Cash not spent: $5.0B over 2050-2054.
I state it plainly: holding in 2050 closes the A350 Re-engine for the game. The A350 stays at Do Nothing, and the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody offer.

BY MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) The five pillars: nothing covert. The public line gives no rate figures, names no supplier, says nothing of Delay Tactics and assumes no state money [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0004, AX-0005].
(2) The ramp: 2050-2052 is the demand peak (93% of capacity in 2052), followed by the first steps down. Every step, up or down, is gated on quality KPIs. No line is kept that demand will not need, and the workforce is managed through recruitment and redeployment [AX-0010, AX-0015, AX-0056, A-0366, A-0485].
(3) The 2030s and beyond: prepared through the technology roadmap and the Board's strategy off-site, on technology gates and two engine sources, with no launch on this board [AX-0020, AX-0006].
(4) The Board: it approves the defaults, asks for no override and asks for a reasoned hold with the forgone value on the record. All three are given.

BOARD-GATE LINES
- The package carries no Board item. ngsa hold, rea350 hold and delay_tactics none are defaults, and a320_plan alt was approved in round 1.
- For the record, the item considered and not brought is rea350 launch, about EUR 4.55bn, which would need a Qualified Majority:
  - five pillars: pass;
  - Toepfer: fail (item robustness, binding);
  - Wagner: fail (engine readiness, binding; passes on safety, quality, ramp and supply crunch);
  - grid ΔPV: +0.58 in S1-S5, -0.41 in S6-S7.
  It is not brought because it carries two unresolved ExCo objections that no override can carry, which is on the Board's would-veto list.
- Delay Tactics, for the record:
  - five pillars: fail for bottleneck and both;
  - Toepfer and Wagner: red line;
  - grid: -7.80 in S1 and S6.
- The payout and buyback proposals go to the Board as reserved matters, not as orders.

BOEING AND OUR OWN CLOCK
- Boeing's last window moves nothing for us. An fps launched now enters service in 2057 or 2060, after NGSA's counted window ends in 2056, so S2-S5 are value-neutral on this grid.
- Only a 787 Re-engine (S6-S7) separates the rows, and only against the Re-engine row.
- Boeing's line ('stable' widebody lines, no fps date, the business case 'isn't' there) leans to S1. I keep my weights unchanged. The bulletin rules out no column.

CONFIDENCE
Toepfer's and Wagner's tests are role-derived (Low and Very low confidence). My own decision rules are inference from pay design and the Board's account. Here, every source points the same way.

decision.predictions:
BOEING IN 2050, its last round:

- If Boeing launches fps, the 10-year route is likelier than the 7-year one. Either way, it enters service after NGSA's counted window.

That is Ali's watch item. So the spares and kit supply for the installed LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A fleets is contracted jointly with Safran, against shop-visit forecasts, ahead of any development parts. They never draw on fleet spares, and the tail stops at what is covered, under the airframer's own rule. No supplier is named, and we have no current supplier data. other_moves.detail: Members: engineering, quality and supply chain; fleet support with field data; the safety review; Safran engineering [CX-0012]. This review reported a standing gap. Nothing on the record since 2045 shows gate point (b), a core or engine test, or (c), acceptance by the airframer and the regulator. There are no Ducted harsh time-on-wing data, and nothing shows a failure. A gap isn't a pass. The review keeps reporting harsh time on wing for the Ducted, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and GEnx fleets to the full Board, against the mature LEAP-1A with the CFM56 as yardstick. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts continues in new make and MRO as part volume falls. other_moves.detail: Ground and flight testing continue jointly, durability and dust first. RISE is not cancelled for cost, and it doesn't launch as a product ahead of an airframer. It becomes a product when an airframer wants it. If an airframer launches a new single-aisle, the product case comes to the full Board then, jointly with Safran and on test results [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0174, CX-0398]. The only public timing: an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. No year. The next-generation bar stays at least 20% better fuel burn without trading durability [CX-0217, CX-0208]. Test results go to the Board as they come off test. None after 2025 are on our record.

That covers the new single-aisle airplane in service and any new single-aisle airplane Boeing launches under its 'more than one engine source' requirement. The work with Embraer goes on, non-exclusive, in addition to our two big customers and not in place of either. No airframer is refused or locked out [CX-0587, CX-0185, CX-0564]. other_moves.detail: Standard terms only. No launch-era pricing, and no concession to win or hold any engine code [CX-0930, CX-0609]. cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That hasn't changed, and it won't.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: the new single-aisle airplane is flying, and CFM is on it with our partner Safran. Our ducted engine is in service on the airplanes that chose it. It's the right engine for those airplanes, and we offer it to both airframers. It isn't the next generation. That's the open fan. Our work with Embraer goes on. It adds to what we do for our two big customers and takes nothing away from them.

Job one is still the fleet. As today's airplanes give way to the new ones, the fleets in service still need us. LEAP, ducted and GEnx engines have to stay on wing. The kits and spares they need get first call, and spares never crowd out the new engines our customers are waiting on. We'll tell you how the fleet is doing when the field data shows it, and not before.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one. When that is, it's really not for us to say.

What we don't know is when the next new airplane comes, or what it will ask of us. We don't have a birthright on that order. When it comes, we'll compete for it on the product and on durability.

We're not going for share for its own sake. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. The balance sheet stays strong, and we keep returning cash to our shareholders.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467, CX-0319]. This is the last round, and the game is the installed base we already have. No slot is open on this board.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, with all three makers fitted.
- Our Ducted (ready 2041), Embraer (counting since 2042) and GEnx upgrade (counting since 2042) can only hold.
- Boeing has not launched the fps, for the fourth round. An fps launched now enters service in 2057 or 2060, after the 2056 narrowbody window.
We win by closing out well: safety and durability of the fleets first, kits and spares first, RISE whole as technology with Safran, the balance sheet and payout untouched, and a straight account to the Board. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages" [CX-0630].

DECISION: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions, genx).
- No Board item.
- Premium $0.0B, and the game total is $0.0B of $4.0B.
- The RISE allowance is unused.
- No overrides. Both memos recommend hold, and no binding veto stands against it.

THE TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Grid rows, S1 / S2:
- Hold: -24.41 / -24.41. The best plan in both columns.
- Open Fan: -38.13 / -38.13, or -13.72 against hold in each column.
  - That is its $8B bill plus $5.72B of wait penalty.
  - Rahul rebuilt the wait at $5.73B: every CFM engine on NGSA from 2050 to 2056, about 4,750 engines at 26.98% of NGSA.
  - Nothing else is in it: no new strain, because the $2B is booked, no write-off, and no WB or MAX effect.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.45 / -37.45, or -13.04 against hold. That is $9B plus $4.04B. Lobby caps the loss at 20 of our 28.33 raw points, and 4.04 / 5.72 = 0.706.
- Lobby next to the Open Fan alone: +0.68. It falls with the Open Fan.
- Lobby alone: off the grid, -1.00 in each column.
- S1 cost of any Open Fan: its whole bill plus the wait, and nothing bought. Worst column = S1 = S2.
- The columns are identical on every row, so hold is best on any weights. Weighted at 0.70 / 0.30, hold is -24.41.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, from the public record.
- Boeing says "the business case isn't" there and gives no date, for the fourth round.
- Its MAX runs down, and it restated "more than one engine source" with headroom in the date. Neither is a launch.
- Rahul's weights are 0.70 / 0.30, the same as mine. The call doesn't turn on them.

(3) The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]. This round's one new point is that $13.72B, or $13.04B with Lobby, now fits under the $15B RISE allowance. I said in the frame that the last round would tempt us, and I tested it hard.
- Fitting is one gate of five (G5).
- G1 is a committed airframer on a path with no wait penalty. It fails in every column.
  - NGSA has flown since 2037.
  - A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, 23 years late in S1 and S2 alike.
  - The window closes in 2056, so the engine never earns a dollar on this board.
  - No airframer has asked for it.
- Without the allowance, $13.72B counts against the $2.0B round cap and fails it.
- Held. Ali confirms 2060 passes his date test, so the date isn't the ground. The airframer path is.

(4) Ducted only as a defence (H3). Hold only. It is live, offered to both airframers, and never called the next generation.

(5) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]. Hold adds no project, and the $2B strain is booked. The supply read below is doctrine, not my record.
- In 2049 the MAX was 938 of our 1,622 NB engines.
- Our NB engines fall to 1,530 (2050), 1,070 (2055) and 424 (2060). OE load falls, but the 1B and 1A fleets keep needing kits and shop visits.
- Order: safety first, then fleet kits and spares, and spares never crowd out OE. The A320 tail never draws on fleet spares.
- The spares tail is contracted with Safran ahead of any development parts.
- Ali's advice holds as well: an Open Fan would load the same constrained suppliers while the 1B tail needs them.

(6) Next generation and durability [CX-0217, CX-0208].
- Ali reports no RISE ground or flight-test result after 2025. The record stops at more than 350 tests, compact-core dust testing from October 2025, and noise below LEAP (2024).
- The 20% is a design target, not a test result. So my 20% line stays unrebutted on test, and any RISE product launch would fail it.
- Hold trades no durability for anything.

(7) Tie-break [CX-0658]. Not needed: hold leads by $13.04B.

SAFETY AND THE DUCTED GATE, CANDIDLY.
- Ali raises no safety flag and no durability flag. Nothing has been turned on and left on.
- Gate points (b) core or engine test and (c) airframer and regulator acceptance: nothing has come onto the record since 2045. I can't report either as passed, and nothing shows either failed. A gap isn't a pass.
- Harsh time on wing:
  - Yardstick, 2023: about 4,800 harsh cycles for LEAP against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56.
  - LEAP-1A: the HPT kit was certified in December 2024 and more than doubles time on wing, to the CFM56 level. That is in my July 2025 words, with no field confirmation since in the record.
  - LEAP-1B: the kit went to certification for 1H 2026, a year late. Its outcome isn't in the record.
  - GEnx and the Ducted: no data.
- My answer on evidence: the gate stays standing as the cross-functional fleet review [CX-0012]. It reports to the full Board, and enhanced inspection continues as part volume falls. Any flag goes to the full Board at once and changes fleet priorities and kits, never on a date.

2045 POST-MORTEM, in one line: we booked -25.0 and hold stayed at -24.41. The $0.59B went undrawn because none of the named moves came: no code-4 fps, no Trent 1000 upgrade, no UltraFan WB, no re-engine.
- The method was right: named moves, each weighted at 0.25 or less.
- But $0.21B had no name on it, and 0.25 on a Trent upgrade was heavy after three quiet rounds.
- This round: no unnamed margin, and the Trent upgrade at 0.20.

BOOKING: -24.6, the hold row less Rahul's weighted named widebody set.
- Trent 1000 upgrade counting from 2053: -0.41 x 0.20.
- UltraFan WB behind a re-engine: -0.50 x 0.05.
- A350 re-engine, EIS 2055: -0.25 x 0.15.
- 787 re-engine with a rival engine: -0.17 x 0.05.
- Total: $0.15B, giving -24.56, rounded down to -24.6.
- Named downside: -25.16 (UltraFan WB behind an A350 re-engine).
- Any fps now lands after 2056, with no NB effect.
- No upside is booked.

BIASES, NAMED.
- Money guided low: the booking sits below hold.
- The installed-base lens [CX-0555] would call a last-round RISE launch "seeding the next 30 years". The board stops counting in 2056 and no airframer has asked, so I book none of it.
- Deference to airframers costs nothing on this board.
- Ramp optimism isn't triggered.
- Doctrine, not my record, drove the supply read, the Lobby handling and the Embraer hold.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold needs none. RISE continuing as joint funded technology, the spares tail contracted jointly, and NB price and capacity kept joint are all joint practice, so consent is assumed. GEnx is GE alone. I see no reason Safran would agree to an Open Fan or Lobby order, which is one more reason none was brought.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed fully, and taken as the money record. Rahul checked every row and rebuilt the Open Fan wait from first principles: $5.73B against the grid's $5.72B, with the Lobby ratio of 0.706 tying out. He confirmed that the $2B strain is booked and that an Open Fan adds none. His tests, in order:
- Pays-for-itself fails for both Open Fan rows and for Lobby.
- Volumes-first fails for the Open Fan rows, because no airframer has asked.
- The payout floor passes: $0.8B a year, or $0.9B with Lobby, against about $2.55B of room. So the floor is not the binding test.

His binding vetoes on the Open Fan rows and on Lobby alone stand, and I don't contest them. I order none of those items, so no override is needed. His terms veto on any concession, or on price or capacity talk without Safran, is met by the final text and the other moves. I took his post-mortem as he scored it, including the over-provision: $0.21B of unnamed margin and a heavy 0.25 Trent weight. I took his booking of -24.6 (named set $0.15B, downside -25.2) and his 0.70 / 0.30 weights. I also took his advice to book a durability reserve in the quarter the need is found. His profit calls land, and his volume dates slip [CX-0910, CX-0987]. There's no volume date in this call.

- Dates: all pass on turn on, turn off. Ducted 2041 (launch + 6), Embraer 2042, GEnx 2033. An Open Fan launched now is ready in 2060, 23 years behind NGSA and four past the window. Accepted.
- The Ducted gate: a standing gap on points (b) and (c), with no Ducted field data and nothing showing failure. I report it as he gave it. A gap isn't a pass.
- Fleets: LEAP-1A kit more than twofold (July 2025); LEAP-1B kit a year late, outcome unknown; nothing on GEnx. Accepted with the same caveats.
- No safety or durability flag, so there's nothing to resolve.
- RISE: no test result after 2025, and 20% is a design target. My 20% line stays a bar, not a pass.

Grounds: (a) Bounded downside fails in every plausible column. (b) Airframer path fails: under part (a), NGSA has been in service since 2037 and the engine is ready in 2060, so the wait applies in every column, S2 included. That part (b) now fits under $15B does not open the allowance. (c) Premium cap: $13.72B against the $2.0B round cap. (d) CFM parity rule (Safran consent): a RISE product launched ahead of any airframer is outside joint practice, and no reason has been stated why Safran would agree. (e) Unresolved objection, unless rebutted on test: Culp's red line requires at least 20% better fuel burn without trading durability, and Ali's record has no RISE test result after 2025 that backs it. The payout floor ($0.8B a year) and Ali's date test (2060 is not before 2045) pass; they are not the grounds. Acceptable alternative: hold.

open_fan: launch with lobby_emissions: launch. Against hold the pair is -13.04 / -13.04, $4.04B beyond its $9B bill. Grounds: bounded downside; airframer path, part (a), because the wait applies in every column; premium cap; CFM parity rule (Safran consent); and the 20% red line unless rebutted on test. The $13.04B fits under the $15B allowance, but the allowance opens only through the airframer path, and part (a) fails. The Lobby item (+0.68 / +0.68 against the Open Fan alone) falls with the vetoed Open Fan, because Lobby needs an Open Fan launched this round or already live. Acceptable alternatives: hold on both.

lobby_emissions: launch alone. It does nothing on the board without an Open Fan, so it is -1.00 in each column (our computation). Grounds: not paid for the risk, and the Lobby rule (no Open Fan launched or live). Any SAF or emissions advocacy can stay an unpriced other move within GE's ordinary public-policy activity. Acceptable alternative: hold.
Any premium_b above $2.0B net of a RISE allowance, and any RISE allowance claimed this round, because no Open Fan has an airframer path.

Any launch carrying an unresolved safety or durability flag from Ali, a binding Ghai or Ali veto still standing, or a Culp red line (20% fuel burn; durability not traded) neither struck nor rebutted on evidence.

recommendations.text: Safety first, on the fleet in service. At this review, bring what the record now holds on Ducted gate points (b) core or engine test and (c) airframer and regulator acceptance. Also bring harsh time on wing for the Ducted, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and GEnx fleets, against the mature LEAP-1A with the CFM56 as yardstick. The 737 MAX steps down to none by 2060 and the A320 family leaves the lines, so keep the LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A spares tail contracted jointly with Safran ahead of any development parts. Keep fleet kits and spares on first call, and never let spares crowd out new engines. Any safety or durability flag comes to the full board at once, as a cross-functional call answered on evidence.

Hold on every field. The grid gives the Open Fan no share gain, and a 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the board's narrowbody window has closed. The figures against hold: Open Fan -13.72 / -13.72, Open Fan plus Lobby -13.04 / -13.04. RISE stays all in as funded technology with Safran, with no product launch and no cancel for cost. It becomes a product when an airframer wants it. If an airframer launches a new single-aisle, bring the RISE product case to the full board then, jointly with Safran and on test results. Do not bring it on sealed orders ahead of that launch. Bring any RISE ground or flight-test result that bears on the 20% bar.

Cost and balance sheet. Holding needs no new R&D. State premium_b as $0.0B and the game total as $0.0B of $4.0B. In premium_reason, state the RISE allowance as unused and say why: the cost fits under $15B, but there is no airframer path. Keep at least 70% of free cash flow returned and the A-range rating untouched. Book expected_pv_b at or below hold (-24.41), sized only to named rival moves, chiefly on the widebody. Add one line on why the 2045 provision of $0.59B was not drawn.

Customers and airframers. Keep the Ducted and LEAP on offer to both airframers, including any new single-aisle Boeing launches under its restated 'more than one engine source' requirement. Offer them on standard terms, with no launch-era pricing or concession to win a code. Keep Embraer non-exclusive. Narrowbody price and capacity stay joint with Safran. Bring first-hand airframer findings only when you have them.

Public statement. Name no rival, the Joint Venture included, and blame no one. Give no open fan year: say only 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer'. Make no Ducted durability claim beyond what test and field data show, and never call the Ducted the next generation. No price or capacity talk without Safran. Last round's statement passed on every point. Keep it so.

Objectives, reported honestly at the game's close. No order on offer can meet either objective. NB share at hold is 45.6% in 2050, and an Open Fan launched now is ready in 2060 and would cut share. Carry no objective premium. Do not use emissions lobbying as a $1B order on the board. Any advocacy stays an unpriced other move within GE's ordinary public-policy activity.

frame.situation:
ROUND: decision year 2050, round 4 of 4. It's the last round. The board counts the narrowbody engine market to 2056 and the widebody to 2061.

PUBLIC RECORD (round-4 bulletin). Round 3 brought no public events.
- NGSA (Airbus): in service since 2037, code 7, with CFM, P&W and RR all fitted. It is in a quality-gated ramp. The last A320 family aircraft leave the lines. Airbus says engines for any A320 built from 2046 must be confirmed without drawing on fleet spares. On the widebody, Airbus 'continues to assess' the A350's evolution 'on our own timetable'.
- Boeing: no fps launch, for the fourth round running. 'The business case isn't' there, and Boeing gives no date. It has restated its engine requirement as 'more than one engine source', from engines ready at entry into service, with headroom in the date. It withdrew '57 a month': the MAX steps down one step at a time with the FAA, to none by 2060 (game assumption).
- Rival narrowbody engine: the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine, ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA, offered on standard terms. Observed 2049 NB engine shares: CFM 46.7%, P&W 26.7%, RR 26.7%. NB deliveries in 2049: Boeing 469, Airbus 1,267.
- No rival widebody move is on the record: no Trent 1000 upgrade, no UltraFan WB, no re-engine.
- Ours, all hold only: GEnx upgrade (ready 2033, WB share 44.8%, 152 engines a year), Ducted (ready 2041) and Embraer (counting since 2042). Nothing of ours can be cancelled.

OUR POSITION AT HOLD:
- dPV -24.41 in both columns; yield 84.74%.
- Components: engine value -18.41, R&D -4.00, strain -2.00 (already booked).
- NB share: 45.6% (2050), 41.5% (2052), 38.1% (2055), 36.5% (2056).
- NB engines: 1,530 (2050), 1,070 (2055), 961 (2056), 424 (2060).

OBJECTIVES:
- Dominate NB (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050): not met. 2040 was 68.8%, 2045 was 49.6%, and 2050 is the worst year at 45.6%.
- Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: not met, and out of reach. A launch now is ready in 2060.
- No order on offer lifts NB share. An Open Fan lowers it. On Ghai's 2045 estimate that is about 20 points of total NB share in 2050, or about 14 with Lobby; he will confirm it for a 2050 launch.

GRID (S1: rivals hold. S2: Boeing launches a 10-year fps with code 7, entering service in 2060, after the window.)
- Hold: -24.41 / -24.41. The best plan in both columns.
- Open Fan: -38.13 / -38.13, which is -13.72 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus $5.72B of wait penalty. It adds no new strain.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.45 / -37.45, which is -13.04 against hold: the $9B bill plus $4.04B.
- Lobby next to the Open Fan alone: +0.68 in each column.
- Lobby alone is not on the grid. I read it at -1.00 in each column.
- The columns are identical on every row, so hold is best on any weights.
- The wait penalty is smaller than in 2045 ($11.22B) only because six or seven years of the window are left, not twelve.

2045 POST-MORTEM, in one line: we booked -25.0, and hold stayed at -24.41. The $0.59B provision went undrawn because none of the moves we named came: no code-4 fps, no Trent 1000 upgrade, no UltraFan WB, no re-engine. We guided low and landed above, sized to named moves. That was right in method, and nothing came.

DUCTED GATE (Board ask, standing): no core or engine test result for gate point (b), no airframer or regulator acceptance for (c), and no harsh time-on-wing data are on our record. Nothing shows a failure either. A gap isn't a pass. Ali reports at this review.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision):
- Would approve: hold on every field, which is never vetoed. It would approve no Open Fan and no Lobby.
- Would veto:
  - The Open Fan alone (-13.72 / -13.72), on these grounds: bounded downside; the airframer path (the wait applies in every column, S2 included); the premium cap; the Safran parity rule; and my 20% line unless rebutted on test. That $13.72B fits under $15B does not open the allowance.
  - The Open Fan + Lobby (-13.04 / -13.04), on the same grounds.
  - Lobby alone (-1.00).
  - Any premium above $2.0B net of a RISE allowance, and any RISE allowance this round.
  - Any launch with an unresolved Ali flag, a standing Ghai or Ali veto, or a red line neither struck nor rebutted.
- Wants to see:
  - the expected scenario with weights;
  - Ghai's tests in numbers (pays for itself, payout floor, strain);
  - Ali's ready years, gate points (b) and (c), harsh time on wing for four fleets, any flag and my answer, and any RISE test result after 2025;
  - the Safran gate;
  - premium $0.0B, the game total, and the allowance stated unused with the reason;
  - an honest objective note;
  - an answer to each recommendation, with the 2045 post-mortem;
  - a booking at or below -24.41 sized to named moves, chiefly widebody.

It stays on offer, with LEAP, to both airframers, including any new single-aisle Boeing launches under 'more than one engine source', on standard terms (H1). It is never called the next generation (H3).

open_fan: hold | launch. $8B. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060 (2050 + 10). NGSA has been in service since 2037, so we lose 35 pp on NGSA (20 pp with Lobby) for the rest of the window, which floors at our NGSA share. It adds no new strain, because the $2B is booked. It serves RISE, so the Safran gate applies. It passes only with an Open Fan launched this round or already live.

cancel: not offered. Nothing of ours can be cancelled, and RISE is never cancelled for cost (H5).
options_to_test: A. Hold every field (my lean). Row -24.41 / -24.41, the best plan in both columns. It adds no R&D and no strain. Premium $0.0B; game total $0.0B of $4.0B. Weighted -24.41 on any weights. Not a Board item.

B. Open Fan alone, declared as the one RISE allowance. Row -38.13 / -38.13, which is -13.72 against hold: the whole $8B bill plus $5.72B of wait penalty, with nothing bought in any column. E. Unpriced other moves alongside the hold (no board effect). (i) Fleet first as the MAX and the A320 family run out. Kits and spares for LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B, Ducted and GEnx get first call, and spares never crowd out OE [CX-0529, CX-0607, CX-0422]. F. What the grid can't show, for the booking. Book only named moves, no upside. (i) A Trent 1000 upgrade launched now counts from 2053: about -$0.41B. (ii) UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2056 and counts only once a re-engine is in service, at the earliest 2055: about -$0.50B. It excludes the Trent upgrade. (iii) An A350 re-engine launched now enters in 2055 and gains 1.5 pp of WB airframe share a year: my rough figure is -$0.27B on GEnx, an inference for Ghai to size. Airbus says it is still assessing. (iv) A 787 re-engine and what it does to the GEnx fit. (v) Any fps launched now enters after 2056 and has no NB effect on this board. My provisional is about -24.6, with a named downside of about -25.2.

H2: no Open Fan while a new NB enters service before it is ready. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and a 2050 launch is ready in 2060, so H2 bars it in every column. The cost now fits under the $15B RISE allowance, but the exception needs a launch I can judge strategic on an airframer path. H6 (through Ali's test): no date without test evidence. The open fan comes 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer', with no year. No Ducted durability claim goes beyond what test and field data show [CX-0009].

H9: premium cap of $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game (game total to date $0.0B), plus one RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full. This round I expect it unused.
My own line: a next engine needs at least a 20% reduction in fuel burn [CX-0217]. It governs RISE. Nothing on test in our record after 2025 backs it, so it stays a target and a wording check.
My own line: durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208], nor for a date, nor for the last round. It binds every fleet in service, the Ducted and the LEAP-1B tail first.
Tie-break within $1B: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658].
frame.asks_ops:
Mohamed, what the tests and the fleet say, not the analysis. Turn it on, turn it off [CX-0009]. This is the last review in the game, so give the Board the plainest account you can.

(1) The Ducted gate (the Board's first ask, again).
- Gate point (b): core or engine test.
- Gate point (c): acceptance by the airframer and the regulator.
- Has anything come onto the record since 2045? If not, say so plainly. A gap isn't a pass, and nothing shows a failure. I won't dress it up.

(2) The fleets in service. Harsh time on wing for the Ducted, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and GEnx, against the mature LEAP-1A with the CFM56 as yardstick. Your 2023 yardstick was about 4,800 harsh cycles for LEAP against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56. The LEAP-1A kit more than doubled it. The LEAP-1B kit came a year late, and its outcome is not in the record. Any safety or durability flag comes as a cross-functional call [CX-0012] and goes to the full Board at once. I answer it on evidence. A flag changes fleet priorities and kits, and a date never decides it.

(3) Ready years.
- An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037. S2's fps enters in 2060.
- Confirm the Open Fan cannot be ready by the first new NB's entry in any column, and that 2060 falls after the board's 2056 window.
- Confirm Ducted (2041), Embraer (2042) and GEnx (2033, counting from 2042) all pass.

(4) RISE on test (a Board ask). Is there any ground or flight-test result after 2025 that backs at least 20% better fuel burn without trading durability, dust first? Your words end in March 2024 and the brief carries none. If that's where it stands, say so. No product date.

(5) Supply load. Your record here is my description of your job [CX-0633], so this part is doctrine.
- Hold adds no project, and the $2B strain is booked.
- The MAX steps down to none by 2060, so LEAP-1B OE runs out while the 1B fleet still needs kits and shop visits.
- The A320 family leaves the lines. Airbus wants engines for any A320 built from 2046 confirmed without drawing on fleet spares.
- Our NB engines go 1,530 (2050), 1,070 (2055), 424 (2060).
Confirm the order: safety first, then fleet kits and spares for LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B, Ducted and GEnx; spares never crowd out OE, and the OE tail never draws on fleet spares. Confirm the spares tail is contracted jointly with Safran ahead of any development parts. Flag any constrained supplier, though no supplier is named in the record.

(6) Dates and wording in the public line. My draft carries no year. The only timing is 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer'. It makes no Ducted time-on-wing claim, and the Ducted 'isn't the next generation'. Flag any date no test backs, and any durability wording that runs ahead of the data.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding). The Board wants:
- your ready years against the new NBs;
- the status of gate points (b) and (c);
- harsh time on wing for all four fleets;
- any flag, with my answer to it on evidence;
- any RISE test result after 2025 bearing on the 20% bar.
It vetoes any launch carrying an unresolved safety or durability flag from you.
frame.initial_lean:
LEAN: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions, genx).
- Hold is the best grid plan in both columns: -24.41 / -24.41.
- The nearest alternative, Open Fan + Lobby, is $13.04B behind. No tie-break is needed.
- RISE stays all in as funded technology with Safran: no cancel for cost (H5), and no product launch ahead of an airframer (H2). It becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469].

EXPECTED COLUMN (provisional): S1, rivals hold. Weights: S1 0.70 / S2 0.30.
- Boeing says the business case isn't there and gives no date, for the fourth round.
- The columns are identical on every row, so hold is best on any weights.

PREMIUM: $0.0B, and the game total is $0.0B of $4.0B.
- The RISE allowance is unused. Its cost now fits ($13.72B, or $13.04B with Lobby, under $15B), but there is no airframer path: NGSA has flown since 2037, the engine would be ready in 2060, and the window closes in 2056.
- It buys nothing on the board and serves no objective. Fitting under the cap is not a reason to spend it.

SAFRAN GATE:
- Hold needs none.
- RISE continuing as joint funded technology is joint practice.
- An Open Fan or Lobby order would fail the gate. A RISE product launched ahead of any airframer, waiting in every column, is outside joint practice, and I see no reason Safran would agree.
- GEnx is GE alone.

BOOKING: provisional about -24.6, below hold, sized only to named widebody moves (Trent 1000 upgrade, UltraFan WB behind a re-engine, an A350 re-engine). The named downside is about -25.2. Ghai sizes it.
- 2045 post-mortem: we booked -25.0 and hold stayed at -24.41. The provision went undrawn because no named move came.

OBJECTIVES, CANDIDLY: neither can be met by any order this round.
- NB share is 45.6% in 2050.
- The Open Fan can't be ready by 2050, and launching it would cut share.
- No objective premium.

BIASES, NAMED:
- The installed-base lens [CX-0555] says a last-round RISE launch 'seeds the next 30 years'. The board stops counting in 2056, and no airframer has asked. I book none of it.
- Deference to airframers [CX-0452]: on this board it costs nothing now. Any fps enters after the window.
- Money guided low: the booking sits below hold.
- Ramp optimism isn't triggered: no ramp is promised.
- Doctrine, not my record, drives the supply read and the Lobby handling.

WHAT CHANGES THIS:
- Nothing on the grid.
- A safety or durability flag from Ali changes fleet priorities, not orders. It goes to the full Board at once, as a cross-functional call.

PUBLIC LINE (draft):
- Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.
- What we know and what we don't.
- Job one is keeping LEAP, Ducted and GEnx engines on wing as today's airplanes leave the lines. Kits and spares first, and spares never crowd out new engines.
- The Ducted is the right engine for the airplanes that chose it, offered to both airframers, and not the next generation.
- RISE is all in with Safran. An open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with one, not ahead of one. No year.
- No birthright on the next order.
- No rival named, and no price or capacity talk.
- 'It's that simple, ain't that hard.'
