tests.numbers: Hold rests only on the record: NGSA on code 7 with all three fitted, Airbus's Alt plan and the 737 MAX phase-out (a public game assumption). Backed out of the brief, the MAX is about 428 aircraft in 2050, 214 in 2055, 172 in 2056 and none from 2060. NGSA is about 1,250 (2050), 1,190 (2055) and 1,145 (2056). Airbus has been all NGSA since 2044, so the A320 tail carries no CFM OE on the board, and LEAP-1A is now a services business. No unannounced selection is assumed.

tests.name: Strain and no second stack (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: Flag any plan that stacks two or more projects (the $2B strain). GE9X losses are not treated as live. Advice only.
tests.numbers: Confirmed: strain is -2.00 in the hold components and already booked. The Open Fan row decomposes exactly as -24.41 - 8.00 - 5.72 = -38.13, which leaves no room for a strain term. Open Fan + Lobby decomposes as -24.41 - 9.00 - 4.04 = -37.45. I read no new $2B. If I did, the wait would have to be $3.72B, and my rebuild of the lost engines says $5.73B. Hold adds no project. The GE9X is long past its peak losses.

tests.name: No overcapitalization: new R&D per year against the payout floor (Culp ask 3)
tests.threshold: New R&D committed this round, spread over its development years, must fit in the cash left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 free cash flow: about $2.55B a year. (inference: analogy from capex at 2-3% of revenue; it cannot fail on the board's numbers)
tests.numbers: Hold: $0.0B a year. Open Fan: $8B / 10 = $0.80B a year over 2050-60. With Lobby: $0.90B a year spread, or $1.80B in 2050 if the 'immediate' $1B lands at once, then $0.80B. All are under about $2.55B, so the floor is not the binding test; pays-for-itself, volumes-first and the premium are. At hold, the 70% payout and the A-range rating are untouched.

tests.name: Premium in dollars and the RISE allowance (Culp ask 4)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium of at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game, against the best grid plan in the expected column. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, and only through the open_fan gates. (company doctrine, hard rule 9; profile.md §6, G1-G5)
tests.numbers: Hold: $0.0B in S1 and S2. Game total: $0.0B of $4.0B. RISE allowance: unused. The new point is that $13.72B, or $13.04B with Lobby, now fits under $15B. That satisfies only G5, one gate of five. G1, a committed airframer, fails in every column: NGSA has flown since 2037, the engine would be ready in 2060, the window closes in 2056, and S2's fps enters in 2060 with the grid still charging the full wait. G3 has no airframer to choose. Hard rule 2 bars the launch. 'Ready by 2050' cannot be met, so no objective premium attaches. Nothing in my tests opens the allowance. Without it, the $13.72B and $13.04B count against the $2.0B round cap and fail it.

tests.name: Terms: no launch-era pricing, no concession, narrowbody price and capacity only with Safran (Culp ask 9)
tests.threshold: No public statement or other move offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or talks CFM narrowbody price or capacity without Safran.
tests.numbers: Culp's draft line has no price, no capacity figure, no concession and no rival named. Other move E(iv) keeps the Ducted and LEAP on offer to both airframers, including any new Boeing single-aisle, on standard terms with no concession to win a code. E(i) contracts the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B spares tail jointly with Safran against shop-visit forecasts, so capacity stays joint, and no cost is booked until those volumes are agreed. GEnx is GE alone. At least 70% of free cash flow is returned, and the A-range rating is untouched. I re-test the final text at the veto check.

tests.name: Weights (Culp ask 5)
tests.threshold: Information: my own weights from the public record.
tests.numbers: Mine: S1 0.70 / S2 0.30, unchanged, against Culp's provisional, which is the same. Against a launch: 'the business case isn't' there, there is no date, and this is the fourth round without a launch. For one: the MAX runs out by 2060, and Boeing restated an engine requirement with headroom in the date. Neither is confirmed data, so I don't move. Expected column: S1. Weighted hold is -24.41 on any weights, and Open Fan / Open Fan + Lobby are -13.72 / -13.04 on any weights, because the columns are identical on every row.

tests.name: 2045 post-mortem (Culp ask 6, Board ask)
tests.threshold: Information. Score the 2045 booking against the outcome, and own any miss.
tests.numbers: We booked -25.0, and hold stayed at -24.41: a $0.59B provision, undrawn. Of it, $0.38B was the weighted named set (code-4 fps about $0.02B; Trent 1000 upgrade, UltraFan WB and a rival-engined 787 re-engine about $0.36B) and $0.21B was margin with no name on it. None of the named moves came. The method was right: sized to named moves, each weighted at 0.25 or less, so the likeliest single outcome was that nothing came, and landing above a low guide is the design. It was over-provisioned by the $0.21B unnamed margin, and my 0.25 on a 2045 Trent upgrade was heavy (three rounds, no widebody move). This round I trim both.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (Culp ask 7)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores, each sized.
tests.numbers:
Worst grid column: S1 = S2 = -24.41, a gap of $0.00B. Un-gridded, sized on the brief's engine values (WB $11.2M x 1.6, 340 WB engines a year, our 47 of 105 raw points):
(a) Trent 1000 upgrade launched 2050, counting 2053-61: we go from 44.8% to 40.0%, losing 16 engines a year, -$0.41B (confirmed). Weight 0.20.
(b) UltraFan WB, ready 2056, counting 2056-61 only behind a re-engine launched now (EIS 2055). It needs two moves this round and excludes (a): 32 engines a year, -$0.50B. Weight 0.05.
(c) A350 re-engine, EIS 2055: +1.5 pp a year of WB airframe share from the 787, which takes GEnx at our 71% of the 787. That is -$0.18B if the first gain lands in 2056, -$0.25B if in 2055. I use -$0.25B; Culp's -$0.27B is a touch heavy but within rounding. Weight 0.15.
(d) 787 re-engine, EIS 2055: if a rival engine takes it, the GEnx fit gain ends (about 9 engines a year), -$0.17B. If GEnx keeps the fit, the 787 gains 1 pp a year, about +$0.16B, which I don't book. If both re-engine in the same year, airframe share doesn't move. Weight 0.05 on the downside.
(e) Confirmed: an fps launched now enters in 2057 (7-year) or 2060 (10-year or via Embraer), after the 2056 window, with no NB effect. The identical columns show it.
Weighted: 0.082 + 0.025 + 0.037 + 0.009 = $0.15B. Worst named stack: UltraFan WB behind an A350 re-engine, -$0.75B, giving -25.16. A Trent upgrade plus an A350 re-engine is -$0.66B. Also left out: a demand slowdown or recession, the pace of the MAX phase-out, and supply.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence
tests.threshold: For each launch: bill years, ready year and first year of share gain, inside the board's horizon (NB to 2056, WB to 2061). (inference; ready years are Ali's to confirm)
tests.numbers: Hold: every live programme is in its paying years. The Ducted was billed 2035-41, has been ready since 2041 and gains +10 pp on NGSA where CFM is fitted. Embraer has counted since 2042. GEnx has counted since 2042, at 44.8% WB and 152 engines a year to 2061. An Open Fan launched in 2050 would be billed 2050-60 and ready in 2060. It would have no share-gain year on the board and losses every year 2050-56, which fails as advice (the test passes only for the hold recommended).

tests.name: Objective check (Culp ask 8)
tests.threshold: Information. No objective premium.
tests.numbers: Confirmed at hold: 45.6% in 2050, the worst year (2040 was 68.8% and met; 2045 was 49.6%). No order on offer lifts it. An Open Fan launched now cuts total NB share by about 20.1 pp in 2050, to 25.5%, or 14.2 pp with Lobby, to 31.4%. The cut widens to 23.5 / 16.6 pp by 2056. That confirms my 2045 estimate of 20.2 / 14.3 for 2050. The 35 pp apply on NGSA and floor at our 27.0%. 'Ready by 2050' cannot be met, since the engine is ready in 2060. No objective premium.

tests.name: Guide low (booking)
tests.threshold: Recommend a low expected PV, at or below the hold row, sized to named moves, with no upside booked before it is confirmed. (inference: my guidance habit applied to the board)
tests.numbers: Book -24.6, the same as Culp's provisional: hold -24.41 less $0.19B. That covers the weighted named set of $0.15B (-24.56) with $0.04B of rounding and no unnamed margin. Named downside: -25.2 (UltraFan WB behind an A350 re-engine, -$0.75B). No upside is booked from S2, from a 787 re-engine with GEnx kept (+$0.16B) or from a quiet 2050.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch (alone), whether or not it is declared as the RISE allowance
vetoes.ground: Capex, binding grounds 1 and 2. It does not beat hold in any column: -13.72 / -13.72, the $8B bill plus $5.72B of wait (I rebuild it at $5.73B as every CFM NGSA engine lost 2050-56). Volumes first fails: no airframer has asked for it, so there are no volumes to agree. The $13.72B fits under $15B, but that is gate G5 only. The allowance opens through G1, a committed airframer, and that fails in every column: NGSA has flown since 2037, the engine would be ready in 2060, and the window closes in 2056. Without the allowance, the premium is $13.72B against the $2.0B round cap. RISE stays funded as joint technology and is never cancelled for cost (hard rule 5). Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch with lobby_emissions: launch, whether or not it is declared as the RISE allowance
vetoes.ground: Capex, binding grounds 1 and 2. -13.04 / -13.04 against hold ($9B plus $4.04B). It fails pays-for-itself and volumes-first in every column. The $13.04B fits under $15B but rests on an airframer path that fails in every column, and it buys no objective, so it counts against the $2.0B cap and fails it. Lobby's +0.68 falls with the Open Fan. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch (alone)
vetoes.ground: Capex, binding ground 1. It is off the grid: $1B with no board effect and no Open Fan launched or live, so -1.00 in each column, below hold. No doctrine or objective supports declaring it as a premium. Any SAF or emissions advocacy goes as an unpriced other move. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a concession to win a code on any new Boeing single-aisle, or talks CFM narrowbody price, capacity or the LEAP spares tail without Safran. None appears in Culp's draft; I re-test the final text.
vetoes.ground: Terms, binding ground 3 (hard rules 4 and 7). Launch-era pricing is behind us, and narrowbody pricing 'is a joint decision' with Safran. An fps launched now enters after 2056 and is worth $0.00B to us on this board (S1 = S2), so a concession buys nothing. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: expected_pv_b booked above -24.56, or Board wording that treats the $15B allowance as 'available' because the cost fits
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. Book -24.6: hold less the weighted named set of $0.15B, with -25.2 as the downside. The allowance stays closed on the airframer path, not on its size. On the spares tail, book no cost until shop-visit volumes are agreed with Safran. But if Ali finds a durability need, the reserve goes into the quarter it is found, not later.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Nothing on this grid moves the orders. Hold is best in both columns by $13.04B or more, the columns are identical, and no order on offer lifts share. To open the RISE allowance, the record would need an airframer committed to a new narrowbody on an open fan, entering no earlier than the engine's ready year and inside the 2056 window. That cannot happen this round, because a 2050 launch is ready in 2060. The booking moves only on confirmed data. I lower it if a Trent 1000 upgrade (-$0.41B), an UltraFan WB behind a re-engine (-$0.50B) or an A350 re-engine (-$0.25B) goes on the record. I raise it toward -24.41 once none has come. A safety or durability flag from Ali changes fleet priorities and reserves, booked in the quarter the need is found, not these orders. Any launch-era pricing, concession, or price or capacity talk without Safran in the final text is a terms veto.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the short answer: hold every field. Your numbers check, and I pushed on each one.

The Open Fan is -13.72 against hold in both columns: the $8B bill plus $5.72B of wait. I rebuild the wait at $5.73B. It is every engine we have on NGSA, about 4,750 of them from 2050 to 2056. Nothing else is in it, and there's no new strain, because the $2B is booked. With Lobby it's -13.04. Lobby's +0.68 falls with the Open Fan, and on its own it's -1.00.

The one new point: $13.72B fits under $15B. That is one gate of five. The allowance opens on a committed airframer, and there isn't one in any column. Fitting under the cap is not a reason to spend it. Premium $0.0B, game $0.0B of $4.0B, allowance unused. At $0.8-0.9B a year, the payout floor isn't binding.

On 2045, there's nothing to hide. We booked -25.0 and landed at -24.41. The method was right: $0.38B was named moves, and none came. But $0.21B had no name on it, and my 0.25 on a Trent upgrade was heavy. I trim both.

Weights stay 0.70 / 0.30, and the columns are identical. Named widebody moves weigh about $0.15B. Book -24.6, with -25.2 as the downside: an UltraFan WB behind an A350 re-engine. Any fps now lands after 2056.

Standard terms, with price and capacity joint with Safran. But the good news is the installed base keeps paying. We keep this flywheel going.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: the ready year of every engine on the board (Culp ask 3)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted: launch + 6. Open Fan: launch + 10, and not before 2045. Embraer: counts 7 years after launch. GEnx: 3 years after launch, not before 2035. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. This is my binding date ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2035, ready 2041 (2035 + 6). Partner Embraer: launched 2035, counting from 2042 (2035 + 7). GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033 (2030 + 3), counting from 2042, which is after 2035. All three can only hold. Open Fan: a 2050 launch is ready in max(2050 + 10, 2045) = 2060. The grid's Open Fan rows (-38.13 / -38.13, and with Lobby -37.45 / -37.45) are computed at 2060, not earlier. Hold (-24.41 / -24.41) adds no ready year. 'Ready by 2050' would have needed a launch by 2040, so any order valued on meeting it would rest on a year ten years early and would fail ground 1. No order on offer does that.

tests.name: Test, not analysis: the dates in Culp's draft public line (Culp ask 6)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back. No Open Fan entry before 2045, and no ready date before launch plus development years (binding ground 2, inference).
tests.numbers: The draft carries no year. Its only timing is 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer', which states launch + 10 as a floor and passes. It makes no Ducted time-on-wing claim. 'Kits and spares first' is a priority, not a number. The frame's years (NGSA 2037, Ducted 2041, Embraer and GEnx 2042, window 2056, Open Fan 2060) are board mechanics for internal use and not public commitments. Advice, not a veto: keep 'the 737 MAX steps down to none by 2060' out of the public line. That is Boeing's programme and a game assumption, Boeing published no rate, and no test of ours backs it. At step 4 I veto, on ground 2, any Open Fan ready or entry year earlier than 2060 for a launch now, and any RISE product year.

tests.name: Ducted gate points (b) and (c), reported against last round's promise (Culp ask 1; Board ask)
tests.threshold: (b): passed on core or engine test. (c): accepted by the airframer and the regulator. The proof is turn on, turn off on test, never analysis.
tests.numbers: Nothing has come onto the record since 2045. In 2045 I said the gate would report at each review. It reports a standing gap. Neither the brief nor my record carries a core or engine test result, an airframer or regulator acceptance, or any Ducted field data. I cannot report (b) or (c) as passed, and nothing on the record shows either one failed. The board has counted the Ducted on NGSA since 2041 (+10 pp where CFM is fitted). That is the game's mechanic, not evidence of acceptance. A gap is not a pass.

tests.name: Durability first: harsh time on wing for the four fleets (Culp ask 2; Board ask)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn, a date or the last round. The Ducted bar is harsh time on wing no worse than the mature LEAP-1A, with the CFM56 as yardstick (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: Hold trades nothing, and the draft makes no durability claim. Yardstick, 2023: LEAP fleet leaders in harsh service ran about 4,800 cycles, against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56. In milder service, 9,882 against about 17,000. (1) LEAP-1A: the HPT kit was certified by FAA and EASA in December 2024. It goes into all deliveries and shop visits and improves time on wing more than twofold, to the CFM56 level. That figure is in Culp's July 2025 words. No field confirmation after 2025 is in my record. (2) LEAP-1B: I said 2025. By July 2025 the kit was in certification for 1H 2026, a year late. The outcome is not in my record. (3) GEnx: no in-service durability data. The upgrade has counted since 2042: WB share 44.8%, 152 engines a year. (4) Ducted: no harsh time-on-wing data, so it cannot be compared with the mature LEAP-1A. Kits reach the fleet at shop visits: 'years, not months'. My record has nothing after November 2025 on any fleet.

tests.name: Safety call: cross-functional, and any flag to the full Board (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: If a problem or an order touches safety or durability, a cross-functional team makes the call, not one person.
tests.numbers: No safety flag and no durability flag: nothing has been turned on and left on. The frame routes any flag to the full Board as a cross-functional call, answered on evidence and never decided by a date. That meets the standard. Keep the gate standing as the fleet review. Its members: engineering, quality and supply chain; fleet support with field data; the safety review; Safran engineering. Keep enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new make and in MRO as the MAX runs out and part volume falls: 'find problems before problems find us'.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan, and the RISE allowance from the readiness side (Culp ask 3; advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. If the Open Fan is ready after the first new NB's EIS, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. NGSA has been in service since 2037, so the Open Fan is 23 years late in S1 and in S2. The S2 fps (10-year) enters service in 2060, the same year, but NGSA came first, so the wait applies anyway. 2060 is also 4 years after the 2056 NB window closes, so the engine never earns on this board. Against hold: Open Fan -13.72 / -13.72 ($8B bill plus $5.72B of wait penalty). Open Fan + Lobby: -13.04 / -13.04 ($9B plus $4.04B). Lobby next to the Open Fan alone: +0.68. On dates, the RISE allowance's airframer path fails in every column. Fitting under $15B changes no ready year.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted, Embraer and GEnx (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted: ready 2041, 4 years after NGSA's 2037 entry. It has earned +10 pp on NGSA since then, and it was ready 19 years ahead of S2's 2060 fps entry, so it stays on offer to both airframers. Embraer: counting since 2042. GEnx: ready since 2033 and counting from 2042, with the WB counted to 2061. No rival widebody move is on the record. All hold only.

tests.name: Physics, and RISE on test (Culp ask 4; Board ask)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so the Ducted is never the next generation. With no fuel-burn data in the brief, this is a wording check (inference).
tests.numbers: Wording passes: the draft calls the Ducted 'not the next generation', and RISE keeps the 20% bar. On test, the brief and my record hold no RISE ground or flight-test result after 2025. My record stops at four points. More than 350 programme tests, with an early focus on durability (July 2025). Dust testing on the compact-core HPT blades, begun October 2025. Open-fan noise below today's LEAP, shown with Airbus (2024). Ground and flight test 'this decade', after the fly demo slipped from 'by the middle of this decade'. The 20% is a design target on physics, not a test result. Nothing on test backs 20% without trading durability, so Culp's 20% line stays unrebutted on test. No product date follows.

tests.name: Supply load: hold, as the 737 MAX runs out and the A320 family leaves the lines (Culp ask 5; doctrine, not my record)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; the board's strain rule).
tests.numbers: The $2B strain is booked, and hold adds no project. In 2049 the MAX was 469 aircraft, or 938 LEAP-1B engines: 57.8% of our 1,622 NB engines. The other 684 went on Airbus airframes, 27.0% of its 2,534 engines. On the bulletin's straight line to none by 2060 (inference): about 855 1B engines in 2050 (55.9% of 1,530), about 428 in 2055 (40.0% of 1,070) and none in 2060 (of 424). Our NB engines fall 5.7% from 2049 to 2050, 30.1% from 2050 to 2055, and 72.3% by 2060. OE load falls, but the installed 1B and 1A fleets still need kits and shop visits. I confirm the order: safety first; then fleet kits and spares for LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B, Ducted and GEnx; spares never crowd out OE; and the OE tail never draws on fleet spares. Engines for A320s built from 2046 are confirmed before build from new-make capacity only. If supply cannot cover both, Airbus's own rule stops the tail at what is covered, and fleet spares hold. Contract the spares tail jointly with Safran, ahead of any development parts. Constrained suppliers: my only record is Culp's 2024 line, 80% of shortages from 9 suppliers. I have no current data and name no supplier. Watch item: 1B part volume falls toward sub-scale while shop-visit demand continues. No evidence in my own words: following doctrine.

tests.name: Supply load: Open Fan, alone or with Lobby (advice)
tests.threshold: A further project must pay on the grid for the load it puts on the constrained suppliers (inference; doctrine).
tests.numbers: On the grid it adds no new strain, and nothing pays for it: -13.72 / -13.72 alone, -13.04 / -13.04 with Lobby. Physically, it would put development parts on the same constrained suppliers while the LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A tails need kits and spares. Recommend against.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the WB, prefer the upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the NB, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: WB: the GEnx upgrade is live on the GE90/GEnx architecture, holds and carries no flag. NB: targeted component upgrades keep flowing into the LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and Ducted fleets at shop visits, carrying RISE technology as it matures on test. RISE stays whole as joint technology with Safran.

vetoes.plan: Conditional, and not in the frame's draft: any public statement or other move that gives an Open Fan ready or entry year earlier than 2060 for a launch now (for example 'ready by 2050', 'in the 2050s' or 'this decade'), any RISE product year, or any ready year earlier than launch plus development years. The same applies to any order whose value rests on meeting 'ready by 2050'.
vetoes.ground: Dates not backed by real testing (binding grounds 1 and 2). A 2050 launch is ready no sooner than 2060 (2050 + 10). The record holds no RISE ground or flight-test result after 2025, and the fly demo has slipped before ('by the middle of this decade', then 'this decade'). My veto over programme dates is an inference: my words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and they concern durability-fix results. The team rule makes the veto binding unless Culp answers it with evidence. The draft ('no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer ... No year') passes, so nothing stands today.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice only. The ready year, 2060, passes my date test, so this is not binding. But it is 23 years behind NGSA (in service since 2037) in both columns, level with the S2 fps, and 4 years past the 2056 window. Against hold it is -13.72 / -13.72 alone and -13.04 / -13.04 with Lobby. Fitting under the $15B allowance changes no ready year. Durability item: should a launch be ordered, the record holds no RISE durability or dust result after 2025 that backs 20% without trading durability. I would carry that to the full Board as an open cross-functional item, answerable only on test. It would also load the constrained suppliers while the LEAP-1B tail needs them. Keep RISE all in as funded technology with Safran: no launch ahead of an airframer, and no cancel.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch alone
vetoes.ground: Advice only. No evidence: following Culp and doctrine. Without an Open Fan it does nothing on the board (-1.00 in each column, by Culp's reading). For any unpriced advocacy, the technical facts I can supply are these: RISE is designed SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable, and open-fan noise was shown below today's LEAP with Airbus. I give no product date.

vetoes.plan: Public statement wording on the Ducted, the fleets and the MAX run-down
vetoes.ground: Advice only. Durability first and the date of another company's programme are not my date ground. With no test or field data on the Ducted, publish no time-on-wing figure and no 'matches LEAP-1A' or 'CFM56-level' claim for it. 'The right engine for the airplanes that chose it' is a statement of fit, not a durability claim, and should stay that way. Never call the Ducted the next generation. Keep 'the MAX steps down to none by 2060' out of our public line: it is Boeing's to say, and no test of ours backs it.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test and field data only, never analysis. (1) Ducted, against: harsh time-on-wing field data below the mature LEAP-1A, or a failure turned on in test or in service that the design does not turn off (HPT distress, nozzle coking, dust). I would raise a cross-functional durability flag to the full Board at once. That changes fleet priority and kits, not this round's orders. (2) Ducted, for: a core or engine test result and airframer and regulator acceptance on the record. I would report gate points (b) and (c) closed and back a durability statement no wider than the test. (3) LEAP-1B: field data on the 1H 2026 kit. Short of the LEAP-1A result, it would raise a flag on the 1B tail. (4) RISE: ground and flight-test results that turn durability and dust on and off at 20% or better. I would back 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer' as a commitment. An Open Fan order still needs an airframer, which is Culp's call, and a 2050 launch is still ready only in 2060. (5) Supply: supplier data showing LEAP-1B or LEAP-1A kits and spares slipping as OE runs down, or the A320 tail drawing on fleet spares. I would raise a supply flag ahead of anything else. Nothing on this grid changes my orders.
ops.memo:
Last round I promised the gate would report each review. Here it is, plainly.

Dates. Every year passes turn on, turn off. Ducted ready 2041, launch plus six. Embraer counting from 2042. GEnx ready 2033, counting from 2042. An Open Fan launched now is ready in 2060: twenty-three years behind NGSA, level with the S2 fps, four years after the window closes. The date passes my test. Against the airframe it fails in every column. Fitting under $15B moves no ready year.

The gate. Points (b) and (c): nothing new on the record since 2045. No core or engine test, no airframer or regulator acceptance, no harsh time on wing for the Ducted. Nothing shows a failure. A gap is not a pass.

The fleets. LEAP-1A: HPT kit certified December 2024, more than twofold, to the CFM56 level. LEAP-1B: I said 2025; it went to certification for first half 2026. The outcome is not in my record. GEnx and Ducted: no data. No safety flag. No durability flag. Nothing turned on and left on.

RISE. Over 350 tests, dust on the compact core from October 2025, noise below LEAP. Nothing after 2025. Nothing on test backs 20% yet. No product date.

Supply, on doctrine. Hold adds nothing. The MAX was 938 of our 1,622 narrowbody engines in 2049, and goes to none. The 1B fleet keeps flying. Contract its spares first, with Safran. The A320 tail never draws on fleet spares.

Hold every field. No binding veto stands.

other_moves.move: Fleet first: kits and spares keep first call as the fleets change over
other_moves.detail: Targeted durability upgrades continue at shop visits into the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B fleets and the GEnx fleet. They go into the ducted fleet as field data warrants [CX-0607, CX-0422]. Supply order: safety first, then fleet kits and spares. Spares never crowd out new engines [CX-0529]. Lean before capital at the constrained suppliers [CX-0540, CX-0653]. CFM narrowbody capacity decisions are made jointly with Safran [CX-0184]. We publish no time-on-wing figure beyond what testing and field data show. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A spares tail contracted jointly with Safran, ahead of any development parts
other_moves.detail: In 2049 the MAX took 938 of our 1,622 NB engines. LEAP-1B new-engine volume runs down, and 1B part volume falls toward sub-scale, but shop-visit demand goes on. That is Ali's watch item. So the spares and kit supply for the installed LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A fleets is contracted jointly with Safran, against shop-visit forecasts, ahead of any development parts. No cost is booked until those volumes are agreed with Safran. If a durability need is found, its reserve goes into the quarter it is found (Ghai). Engines for any late A320 family build come from new-make capacity only, confirmed before build. They never draw on fleet spares, and the tail stops at what is covered, under the airframer's own rule. No supplier is named, and we have no current supplier data. Doctrine drives this, not my record [CX-0613, CX-0633, CX-0529, CX-0184].

other_moves.move: Ducted gate kept standing as the cross-functional in-service fleet review
other_moves.detail: Members: engineering, quality and supply chain; fleet support with field data; the safety review; Safran engineering [CX-0012]. This review reported a standing gap. Nothing on the record since 2045 shows gate point (b), a core or engine test, or (c), acceptance by the airframer and the regulator. There are no Ducted harsh time-on-wing data, and nothing shows a failure. A gap isn't a pass. The review keeps reporting harsh time on wing for the Ducted, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and GEnx fleets to the full Board, against the mature LEAP-1A with the CFM56 as yardstick. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts continues in new make and MRO as part volume falls. Any safety or durability flag goes to the full Board at once as a cross-functional call, answered on evidence. A date never decides it [CX-0009, CX-0208].

other_moves.move: RISE all in as a funded technology programme with Safran
other_moves.detail: Ground and flight testing continue jointly, durability and dust first. RISE is not cancelled for cost, and it doesn't launch as a product ahead of an airframer. It becomes a product when an airframer wants it. If an airframer launches a new single-aisle, the product case comes to the full Board then, jointly with Safran and on test results [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0174, CX-0398]. The only public timing: an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. No year. The next-generation bar stays at least 20% better fuel burn without trading durability [CX-0217, CX-0208]. Test results go to the Board as they come off test. None after 2025 are on our record.

other_moves.move: CFM engines offered to both airframers
other_moves.detail: CFM's ducted engine stays on offer, with LEAP, to both airframers. That covers the new single-aisle airplane in service and any new single-aisle airplane Boeing launches under its 'more than one engine source' requirement. The work with Embraer goes on, non-exclusive, in addition to our two big customers and not in place of either. No airframer is refused or locked out [CX-0587, CX-0185, CX-0564]. No price, volume, capacity or date is published.

other_moves.move: Terms and private airframer engagement for any new single-aisle campaign
other_moves.detail: Standard terms only. No launch-era pricing, and no concession to win or hold any engine code [CX-0930, CX-0609]. An fps launched now enters service after 2056, so a concession would buy nothing on this board. Narrowbody price and capacity are joint decisions with Safran [CX-0184]. Embraer volume, price and capacity stay joint and private until agreed. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Their purpose is first-hand data on product and durability, never price. Findings go to the Board as they come. None are claimed today.

other_moves.move: SAF and emissions advocacy within GE's ordinary public-policy activity
other_moves.detail: Unpriced, with no board order (lobby_emissions held). We support SAF readiness and sensible emissions policy through industry bodies [CX-0451, CX-0508]. Technical claims stay limited to what test shows: RISE is designed SAF-ready, and open-fan noise has been shown below today's LEAP [CX-0001, CX-0013]. No product date, and no rival named.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That hasn't changed, and it won't.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: the new single-aisle airplane is flying, and CFM is on it with our partner Safran. Our ducted engine is in service on the airplanes that chose it. It's the right engine for those airplanes, and we offer it to both airframers. It isn't the next generation. That's the open fan. Our work with Embraer goes on. It adds to what we do for our two big customers and takes nothing away from them.

Job one is still the fleet. As today's airplanes give way to the new ones, the fleets in service still need us. LEAP, ducted and GEnx engines have to stay on wing. The kits and spares they need get first call, and spares never crowd out the new engines our customers are waiting on. We'll tell you how the fleet is doing when the field data shows it, and not before.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one. When that is, it's really not for us to say.

What we don't know is when the next new airplane comes, or what it will ask of us. We don't have a birthright on that order. When it comes, we'll compete for it on the product and on durability.

We're not going for share for its own sake. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. The balance sheet stays strong, and we keep returning cash to our shareholders.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467, CX-0319]. This is the last round, and the game is the installed base we already have. No slot is open on this board.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, with all three makers fitted.
- Our Ducted (ready 2041), Embraer (counting since 2042) and GEnx upgrade (counting since 2042) can only hold.
- Boeing has not launched the fps, for the fourth round. An fps launched now enters service in 2057 or 2060, after the 2056 narrowbody window.
We win by closing out well: safety and durability of the fleets first, kits and spares first, RISE whole as technology with Safran, the balance sheet and payout untouched, and a straight account to the Board. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages" [CX-0630].

DECISION: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions, genx).
- No Board item.
- Premium $0.0B, and the game total is $0.0B of $4.0B.
- The RISE allowance is unused.
- No overrides. Both memos recommend hold, and no binding veto stands against it.

THE TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Grid rows, S1 / S2:
- Hold: -24.41 / -24.41. The best plan in both columns.
- Open Fan: -38.13 / -38.13, or -13.72 against hold in each column.
  - That is its $8B bill plus $5.72B of wait penalty.
  - Rahul rebuilt the wait at $5.73B: every CFM engine on NGSA from 2050 to 2056, about 4,750 engines at 26.98% of NGSA.
  - Nothing else is in it: no new strain, because the $2B is booked, no write-off, and no WB or MAX effect.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.45 / -37.45, or -13.04 against hold. That is $9B plus $4.04B. Lobby caps the loss at 20 of our 28.33 raw points, and 4.04 / 5.72 = 0.706.
- Lobby next to the Open Fan alone: +0.68. It falls with the Open Fan.
- Lobby alone: off the grid, -1.00 in each column.
- S1 cost of any Open Fan: its whole bill plus the wait, and nothing bought. Worst column = S1 = S2.
- The columns are identical on every row, so hold is best on any weights. Weighted at 0.70 / 0.30, hold is -24.41.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, from the public record.
- Boeing says "the business case isn't" there and gives no date, for the fourth round.
- Its MAX runs down, and it restated "more than one engine source" with headroom in the date. Neither is a launch.
- Rahul's weights are 0.70 / 0.30, the same as mine. The call doesn't turn on them.

(3) The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]. This round's one new point is that $13.72B, or $13.04B with Lobby, now fits under the $15B RISE allowance. I said in the frame that the last round would tempt us, and I tested it hard.
- Fitting is one gate of five (G5).
- G1 is a committed airframer on a path with no wait penalty. It fails in every column.
  - NGSA has flown since 2037.
  - A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, 23 years late in S1 and S2 alike.
  - The window closes in 2056, so the engine never earns a dollar on this board.
  - No airframer has asked for it.
- Without the allowance, $13.72B counts against the $2.0B round cap and fails it.
- Held. Ali confirms 2060 passes his date test, so the date isn't the ground. The airframer path is.

(4) Ducted only as a defence (H3). Hold only. It is live, offered to both airframers, and never called the next generation.

(5) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]. Hold adds no project, and the $2B strain is booked. The supply read below is doctrine, not my record.
- In 2049 the MAX was 938 of our 1,622 NB engines.
- Our NB engines fall to 1,530 (2050), 1,070 (2055) and 424 (2060). OE load falls, but the 1B and 1A fleets keep needing kits and shop visits.
- Order: safety first, then fleet kits and spares, and spares never crowd out OE. The A320 tail never draws on fleet spares.
- The spares tail is contracted with Safran ahead of any development parts.
- Ali's advice holds as well: an Open Fan would load the same constrained suppliers while the 1B tail needs them.

(6) Next generation and durability [CX-0217, CX-0208].
- Ali reports no RISE ground or flight-test result after 2025. The record stops at more than 350 tests, compact-core dust testing from October 2025, and noise below LEAP (2024).
- The 20% is a design target, not a test result. So my 20% line stays unrebutted on test, and any RISE product launch would fail it.
- Hold trades no durability for anything.

(7) Tie-break [CX-0658]. Not needed: hold leads by $13.04B.

SAFETY AND THE DUCTED GATE, CANDIDLY.
- Ali raises no safety flag and no durability flag. Nothing has been turned on and left on.
- Gate points (b) core or engine test and (c) airframer and regulator acceptance: nothing has come onto the record since 2045. I can't report either as passed, and nothing shows either failed. A gap isn't a pass.
- Harsh time on wing:
  - Yardstick, 2023: about 4,800 harsh cycles for LEAP against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56.
  - LEAP-1A: the HPT kit was certified in December 2024 and more than doubles time on wing, to the CFM56 level. That is in my July 2025 words, with no field confirmation since in the record.
  - LEAP-1B: the kit went to certification for 1H 2026, a year late. Its outcome isn't in the record.
  - GEnx and the Ducted: no data.
- My answer on evidence: the gate stays standing as the cross-functional fleet review [CX-0012]. It reports to the full Board, and enhanced inspection continues as part volume falls. Any flag goes to the full Board at once and changes fleet priorities and kits, never on a date.

2045 POST-MORTEM, in one line: we booked -25.0 and hold stayed at -24.41. The $0.59B went undrawn because none of the named moves came: no code-4 fps, no Trent 1000 upgrade, no UltraFan WB, no re-engine.
- The method was right: named moves, each weighted at 0.25 or less.
- But $0.21B had no name on it, and 0.25 on a Trent upgrade was heavy after three quiet rounds.
- This round: no unnamed margin, and the Trent upgrade at 0.20.

BOOKING: -24.6, the hold row less Rahul's weighted named widebody set.
- Trent 1000 upgrade counting from 2053: -0.41 x 0.20.
- UltraFan WB behind a re-engine: -0.50 x 0.05.
- A350 re-engine, EIS 2055: -0.25 x 0.15.
- 787 re-engine with a rival engine: -0.17 x 0.05.
- Total: $0.15B, giving -24.56, rounded down to -24.6.
- Named downside: -25.16 (UltraFan WB behind an A350 re-engine).
- Any fps now lands after 2056, with no NB effect.
- No upside is booked.

BIASES, NAMED.
- Money guided low: the booking sits below hold.
- The installed-base lens [CX-0555] would call a last-round RISE launch "seeding the next 30 years". The board stops counting in 2056 and no airframer has asked, so I book none of it.
- Deference to airframers costs nothing on this board.
- Ramp optimism isn't triggered.
- Doctrine, not my record, drove the supply read, the Lobby handling and the Embraer hold.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold needs none. RISE continuing as joint funded technology, the spares tail contracted jointly, and NB price and capacity kept joint are all joint practice, so consent is assumed. GEnx is GE alone. I see no reason Safran would agree to an Open Fan or Lobby order, which is one more reason none was brought.

- Pays-for-itself fails for both Open Fan rows and for Lobby.

His binding vetoes on the Open Fan rows and on Lobby alone stand, and I don't contest them. I order none of those items, so no override is needed. His terms veto on any concession, or on price or capacity talk without Safran, is met by the final text and the other moves. I took his post-mortem as he scored it, including the over-provision: $0.21B of unnamed margin and a heavy 0.25 Trent weight. - No safety or durability flag, so there's nothing to resolve.
- RISE: no test result after 2025, and 20% is a design target. My 20% line stays a bar, not a pass.

- His advice not to publish 'the MAX steps down to none by 2060' is taken. It's Boeing's to say, and the line carries no year. His conditional date veto is met: the statement gives no year, only 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer'.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
The bad news first. The move from one generation of single-aisle aircraft to the next cost us volume. Our share of narrowbody engines dipped in 2039 and 2040; it has since come back, to 26.7 percent of the narrowbody engines delivered in 2049. Our competitors answered with new engines of their own, as they should, and what we have earned on the money we spent to get here has come in short of what we planned. We own that, and we are not going to dress it up.

The GTF fleet on the A320neo comes first: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into that fleet at shop visits. New production never crowds out its spares, and we confirm new engines only where the fleet's spares are covered. Control what you can control.

The Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, built on GTF2, has been in service on NGSA since 2037. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself. Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign is complete. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We offer the Joint Venture engine to an airframer only where it is ready by that airframe's entry into service, and it is ready now. We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes, dates, rates and engine choices, and we will not get out ahead of them. The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. `premium_b` is 0 and `overrides` is empty. Neither order is a Board item.

THE GRID
The brief's grid has one row: -2.16 in S1 (rivals hold) and -2.16 in S2 (Boeing launches the fps on a 10-year programme, code 7). Expected, worst and booked are all -2.16, on any weights.
- S2 moved from -2.17 (2045) to -2.16 because an fps launched in 2050 enters service in 2060 (2057 on a 7-year programme). The board stops counting narrowbody engines in 2056.
- No Board item exists. Both fields offer only `hold`, and a round of all holds does not reach review.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Eddy's proposal is hold/hold, the only legal values. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 with a $0 write-off. The Joint Venture formed that year, so `withdraw` is barred and `commit` is spent.
2. Binding vetoes: none stands.
- Mitchill clears all four grounds. His two conditional binding vetoes (ground 4 on statement wording, ground 3 on terms) are not triggered by the package as returned.
- Eddy invokes neither of his grounds. His conditional ground-1 veto (on T1) and ground-2 veto (the spares gate) are not triggered, because the other moves keep both.
3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]:
- the engine in service stays GTF2 as tested;
- no block upgrade or fps-specific change enters service without its own campaign;
- no OE draws on fleet spares.
Hold/hold meets the constraint, so it is also the best PV inside it.
4. Tie-breaks:
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: there is no new engine to weigh.
- Miss a cycle against visible demand [PX-0071][PX-0109]: we are in this cycle on NGSA. Any fps code that names us (4, 6 or 7) finds the engine ready. The rule is RTX-wide, and applying it here is inference.
- A rival's discount does not move the answer [PX-0055]: none is on the record, and we offer none.
5. Premium: doctrine $0 plus objective $0, $0 of the $1B cap. The Board's $0.5B allowance is unused. Nothing trails, so there is nothing to declare.

MY TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass. The engine has been ready since 2036 against the 2037 NGSA EIS, and against any fps EIS of 2057 or 2060.
- Visible demand: no launch is offered.
- Miss-a-cycle cost: zero inside the window. We are fitted on NGSA, and an fps adds $0 inside 2056.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no premium.
- Dividend safe: Mitchill confirms. $0 of about $6B used; the dividend is covered; debt stays on its path to pre-ASR levels (not claimed to be there); buybacks are the fill-in.
- Value, not share: standard terms; the kit is charged; no fps concession.
- Objective status: Restore credibility is MET (the Joint Venture engine has been in service on NGSA since 2037). Capitalise is NOT MET at -2.16.

WHAT CHANGED FROM MY FRAME
1. Governing weights. I adopt Mitchill's S1 0.65 / S2 0.35 in place of my 0.60 / 0.40. I trust his numbers over my read, and his reasoning holds: the gating indicator, Boeing's line "the business case isn't [there]... I'm not going to give you a date", has not moved, and Boeing held on the same line in 2045. It changes the expected value by $0.00B.
2. The share line in the statement reads 26.7 percent, the exact record, on Mitchill's and the Board's advice. My draft rounded it up to "about 27%".
3. Mitchill advised keeping fps EIS years and grid figures off the bulletin. The public fps move no longer carries "2057 or 2060" or "S2 equals S1"; both stay in this private record. Last round's public text crossed that line, which is close to my own red line on an airframer's dates [PX-0062]. I own that and have corrected it.

FINAL ACCOUNT OF CAPITALISE (B8)
The booked figure is -2.16 against the status quo: engine value -0.16 and R&D -2.00 undiscounted, unchanged since 2045.

The reset check I set in 2045 has not fired:
- The round-4 year table is identical to round 3 in every year from 2026 to 2060 (my diff, Mitchill's diff).
- In 2045-49 we delivered 830 / 866 / 861 / 887 / 925 engines, to the engine as forecast, and within two engines of the public delivery record.
- Values were 7.5 / 8.0 / 8.1 / 8.6 / 9.1 against status quo 7.2 / 7.8 / 7.9 / 8.4 / 9.1: about +0.13 PV realised. I checked this against the brief.
- Of the +0.41 recovery for 2041-56, +0.27 is realised and +0.137 is still forecast for 2050-56.
- The rounded table sums to -0.105 against the brief's -0.16. The brief governs.

The low end and what lies outside the window:
- If no forecast year arrived, we would be at about -2.30. That is not a column.
- Even if every forecast year lands, the $2.00B is not recovered inside 2056.
- 2057-60 adds about +0.07 PV (S1). It is recorded and not booked. Years after 2056 are not claimed.

The 2045 lesson stays on the record: any engine a rival names in public is priced as the low end, even when no column carries it [PX-0076]. This year the low end equals the booked figure:
- CFM's ducted engine and the Embraer partnership are already in the number;
- RISE is at least ten years from any launch;
- Rolls-Royce is inside the Joint Venture;
- any fps enters service after 2056.

No premium, discount or concession chases the $2.16B gap. Long-term value now comes from running the engine in service well and returning cash in the Board's order.

THE 2045 COMMITMENTS THAT FELL DUE
All are delivered in the other moves:
- the reset check (above);
- the capacity case: there is none, and the peak is met lean;
- the Joint Venture formed terms to the Finance Committee;
- the first annual Joint Venture NPV review;
- the annual durability report to Governance and Public Policy.

BIASES, DECLARED
- Incrementalism: I leaned to Boeing holding and took Mitchill's even lower S2.
- Operating optimism: the 2036 date held, but I publish no time-on-wing figure and no upgrade date.
- Architecture loyalty: the gear and core stay ours, and the engine in service stays as tested.
- Supply-first caution: the 2052 peak is met lean, not built for.

WHERE THE RECORD IS THIN
- The Joint Venture positions are doctrine and inference [P-1233]; I have no Rolls-Royce evidence of my own.
- Eddy's seat rests on one event.
- The board models no parts, dividend or debt.

"The bad news first. The move from one generation of single-aisle aircraft to the next cost us volume. Our share of narrowbody engines dipped in 2039 and 2040; it has since come back, to about 27% of the narrowbody engines delivered in 2049. Our competitors answered with new engines of their own, as they should, and what we have earned on the money we spent to get here has come in short of what we planned. We own that, and we are not going to dress it up.

The GTF fleet on the A320neo comes first: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into that fleet at shop visits. New production never crowds out its spares, and we confirm new engines only where the fleet's spares are covered. Control what you can control.

The Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, built on GTF2, has been in service on NGSA since 2037. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself. Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign is complete. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We offer the Joint Venture engine to an airframer only where it is ready by that airframe's entry into service, and it is ready now. We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes, dates, rates and engine choices, and we will not get out ahead of them. The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service."

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
The order cannot change: `hold` is the only value on both fields, and this is the last round. What would change my record:
1. Field records showing a quality escape, an AOG trend or a life-limited-part shortfall on the Joint Venture engine or the GTF tail. I would book the cost fast, with contingency before the estimate and a dated follow-up [PX-0292][PX-0288].
2. Eddy saying the 2051 step needs supplier capacity. He brings a dollar figure, and I test it against Do Nothing and a buyback at 10%, temporary and back-end-loaded. Without a figure, there is no case.
3. A Boeing launch on the record. It would not change the order and is worth $0 inside 2056. A code-3 (CFM-only) fps would be recorded as the post-2056 low end.
4. A CFM Open Fan launch on the record. It is upside under the rules and in no column, so it is recorded, not booked.
5. Realised 2050-56 years falling short of the +0.14 forecast. I would reset openly, with drivers. The floor is about -2.30.
6. Joint Venture terms drifting toward a balancing payment, a carried share, below-standard modules or unsigned partner money (ground 3).
7. Any statement line adding a Capitalise, return, durability-figure or post-2056 claim (ground 4).
cfo.memo:
Low end first. One legal row, hold/hold: -2.16 in S1 and in S2. My weights stay S1 0.65, S2 0.35. Boeing now says the technology is there, but "the business case isn't", with no date. Expected, worst and booked: -2.16 on any weights. Nothing to fund: 2050 adds $0 of R&D, total R&D is our $2.00B Joint Venture share, no write-off. Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. The stretch was never used.

The reset check. I said in 2045 we'd reset if the years didn't show. They showed. The 2045-49 rows match the 2045 table to the engine, and the public delivery record within two engines. Realised +0.13 PV, so +0.27 of the +0.41 is in and +0.14 is still forecast. The trigger hasn't fired; -2.16 stands. I'm not declaring victory on one clean set of years.

Capitalise is not met and won't be. If every forecast year lands, engine value still ends at -0.16 and the $2.00B is not recovered. 2057-60 adds about +0.07, recorded, not booked. If the forecast failed outright, we'd be at -2.30.

No rival engine on the record moves our number inside 2056. CFM's ducted engine and Embraer partnership are already in it, RISE is ten years from any launch, and any fps enters service in 2057 at the earliest.

The 2051-52 peak: meet it lean. The grid pays nothing for capacity, and capacity for 1,010 sits 43% idle by 2060.

The gate clears on all four grounds.

ops.proposal:
ORDERS PROPOSED: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: hold. These are the only values the brief offers (round4.md section 3). Not a Board item; premium_b 0, overrides empty. I confirm the CEO's reading and have nothing to add. It is the last decision year, so these holds stand to the end of the game.

WHY gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 launched in 2030 and folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 with a $0 write-off. There is no solo programme left to launch or cancel. The Joint Venture engine took GTF2's ready year, 2036.
WHY jv_with_rr: hold. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, so withdraw is barred and commit is spent. Hold keeps the engine we tested as the engine in service on NGSA (fitted CFM + PW + RR). Grid row hold/hold: -2.16 (S1), -2.16 (S2). Weights do not move my technical view.

ANSWERS TO THE CEO'S ASKS
(1) Orders: hold/hold, confirmed. Not submitted: withdraw, commit, cancel, launch, launch_if_selected.

(2) Annual in-service report to Governance and Public Policy (Joint Venture engine, GTF2 as tested). From the record only; I invent no figures.
- Public record: GTF2's 2036 date, set at launch in 2030, held. The engine was fitted at NGSA's 2037 EIS and is still fitted, 13 years later. No P&W quality escape, slip or AOG problem is published in any bulletin from 2035 to 2050, and the GM's 2045 notes say "Public events: none."
- 2030 gates: (a) an Advantage derivative with gear and core carried over is consistent with the record. (b) Severe-environment endurance hours, (c) life-limited parts at full life at EIS, and (d)-(e) the golden rules (all development testing done before service, every new feature instrumented [P-1214][P-1215]) are not on the board and not in my evidence. The committee takes the certification and field records, not my word.
- 2035 gate (T1): no Rolls-Royce-content change has entered service on the record.
- Not in evidence: time on wing, shop-visit rate, AOG count. My last figures are from June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG [PX-0120] and 60% in the latest configuration [PX-0116].
- Share went from 22.1% (2039) to 26.7% (2049). That comes from board mechanics (the NGSA ramp and the equal-share rule) and is not a durability signal.
- The record shows the 2045 and 2050 reports. The years between are not on the record I can see, and I say so.
- I will not say "there's no surprise coming". I said that in June 2023, five weeks before the recall [PX-0112][PX-0290].

(3) GTF A320neo tail.
- The A320neo flies CFM 60% / P&W 40%. The last visible GTF OE lead is 2043: P&W 23.4% against Rolls-Royce 19.6%.
- From 2044 to 2049, P&W equals Rolls-Royce to the decimal every year (24.1, 25.2, 25.6, 25.9, 26.3, 26.7). The equal-share rule applies only on the new types, so the delivered record shows no A320neo GTF OE since 2044 (inference from rules.md). Airbus's own line says 2045 is covered.
- Answer to Airbus: no GTF tail units are left to confirm on the record. If Airbus asks for any unit built from 2046, it is confirmed only where the daily parts review shows the spares gate holds, on standard terms. The board models no parts, so I cannot say the gate holds for a unit nobody has asked for. If it does not hold, the fleet wins and we promise nothing in public.
- Installed base: over 10,000 engines, including orders and options, in 2023 [PX-0129]. The 2050 count is not in evidence. It needs spares and shop visits for decades.
- Freed material goes to spares first, then to Joint Venture OE. GTF OE ended about 2044 on the record, so this has applied for about six years (inference).
- Hot Section kit (about 90-95% of the Advantage durability content [PX-0088]): continues at shop visits, charged. The embodiment percentage is not in evidence, and I give none.

(4) Parts and capacity, 2050-52.
- Pacing parts: about 30 [PX-0123], led by structural castings [PX-0125] and powder-metal disk material [P-1040]. The full 2050 list is not in my evidence. The Joint Venture engine is GTF2, so its OE and the fleet's spares draw on the same material (inference).
- Steps: 913 (2050, -1.3% on 925), 987 (2051, +74, +8.1%), 1,010 (2052, +23). The peak runs 62 (6.7%) and 85 (9.2%) above the 925 delivered in 2049: 147 engine-years, 5.1% of 2050-52 volume. Then 916 in 2053 (-9.3%), and the peak falls 17% by 2056 and 43% by 2060.
- Record: the 2041 step of +141 (+20.1%) and the 2045-49 ramp of +95 (+11.4%) came in with no escape on the record.
- My judgement: the 2051 step is met lean, with no capacity case. Lean means existing qualified suppliers and freed GTF OE material, with no permanent capex (inference). I bring no case to Neil.
- The ramp is gated on GTF and Joint Venture fleet spares, worked daily and reported weekly [PX-0131]. Supplier qualification, first-article inspection and a records review come before each step [P-1040][PX-0039]. If the weekly drumbeat shows a step needs new supplier capacity, it goes to Neil then, priced against Do Nothing and a buyback at 10%. If the gate fails, the OE step waits and the fleet wins [PX-0080].

(5) fps readiness. The engine has been ready since 2036. EIS 2057 (7-year): 21 years of margin. EIS 2060 (10-year or via Embraer): 24 years. Code 4 needs a formed Joint Venture engine ready by EIS, which is met; codes 6 and 7 fit P&W through the Joint Venture engine. Conditions:
- (a) offered as tested; any fps-specific change gets its own durability campaign first;
- (b) the installation work (nacelle, loads, flight test) is real certification work the board does not model, and it is staffed from the Joint Venture, not fleet engineering;
- (c) fps volume sits behind the spares gate, which binds hardest on code 4 (inference).
Nothing on Boeing's dates, sources or code.

(6) T1: no Rolls-Royce-content block upgrade is planned or wanted by me.

(7) Engineering load: Joint Venture fleet support on NGSA, GTF fleet support, the kit, and supplier qualification for the ramp. There is no fps work until Boeing launches, and then it is staffed from the Joint Venture. Nothing pulls fleet engineering off the engines in service. Pass.

(8) Veto check: grounds 1 and 2 both pass on hold/hold and on B1-B8. B2, B4 and B6 are mine and pass as written. In the statement, "about 27%" matches 26.7%. "Ready now" and "in service on NGSA since 2037" match the bulletin. "We confirm new engines only where the fleet's spares are covered" is a rule we control, not an outcome claim; keep it, and keep to it. There is no time-on-wing, full-life or upgrade claim. B5 terms, B7 and B8 are Mitchill's and Calio's.

Operating side of the reset check: the 2045-49 volumes came in at 830/866/861/887/925, which is my 2045 forecast to the engine, and the round-3 and round-4 year tables are identical. Seat doctrine, not my record: the gates, T1, the spares gate.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Any one of these would change my view:
- A P&W quality escape, slip or rising AOG on the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet, in the record or the internal reports. I would contain first, give a dated recovery, hold each ramp step and fail ground 2 on anything that drops the gate.
- Certification records showing a life-limited part not at full life at the 2037 EIS, or testing left open at service. I would report it to Governance and Public Policy at once and strike any durability wording (ground 1).
- The weekly drumbeat showing the 2051 step (+74) cannot be met lean. That goes to Neil, priced against Do Nothing and a buyback.
- Airbus asking for GTF units it builds from 2046 where the spares gate does not hold. The fleet wins.
- Any ask to put a block upgrade or fps-specific change into service before its own campaign (ground 1, binding).
Weights do not move my view.
ops.memo:
The bad number first. We book -2.16 against the status quo, unchanged since 2045, and no order closes it. The account is Neil's. The operating side of it is mine.

Orders: hold and hold, the only legal values. GTF2 folded in 2035, and the Joint Venture formed that year.

Readiness passes. The engine has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. An fps launched now enters service in 2057 or 2060, with 21 or 24 years of margin.

In service, the record shows no escape, slip or AOG problem since 2035. The 2045-49 volumes came in to the engine, 830 to 925. That's the record, not a durability figure, and I publish no time-on-wing number. I won't say there's no surprise coming. I said that once, five weeks before a recall. Governance gets the certification and field records, not my word.

The A320 tail: since 2044 our share has equalled Rolls-Royce's to the decimal, so there are no GTF tail units on the record to confirm. If Airbus asks, a unit gets confirmed only where the spares gate holds. If it doesn't hold, the fleet wins and we say nothing.

The peak: 987 and 1,010 engines, 62 and 85 over last year's 925, then down 43% by 2060. About 30 parts pace it, with castings and powder metal leading. We meet it lean: daily cadence, weekly drumbeat, a records review before each step. There's no capacity case.

No veto. Where I'm thin: one event, June 2023, before the recall. The rest is seat doctrine.

decision.public_statement:
The bad news first. The move from one generation of single-aisle aircraft to the next cost us volume. Our share of narrowbody engines dipped in 2039 and 2040; it has since come back, to 26.7 percent of the narrowbody engines delivered in 2049. Our competitors answered with new engines of their own, as they should, and what we have earned on the money we spent to get here has come in short of what we planned. We own that, and we are not going to dress it up.

The GTF fleet on the A320neo comes first: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into that fleet at shop visits. New production never crowds out its spares, and we confirm new engines only where the fleet's spares are covered. Control what you can control.

The Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, built on GTF2, has been in service on NGSA since 2037. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself. Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign is complete. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We offer the Joint Venture engine to an airframer only where it is ready by that airframe's entry into service, and it is ready now. We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes, dates, rates and engine choices, and we will not get out ahead of them. The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. `premium_b` is 0 and `overrides` is empty. Neither order is a Board item.

THE GRID
The brief's grid has one row: -2.16 in S1 (rivals hold) and -2.16 in S2 (Boeing launches the fps on a 10-year programme, code 7). Expected, worst and booked are all -2.16, on any weights.
- S2 moved from -2.17 (2045) to -2.16 because an fps launched in 2050 enters service in 2060 (2057 on a 7-year programme). The board stops counting narrowbody engines in 2056.
- No Board item exists. Both fields offer only `hold`, and a round of all holds does not reach review.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Eddy's proposal is hold/hold, the only legal values. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 with a $0 write-off. The Joint Venture formed that year, so `withdraw` is barred and `commit` is spent.
2. Binding vetoes: none stands.
- Mitchill clears all four grounds. His two conditional binding vetoes (ground 4 on statement wording, ground 3 on terms) are not triggered by the package as returned.
- Eddy invokes neither of his grounds. His conditional ground-1 veto (on T1) and ground-2 veto (the spares gate) are not triggered, because the other moves keep both.
3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]:
- the engine in service stays GTF2 as tested;
- no block upgrade or fps-specific change enters service without its own campaign;
- no OE draws on fleet spares.
Hold/hold meets the constraint, so it is also the best PV inside it.
4. Tie-breaks:
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: there is no new engine to weigh.
- Miss a cycle against visible demand [PX-0071][PX-0109]: we are in this cycle on NGSA. Any fps code that names us (4, 6 or 7) finds the engine ready. The rule is RTX-wide, and applying it here is inference.
- A rival's discount does not move the answer [PX-0055]: none is on the record, and we offer none.
5. Premium: doctrine $0 plus objective $0, $0 of the $1B cap. The Board's $0.5B allowance is unused. Nothing trails, so there is nothing to declare.

MY TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass. The engine has been ready since 2036 against the 2037 NGSA EIS, and against any fps EIS of 2057 or 2060.
- Visible demand: no launch is offered.
- Miss-a-cycle cost: zero inside the window. We are fitted on NGSA, and an fps adds $0 inside 2056.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no premium.
- Dividend safe: Mitchill confirms. $0 of about $6B used; the dividend is covered; debt stays on its path to pre-ASR levels (not claimed to be there); buybacks are the fill-in.
- Value, not share: standard terms; the kit is charged; no fps concession.
- Objective status: Restore credibility is MET (the Joint Venture engine has been in service on NGSA since 2037). Capitalise is NOT MET at -2.16.

WHAT CHANGED FROM MY FRAME
1. Governing weights. I adopt Mitchill's S1 0.65 / S2 0.35 in place of my 0.60 / 0.40. I trust his numbers over my read, and his reasoning holds: the gating indicator, Boeing's line "the business case isn't [there]... I'm not going to give you a date", has not moved, and Boeing held on the same line in 2045. It changes the expected value by $0.00B.
2. The share line in the statement reads 26.7 percent, the exact record, on Mitchill's and the Board's advice. My draft rounded it up to "about 27%".
3. Mitchill advised keeping fps EIS years and grid figures off the bulletin. The public fps move no longer carries "2057 or 2060" or "S2 equals S1"; both stay in this private record. Last round's public text crossed that line, which is close to my own red line on an airframer's dates [PX-0062]. I own that and have corrected it.

FINAL ACCOUNT OF CAPITALISE (B8)
The booked figure is -2.16 against the status quo: engine value -0.16 and R&D -2.00 undiscounted, unchanged since 2045.

The reset check I set in 2045 has not fired:
- The round-4 year table is identical to round 3 in every year from 2026 to 2060 (my diff, Mitchill's diff).
- In 2045-49 we delivered 830 / 866 / 861 / 887 / 925 engines, to the engine as forecast, and within two engines of the public delivery record.
- Values were 7.5 / 8.0 / 8.1 / 8.6 / 9.1 against status quo 7.2 / 7.8 / 7.9 / 8.4 / 9.1: about +0.13 PV realised. I checked this against the brief.
- Of the +0.41 recovery for 2041-56, +0.27 is realised and +0.137 is still forecast for 2050-56.
- The rounded table sums to -0.105 against the brief's -0.16. The brief governs.

The low end and what lies outside the window:
- If no forecast year arrived, we would be at about -2.30. That is not a column.
- Even if every forecast year lands, the $2.00B is not recovered inside 2056.
- 2057-60 adds about +0.07 PV (S1). It is recorded and not booked. Years after 2056 are not claimed.

The 2045 lesson stays on the record: any engine a rival names in public is priced as the low end, even when no column carries it [PX-0076]. This year the low end equals the booked figure:
- CFM's ducted engine and the Embraer partnership are already in the number;
- RISE is at least ten years from any launch;
- Rolls-Royce is inside the Joint Venture;
- any fps enters service after 2056.

No premium, discount or concession chases the $2.16B gap. Long-term value now comes from running the engine in service well and returning cash in the Board's order.

THE 2045 COMMITMENTS THAT FELL DUE
All are delivered in the other moves:
- the reset check (above);
- the capacity case: there is none, and the peak is met lean;
- the Joint Venture formed terms to the Finance Committee;
- the first annual Joint Venture NPV review;
- the annual durability report to Governance and Public Policy.

BIASES, DECLARED
- Incrementalism: I leaned to Boeing holding and took Mitchill's even lower S2.
- Operating optimism: the 2036 date held, but I publish no time-on-wing figure and no upgrade date.
- Architecture loyalty: the gear and core stay ours, and the engine in service stays as tested.
- Supply-first caution: the 2052 peak is met lean, not built for.

WHERE THE RECORD IS THIN
- The Joint Venture positions are doctrine and inference [P-1233]; I have no Rolls-Royce evidence of my own.
- Eddy's seat rests on one event.
- The board models no parts, dividend or debt.

So, the last decision year. These orders fix the end state, and no later round exists in which to cancel anything. I decided on cash and quality of earnings [RX-0054], by the team rule.

1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL: every field at hold. Grid row 'UltraFan NB: hold' is +9.98 / +9.98 / +9.98 / +10.33 (S1-S4). It is the best plan in every column.

2. WEIGHTS. S1 0.75, S2 0.05, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, confirmed by McCabe and the Board.
- S2 0.05: Boeing will not launch 'until [the business case] is', with no date and no maker named. That is a signal against.
- S3 0.10: nothing is on the record, and Boeing calls its 787 line stable.
- S4 0.10: Airbus's 'continue to assess its evolution' is a soft A350 signal, but S4 also needs a 787 Re-engine nobody has signalled. I round it up, which favours the launch rows.
- On these weights the hold row is +10.02. It is +10.00 on McCabe's guide-low set (0.80/0.05/0.10/0.05) and on last round's set, +10.07 on equal weights and +10.05 on a Re-engine stress. No vote turns on the weights.

3. BINDING VETOES.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on `t1000_upgrade: launch` and on `ultrafan_wb: launch` (binding: hurdle and downside). Both orders stay `hold`.
- Watson: no Civil veto on the all-hold package. Maturity: the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 EIS, and no finding is on the record. Early date: none disclosed. Support: in place by 2036.
- Nothing to revise.

4. THE TWO WIDEBODY ITEMS, against hold, column by column.
- T1000 upgrade: -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.63, -6.72 weighted. Its worst column is 3.37 times its $2B bill. Even before the $5B strain it is -1.73: about $0.27B of engine gain for $2B. It counts only from 2053, so it buys no point of 2050 share. My record says regain the 787 share, 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. On this board the answer is the price. It fails the viable-business-model part of the four-part gate [RX-0030].
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32, -8.90 weighted. Its worst column is 2.25 times its $4B bill. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, so airframers-first fails [RX-0058]. It would be ready in 2056, a year after the 2055 EIS of any Re-engine launched this round.
- Either launch fixes the $5B strain (about £3.7bn) for good. It would turn 'widebody never starved' from met to not met and pull engineers off the 2052 peak.
- Both are far beyond the $3B cap and the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap, so no declared premium can carry either.

5. RED-LINE FLAGS.
- Watson flagged B and C: each loses more than its bill, is beyond the caps, fixes the strain, and C has no Re-engine on the record. McCabe flagged C on the same no-programme ground. I confirm every flag; both items were already struck.
- Final check against the company red lines: no UltraFan launch; no early date; no overlap; no cancel; no concession; no disclosure on airframers' dates, the A350 or P&W's modules. Nothing breaches.
- `overrides` is empty.

6. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. My record has no run-down, capacity or closing-account behaviour. On these I follow company doctrine: McCabe's capital order and guide-low frame as my evidence on cash, and Watson on support, capacity and maturity. The P&W module split and measured-rate sizing go to the Board as an open support item. That is advice, not a veto: support was in place before EIS, and no narrowbody order is live.

7. WHAT HOLD COSTS AND WHAT IT KEEPS.
- Cost on the grid: none. Premium $0.
- It keeps narrowbody at 27.2% and widebody at 55.2% (58.0% in S4), strain at $0, and the value at +9.98 at the worst column.

- The biggest risk to tomorrow's financials [RX-0125] is off the grid: an in-service finding at the peak on modules we do not design. Fleet first, ramp second.

We don't commit that easily [RX-0124]. A milestone on our journey, not our final destination [RX-0062].
