It gives no date or engine choice for Boeing's fps, no comment on Airbus's A350 evolution or NGSA ramp, nothing on P&W's modules, no widebody programme and no time-on-wing target. Watson checked it and it passes. 'Fleet first, ramp second' stays private. 'We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.' stands.

priorities: 1. Product safety and in-service maturity, now at the narrowbody peak. The Joint Venture engine has flown on NGSA since 2037. Our narrowbody volume is 913 engines in 2050 and peaks at 1,010 in 2052, about five times our 188 widebody engines a year. Its gear and GTF Advantage core are P&W modules, so our assurance on them rests on P&W's data. Watson's in-service watch continues to this Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. The fleet comes first and the ramp second: a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. The same rule holds for the Trent XWB, Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 fleets [RG-0027, RG-0025, RG-0019, RG-0049, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0284].

2. Hold on every field, and remember that this is the last decision year: these orders fix the end state. The 'UltraFan NB: hold' row is the best plan in every column, at +9.98 / +9.98 / +9.98 / +10.33 (S1-S4), or +10.02 on our illustrative weights. The narrowbody fields can only hold. Each widebody launch would add the $5B strain, because the Joint Venture is ready and can no longer be cancelled. That strain is charged only if a widebody programme is added, so it belongs in the item value [RG-0033, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214].

3. Defend the widebody core through time on wing, not through a programme. RR widebody share is 55.2% in 2050 in S1-S3 and 58.0% in S4, on the hold row and on both launch rows alike. Neither widebody launch moves the scored 2050 line: the Trent 1000 upgrade would count only from 2053, and UltraFan WB only once a Re-engine is in service, with readiness in 2056. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the widebody franchise test does not trigger. Airbus's new line, that it continues to assess the A350's evolution, is a signal and not an announcement [R-1574, RX-0246, RG-0068, RX-0101, R-0361].

4. The balance sheet and the capital frame. Narrowbody development money is final at $5.71B: the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B fold write-off. That is $1.71B over the $4B bound, stated openly, and no order can change it. No new development spend is proposed. Narrowbody value, a lifecycle value of $14.9B nominal in 2050 against $6.0B under the status quo, goes through the capital order: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity and no leverage for distributions [R-0900, RX-0242, RG-0041, R-0909, RG-0059].

5. Discipline on terms and on disclosure. An fps on code 5 (S2) is now worth exactly 0.00 against S1 (+9.98 both), so no concession, discount or free upgrade can pay. The Joint Venture engine is offered on standard terms, jointly with P&W. The public statement gives nothing on Boeing's fps dates or engine requirement and nothing on Airbus's A350 evolution or ramp, and it announces no widebody programme. 'We won't do anything not profitable' stands [R-1561, R-1582, RX-0081, RX-0097, R-0970, R-1476].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4 of 5, unchanged, in the final round. Our narrowbody development is complete, paid for and in service. The only orders open are two widebody launches, and each stacks a $5B strain on its own bill. We accept no item that can lose more than its own bill in any plausible column. We accept no shortfall beyond the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap or the $3B cap. No vote turns on the weights. Both items fall below their own bill in every column and under every weighting we tried, including equal weights (upgrade -6.71, UltraFan WB -8.75). One-big-programme does not bite as a formal ground: no UltraFan is in development and no `launch_if_selected` is available. The balance-sheet and position-weakening tests do not apply unless McCabe invokes a balance-sheet veto or another move needs equity, leverage above about 1.5x, or borrowing for distributions. On time horizon (2.5), the long view on the widebody core is ours to hold. It acts through the two caps, and this round both items are far outside them.

That includes the $5B strain, but even without it the item is -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.63, so it does not pay on its own [RG-0033]. Second ground, declared premium. The item is -6.72 weighted (-6.71 to -6.73 on every set), beyond the $3B cap. It counts only from 2053, so it does not move the scored 2050 widebody share (55.2%, and 58.0% in S4, the same as hold). The core is not at risk: the widebody franchise test does not trigger. One-big-programme is not a ground, because no UltraFan is in development and none can be triggered. Any missing co-signature from McCabe is a governance ground. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

Any Board item without McCabe's co-signature as we define it, and any package with a binding ExCo veto left unrespected, a red-line flag left unrebutted, or a non-empty `overrides`. Ground: governance [RX-0213, R-1579, RG-0044]. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

recommendations.text: In-service maturity at the narrowbody peak. Continue Watson's in-service watch each round to this Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee: durability, time on wing, shop-visit rates, spares cover, early-service intervention and any open findings, with P&W's data on the gear and GTF Advantage core coming through the Joint Venture. Narrowbody volume peaks at 1,010 engines in 2052, so the years 2050-2052 are when an in-service issue would bite hardest. If one arises, the fleet comes first and the ramp second: a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. 'Product safety ... is and always must be our most important priority.'

Capacity through the peak and the run-down. The brief shows 913 narrowbody engines in 2050 and 1,010 in 2052, then a fall to 574 by 2060 as replacement demand drops after the mid-2050s. Plan both sides. To the peak, place work with high-performing suppliers and keep Trent kits, spares and time-on-wing engineering on first call. After the peak, move OE capacity to repair and the partner-shop aftermarket, sized on measured shop-visit rates, and add no owned capacity that would sit idle. The concentration on P&W for the gear and core stays on the Committee's risk register.

The widebody core, beyond this game's horizon. Hold both widebody fields. Defend the Trent fleets through time on wing inside the existing envelope, on the model of the Trent 1000 durability package. Airbus's new line on assessing the A350's evolution should be watched, not answered. A widebody programme should come to this Board only when a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record and names us, and when the case pays at our hurdles with the $5B strain counted (on McCabe's break-even, a Re-engine gain of about $8B for UltraFan WB or about $4B for the upgrade). UltraFan may be kept as a technology option inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, not as a programme and with no public date. 'We are a long-term business with very long investment cycles', and the long view comes through the caps, not around them.

The capital frame and a closing account. McCabe should report narrowbody development money as final at $5.71B ($4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B fold write-off), $1.71B over the bound. The narrowbody value is engine lifecycle value ($14.9B nominal in 2050 against $6.0B under the status quo, peaking at $16.6B in 2052); it arrives as LTSA balance growth, not straight-line cash. It goes through the capital order: the balance sheet, the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity and no leverage for distributions. Any change to medium-term guidance comes to this Board before release. The closing objective note should record each line as it stands, including the bound we missed.

Commercial discipline in any fps campaign. Boeing now asks for more than one engine source, each ready by the airplane's entry into service. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and meets that requirement. An fps selection on code 5 is worth 0.00 against S1 on this grid (+9.98 both), so offer the engine only on standard terms, jointly with P&W, with no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade. Any fps-specific change to the engine gets its own durability campaign first. Any change of Joint Venture terms, or any inducement, comes to this Board with McCabe's co-signature. Profit and cash over market share.

Disclosure. The 2045 statement can largely stand: the Joint Venture engine is in service, maturity and time on wing come first on every fleet, and widebody is our core. Give no date or engine choice for Boeing's fps and make no comment on its requirement beyond standard terms. Say nothing on Airbus's A350 evolution or NGSA ramp, nothing on P&W's modules beyond what the partners have said, and announce no widebody programme. Keep 'fleet first, ramp second' as a private rule. 'We won't do anything not profitable' stands.

frame.question:
So, 2050 is the last decision year. These orders fix the end state, and no later round exists in which to cancel anything. The question is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. It has two parts.

(1) Do we add a widebody programme in the last round? The only orders open are `ultrafan_wb: launch` and `t1000_upgrade: launch`. The Joint Venture is ready, on the record and impossible to cancel, so either launch pays the $5B strain on top of its own bill, and the strain is now permanent. The grid says no in every column:
- the upgrade is -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.63 against hold;
- UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32 against hold.
Each loses more than its own bill in every column. Neither moves the scored 2050 widebody share: 55.2% in S1-S3 and 58.0% in S4, the same on every row. A launch would also turn 'widebody never starved' from met to not met.

(2) How do we turn the narrowbody entry into cash through the peak without risking safety or the Trent core? We deliver 913 narrowbody engines this year, rising to 1,010 in 2052 and falling to 574 by 2060, against 188 widebody engines a year. The answer is in-service maturity, capacity for both the peak and the run-down, standard terms with P&W, the capital order and an honest closing account.

Actually, the biggest risk to tomorrow's financials [RX-0125] is not on this grid. It is an in-service finding at the peak, on a gear and a core we do not design. Fleet first, ramp second. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058].
frame.situation:
Round 4, decision year 2050, the last round. Round 3 was adjudicated with no public events. We held every field and the Board approved with no items.

PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin):
- NGSA (Airbus): in service since 2037, fitted CFM + PW + RR, in a 'disciplined and controlled ramp-up: rate by rate, quality first'. The last A320s are leaving the lines.
- The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine: formed 2035, ready since 2036, in service on NGSA. Both Solos (GTF2 and UltraFan NB) folded into it in 2035.
- P&W: 'Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules ... and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself.' Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign. It competes on standard terms, offers the engine only where it is ready by EIS, and says 'the development spend is behind us'. The GTF fleet on the A320neo comes first.
- CFM: the ducted engine has been ready since 2041 and is offered to both airframers; the Embraer partnership has been ready since 2042; GEnx upgrade since 2033. RISE stays a technology programme, with an open fan 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer'. Kits and spares keep first call.
- Boeing: no fps. 'The business case isn't [there], and I'm not going to launch an airplane until it is.' No date. The engine requirement is restated as 'more than one engine source, from engines that are ready when the airplane is', with no maker, code or date named. '787 and 777X lines are stable.' The MAX steps down one step at a time. No 787 Re-engine.
- Airbus on widebody: 'the A350 family ... remains our offer. We continue to assess its evolution as engine technology matures, and we will decide on our own timetable.' That is a signal, not an announcement: no programme and no date. No A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- Our 2045 line: Joint Venture engine in service, narrowbody development complete, maturity and time on wing first on every fleet, standard terms jointly with our partner, widebody is our core, 'We won't do anything not profitable.'
- Observed: RR narrowbody engine share 25.2% (2045) to 26.7% (2049). RR widebody 55.2% since 2042, after the GEnx upgrade.

OUR POSITION (brief section 1), if nobody moves:
- ΔPV +9.98 $B, yield 109.07%: engine value +15.70, R&D -4.00, write-offs -1.71.
- Narrowbody engines: 913 (2050), 987 (2051), 1,010 (2052 peak), then 916, 903, 869, 838, 751, 674, 623 and 574 (2060).
- Widebody: 188 a year at 55.2% through 2060.
- Engine lifecycle value: $14.9B nominal in 2050 against $6.0B under the status quo, peaking at $16.6B in 2052.
- The board counts the narrowbody market to 2056 and the widebody to 2061.

OBJECTIVE STATUS (brief section 2):
- Enter NB: met (25.2% in 2045, 27.2% in 2050).
- Keep WB dominance: met (worst year 55.2%).
- Bounded NB risk: NOT met. Final at $5.71B ($4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B fold write-off), $1.71B over the $4B bound. No order can change it.
- WB never starved: met with $0 strain, but only if every widebody field holds. Any widebody launch now charges $5B for good.

SCENARIOS:
- S1: rivals hold.
- S2: Boeing launches the fps 10-yr (EIS 2060) on code 5. It is worth 0.00 against S1 (+9.98 both): EIS falls after the board's 2056 narrowbody count.
- S3: 787 Re-engine (EIS 2055).
- S4: 787 and A350 Re-engines (EIS 2055).

BOARD GUIDANCE:
- Risk appetite 4 of 5, unchanged. Hold every field.
- It would veto `ultrafan_wb: launch` on four grounds: no airframe on the record; worst column below its bill; -8.90 weighted, beyond the $1B sub-cap; Ready-by-EIS fail (2056 against 2055).
- It would veto `t1000_upgrade: launch`: more than three times its bill in every column, -6.72 weighted, beyond the $3B cap, and it does not move 2050 share.
- It would veto any item without McCabe's co-signature, any package with a standing veto or an unrebutted flag, and any non-empty `overrides`.
- It wants Watson's in-service report, the capacity plan through the peak and run-down, McCabe's confirmation that narrowbody money is final at $5.71B, a statement that comments on no airframer's plans, a closing objective note, and `board_response` to its round-3 recommendations as they stand in 2050.

The value is lifecycle value: $14.9B nominal this year, $16.6B at the 2052 peak, $14.2B in 2060, while narrowbody OE falls 43%. It arrives as LTSA balance growth, not a straight line, through the frame: balance sheet, the 30-40% payout, then investment and distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity, no leverage for distributions. We guide low.

A finding on P&W's modules is unpriced. Fleet first.

My record on engine economics is thin; these are the board's numbers. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture engine (in service)
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier if a folded Solo is further along (the bulletin shows 2036). It must be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS. A zero margin passes with a note. A late engine fails, but that is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: Formed 2035, ready 2036 on GTF2's full six-year programme (2030 + 6). NGSA launched 2030 with EIS 2037: 1 year in hand. It has been in service since 2037. S2: an fps 10-yr launched 2050 has EIS 2060, so the engine is 24 years ahead (a 7-yr fps would be EIS 2057). It also meets Boeing's restated 'ready when the airplane is' requirement. S2 is worth 0.00 against S1 (+9.98 both) because an EIS of 2060 falls after the board's 2056 narrowbody count.

tests.name: In-service watch: Joint Venture engine and P&W modules (Board R1; inference from the maturity rule)
tests.threshold: No open in-service finding on the record. If one arises, the fleet comes first and the ramp second: a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. No figure cited that I cannot source.
tests.numbers: In service 13 years (2037-2050). RR narrowbody deliveries ran 7 (2037), 23 (2038) and 80 (2039), so the early-service intervention window was a slow one. Then 257 (2040), 830 (2045), 925 (2049) and 913 (2050); share 0.2% (2037) to 26.7% (2049). The 925-to-913 dip follows airframe deliveries (Airbus: 'rate by rate, quality first'), not an engine finding (inference). Nothing on the record points to a finding. NOT ON THE RECORD: durability, time on wing, shop-visit rates, spares cover, early-service interventions and open findings on the Joint Venture engine. The board has no in-service mechanic, so I report none. P&W MODULES: P&W now says the gear and the GTF Advantage core 'are Pratt & Whitney modules ... and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself.' What that changes: (a) in public we give no assurance on those modules beyond P&W's own words; (b) in private, our assurance rests entirely on P&W's module data reaching the Board and the Committee through the Joint Venture, so that data flow is a standing condition. What it confirms: P&W's rule that any in-service change 'comes only after its own durability campaign ... If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it' matches our maturity rule. P&W's GTF Advantage hot-section kit going into its A320neo fleet is about its own fleet, not ours, but it is the nearest public evidence on the core we fly. Slower ramp into 2052? Nothing on the record justifies one. The rule stands if something does.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan WB (if launched in 2050)
tests.threshold: Ready at launch + 6. It counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. It must be ready by that Re-engine's EIS. A late engine fails as advice inside the ExCo; for an unconditional launch the Board reads the fail as a veto ground.
tests.numbers: Launched 2050, ready 2056. A 787 or A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 (S3, S4) has EIS 2055 (launch + 5), so UltraFan WB is ONE YEAR LATE. Six years is longer than five, so it can never meet a Re-engine launched in its own round. In S1 and S2 there is no Re-engine, so it never counts. In S3 and S4 it counts 2056-2061, which is why its item improves only to -8.68 and -8.32. No Re-engine is on the record. Airbus's 'continue to assess its evolution' is a signal, not a programme. Development 2050-2056.

tests.name: Count year: Trent 1000 upgrade (if launched in 2050)
tests.threshold: Counts at launch + 3, not before 2035. No airframe dependency.
tests.numbers: Launched 2050, counts 2053 on its full three years: nothing is compressed. That is after the scored 2050 line, so 2050 widebody share stays 55.2% (58.0% in S4), the same as hold. Development 2050-2053, which overlaps the narrowbody peak (2050-2052). Passing on timing is not a case for launching it: see Engineering load.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 6 (UltraFan WB: not before 2056) or the Joint Venture engine's ready date as the bulletin shows it (2036). No time-on-wing target until its risk is gone. Nothing on airframers' dates or on P&W's modules beyond P&W's own words.
tests.numbers: Draft line checked: 'Joint Venture engine ... is in service, and our narrowbody development is complete' matches the bulletin (ready 2036, in service 2037). It gives no date, no fps or Re-engine date or engine choice, no comment on Airbus's A350 evolution or NGSA ramp, nothing on P&W's modules, no widebody programme and no time-on-wing figure: PASS. 'Fleet first, ramp second' stays private, as advised in 2045. In public it would read as a comment on Airbus's ramp or a hint of a finding that is not on the record. The public move (standard terms, jointly with P&W) carries no date: PASS.

tests.name: Support before EIS, and at fleet scale (Board R2 support)
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a partner-shop support plan had to exist before the narrowbody EIS (by 2036 for the 2037 EIS). In service it must scale with the fleet on measured rates (inference). Before any new EIS (an fps), the plan must cover that airframe too.
tests.numbers: Before EIS: in place by 2036. Partner MRO on the Singapore joint-venture model by 2032; repair technology, a spare-engine pool and high-performing suppliers by 2035; EIS team and early-service intervention by 2036. PASS. FLEET (RR narrowbody engines delivered, cumulative): 3,765 (end-2045), 7,304 (end-2049), 8,217 (end-2050), 10,214 (end-2052), 13,740 (end-2056), 16,362 (end-2060), against 4,844 Trent engines delivered 2026-2050 on this board. Sized on measured rates? The Joint Venture engine's shop-visit rate and time on wing are not on the record, so I cannot show partner MRO, P&W's shop network, the spare pool and repair technology sized on measured rates from anything I can source. The rule stands: size on measured rates, not on an assumed one. P&W MODULE SPLIT: I cannot show the MRO and spares split for the gear and core as agreed. P&W's 2050 line ('they stay ours') points to P&W keeping module work (inference). Under the round-3 rule it goes to the Board as an OPEN SUPPORT ITEM until it is confirmed. That is advice, not a veto ground: support was in place before the 2037 EIS, and no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit is on this round's orders. Shop visits: for the Trent base I use my 1,100-1,200 a year [RX-0279], not 1,400-1,500 [RX-0223]. Neither is a narrowbody rate.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs a one-off $5B strain whatever the dates. Seat red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference: seat and company rule).
tests.numbers: All hold: strain $0 in S1-S4. CONFIRMED: the Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, and no later round exists, so either widebody launch fixes the $5B for good and turns 'widebody never starved' to not met. Upgrade item: -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.63 (S1-S4); -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.63 before strain; -6.72 weighted on 0.75/0.05/0.10/0.10 (-6.71 to -6.73 on every set); worst column 3.37 times its $2B bill. UltraFan WB item: -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32; -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.68 / -3.32 before strain; -8.90 weighted (-8.75 to -8.93); worst 2.25 times its $4B bill. The seat red lines do not bite: no UltraFan is in development and no Solo exists. LOAD: there is no load reason for a widebody programme to pull engineers from the peak, and every reason against. The upgrade (2050-2053) and UltraFan WB (2050-2056) would both run while the fleet grows from 8,217 to 10,214 engines and OE peaks at 1,010. That is the worst point to compete with in-service support (inference). Advice, not binding.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers (Board R2 capacity)
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. A narrowbody ramp and run-down are flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers: Narrowbody: 913 (2050), 987 (2051), 1,010 (2052 peak), then 916, 903, 869, 838, 751, 674, 623 and 574 (2060), 43.2% below the peak. Widebody: 188 a year to 2061. Total: 1,101 (2050), 1,198 (2052), 762 (2060). Narrowbody is 4.9 times widebody in 2050, 5.4 times at the peak and 3.1 times in 2060. My midterm widebody OE plan was 300-350 a year [RX-0279], so the 2052 total is 3.4-4.0 times it. TO THE PEAK: our share of the work stays with high-performing suppliers [RX-0286], critical parts dual-sourced, and Trent kits, spares and time-on-wing engineering keep first call. AFTER THE PEAK: OE falls while shop visits rise as the fleet ages, so OE capacity moves to repair and the partner-shop aftermarket, sized on measured rates, with no owned capacity that would sit idle (inference). RISK REGISTER: the gear and core come only from P&W through P&W's own chain, and P&W says its GTF fleet and spares come first. That single-partner concentration on the two most critical modules stays on the Committee's register.

tests.name: Widebody dominance (Board R3)
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (inference). Time on wing is the lever.
tests.numbers: 58.0% (2040), 55.2% (2045), 55.2% (2050) in S1-S3 and 58.0% in S4, the same on all three rows. The brief shows 55.2% flat to 2060. The worst cell is 5.2 pp above the line, and no column threatens it. What time on wing inside the envelope protects through 2061: about 4,844 Trent engines delivered 2026-2050 on this board, plus 2,068 more at 188 a year over 2051-2061. The Trent XWB is about 60% of the large-engine fleet [R-1279]. The tools are the Trent 1000 durability package, with fleet retrofit within two years [RG-0068], and longer-life HP turbine blades and life-limited parts on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 [RX-0285]. No programme and no strain. Break-even watch: the UltraFan WB item improves by only +0.68 from S1 to S4 and the upgrade by +0.10, nowhere near McCabe's roughly $8B and $4B Re-engine break-evens.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: Qualitative only. UltraFan technology feeds the Trent fleet. No grid adjustment (inference).
tests.numbers: Kept as a technology inside a flat envelope, with no programme and no date, UltraFan feeds Trent time on wing [RX-0295] and draws no fleet engineers if it stays at technology level. Rule (inference): through 2050-2052, no engineers move from in-service, fleet or Trent time-on-wing teams to UltraFan technology work, and the fleet keeps first call. This is no reason to launch UltraFan WB. No value is added to the grid.

tests.name: fps campaign readiness (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Any fps-specific change to the Joint Venture engine gets its own durability campaign before that airframe's EIS, staffed from the Joint Venture, not fleet engineering, with partner-shop support in place before EIS (inference from the maturity and support rules).
tests.numbers: Confirmed as a rule. The engine has been ready since 2036 in its as-tested configuration and meets any fps EIS (2057 on a 7-yr fps launched 2050, 2060 on a 10-yr). P&W has said the same publicly: changes only after their own durability campaign, installation work staffed from the Joint Venture. Terms are standard, jointly with P&W. An fps on code 5 is worth 0.00, so no concession can pay. No fps is on the record, so nothing is live.

tests.name: Board round-3 recommendations as they stand in 2050 (Civil part: R1, R2, R3, R6)
tests.threshold: Report each as it stands. Not a pass/fail test.
tests.numbers: R1 IN-SERVICE: continued. The watch reports to the Board and the Committee. No finding is on the record, and no durability, time-on-wing, shop-visit or spares figure is on it either, so I report none. P&W's module data must come through the Joint Venture, and P&W now speaks only for its modules. The rule holds: fleet first, a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection. R2 CAPACITY: plan as above, from 913 to the 1,010 peak and down to 574, with Trent first call and OE moved to repair after 2052. OPEN: the MRO and spares split for P&W's modules, and partner MRO sized on measured rates, cannot be shown as done from the record, so both go to the Board as an open support item. R3 WIDEBODY CORE: both fields at hold. Worst cell 55.2%, 5.2 pp above the line. No Re-engine is on the record, and no grid column comes near the break-evens. Time on wing protects the core. R6 DISCLOSURE: the draft line passes, with no date, airframer comment, P&W module claim, widebody programme or time-on-wing target. 'Fleet first, ramp second' stays private.

vetoes.plan: A, the CEO's lean: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`
vetoes.ground: NO CIVIL VETO. (1) Maturity: the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's full six-year programme, a year before NGSA's 2037 EIS, and no in-service finding is on the record. (2) Early date: the draft line gives none. (3) Support: partner-shop support was in place by 2036. NOTES, NOT BINDING: the MRO and spares split for P&W's modules, and partner MRO sized on measured rates, go to the Board as an open support item. P&W module data through the Joint Venture is a standing condition. The P&W concentration stays on the risk register.

vetoes.plan: B: A + `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground: NOT A CIVIL GROUND. It counts in 2053 on its full three years, no date is disclosed, and Trent 1000 support is in place. My seat red line (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development) does not bite. I back the upgrade as a time-on-wing tool [RX-0285], but it fails on value: -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.63 against a $2B bill, and -1.73 even before strain. RED-LINE FLAG (the CEO's company rules, not my veto): the item loses more than its own bill in every column, it is beyond the $3B cap, and it fixes the $5B strain for good, breaking 'widebody never starved'. The CEO must strike it. It is also advice on load: development 2050-2053 overlaps the peak.

vetoes.plan: C: A + `ultrafan_wb: launch`
vetoes.ground: NOT A CIVIL VETO unless a date before 2056 (launch + 6) is disclosed. Ready-by-EIS FAIL as advice: ready 2056 against a 2055 EIS for any Re-engine launched this round, and it never counts in S1-S2. The Board reads this fail as a veto ground for an unconditional launch. RED-LINE FLAGS (company rules, not my veto): no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the public record [R-1574]; -8.90 weighted, far outside the $1B sub-cap; worst column -9.00, 2.25 times its $4B bill; the $5B strain fixed permanently. The CEO must strike it.

vetoes.plan: Conditional, for the final package at the veto check. It applies if any of these appear: a public statement or public move that gives a Joint Venture engine date other than the bulletin's, an UltraFan WB date before 2056, or a time-on-wing target; a rationale or move that counts on an engine before its ready year; any move that shortens an inspection or test regime on the Joint Venture engine or the Trent XWB, Trent 1000 or Trent 7000 fleets to hold the ramp; an fps-specific change offered without its own durability campaign before EIS; or a move that drops the narrowbody support plan
vetoes.ground: Civil veto grounds: compressed maturity (including in service), an early date, or no support. NOT INVOKED: nothing in the CEO's lean breaches them. If any appears in the final orders, statement or moves, I invoke the veto at the check, and the team rule makes it binding. The grounds rest on attributed CMD turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

ops.would_change_mind_if: Three things would change my view. First, an in-service finding on the Joint Venture engine, or on P&W's gear or GTF Advantage core (durability, a life-limited part, a hot-section shortfall). I would report it at once to the Board and the Committee and advise a fix and a slower ramp, and I would invoke the binding Civil veto on any move that shortened an inspection or test regime. Second, if P&W's module data stops reaching the Committee through the Joint Venture, or the MRO and spares split is not agreed, I would put it on the Board agenda as a support gap. Third, on widebody this is the last round, so a launch is permanent. I would back the upgrade or UltraFan WB only if all three of these held: a Re-engine on the record that names us, an engine ready by its EIS, and an item that fits the $3B cap or the $1B sub-cap with the $5B strain counted. None of that is on this grid. I would also act if a column showed the 50% line at risk. Named airline wins for the engine on NGSA would firm up the capacity plan.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen, Civil's 2050 test.

In service. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and has flown on NGSA since 2037. Nothing on the record shows an in-service finding, and I cite no figure I can't source. Pratt says the gear and GTF Advantage core 'stay ours', so our assurance on them rests on Pratt's data through the Joint Venture, and in public we speak only for ourselves. Their rule, a durability campaign before any change, matches ours. Nothing says slow the ramp. If something does, it's a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection.

Support. Our fleet grows from about 8,200 engines this year to 10,200 by 2052 and 16,400 by 2060. Partner shops and spares scale on measured rates. I can't show the MRO split for Pratt's modules as agreed, so it goes to the Board as an open support item.

Capacity. 913 engines this year, 1,010 at the 2052 peak, then down 43% to 574. High-performing suppliers to the peak, Trent kits and spares first, then OE capacity into repair, nothing owned left idle.

Widebody. 55.2%, 58.0% in S4, 5.2 points above the line. I like the upgrade for time on wing, but it's -1.73 before strain and -6.73 with it. UltraFan WB is ready in 2056, a year after any Re-engine launched today: a fail, as advice. Both pull engineers off the peak.

Disclosure. The draft line passes.

Orders: all hold. No veto. We're keeping our engines flying and earning.

other_moves.move: In-service watch on the Joint Venture engine at the narrowbody peak, P&W modules included (Board recommendation 1; Watson's condition)
other_moves.detail: Watson reports each round to the Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee on durability, time on wing, shop-visit rates, spares cover, early-service intervention and open findings. P&W's data on the gear and GTF Advantage core reaching us through the Joint Venture is a standing condition. P&W now says the modules 'stay ours' and 'Rolls-Royce speaks for itself', so in public we give no assurance on them beyond P&W's own words. Today the record shows no in-service finding, and we cite no in-service figure we cannot source. Private rule: the fleet comes first and the ramp second. The answer to a finding is a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime, on the Joint Venture engine and on the Trent XWB, Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 fleets. Any move that shortens one triggers Watson's binding Civil veto.

other_moves.move: Open support item to the Board: P&W module MRO and spares split, and partner MRO sized on measured rates (Watson's advice)
other_moves.detail: Support was in place before the 2037 EIS: partner MRO on the Singapore model, repair technology, a spare-engine pool and an EIS team by 2036. The fleet grows from about 8,200 RR narrowbody engines at end-2050 to about 10,200 at end-2052 and 16,400 by 2060. Watson cannot show from the record that the MRO and spares split for P&W's gear and core is agreed, or that partner MRO, P&W's shop network, the spare pool and repair technology are sized on measured shop-visit rates. Both go to the Board as an open support item until they are confirmed. Rule: size on measured rates, not assumed ones.

other_moves.move: Capacity plan through the 2052 peak and the run-down (Board recommendation 2)
other_moves.detail: Narrowbody OE: 913 (2050), 987 (2051), 1,010 (2052 peak), then 916, 903, 869, 838, 751, 674, 623 and 574 (2060), 43% below the peak. Widebody: 188 a year to 2061. To the peak: our share of the work stays with high-performing suppliers, critical parts are dual-sourced, and Trent kits, spares and time-on-wing engineering keep first call. After the peak: OE capacity moves to repair and the partner-shop aftermarket as shop visits rise with the ageing fleet, sized on measured rates. No owned capacity that would sit idle. The single-partner concentration on P&W for the gear and core stays on the Committee's risk register.

other_moves.move: Widebody core through time on wing; UltraFan kept as a technology (Board recommendation 3)
other_moves.detail: Trent XWB, Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time on wing inside the existing envelope, on the model of the Trent 1000 durability package: longer-life HP turbine blades and life-limited parts, fleet retrofit at shop visits. UltraFan stays a technology inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, redeployed and not added: no programme, no public date, not a game order and not a capital item. Its learning feeds Trent time on wing. Through 2050-2052 no engineer moves from in-service, fleet or Trent time-on-wing teams to UltraFan technology work. A widebody programme comes to the Board only when a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record and names us, and the case pays at our hurdles with the $5B strain counted: on McCabe's break-even, a Re-engine gain of about $8B weighted for UltraFan WB or about $4B for the upgrade, and at least $5B in every plausible column. This grid's best is +0.68. Airbus's line on assessing the A350's evolution is watched, not answered.

other_moves.move: Standard terms for the Joint Venture engine
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce offers the Joint Venture engine on standard terms, jointly with Pratt & Whitney, on NGSA and in any campaign. No launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade. Private notes: an fps on code 5 is worth 0.00 against S1 on this grid (+9.98 both), so no inducement can pay. Any fps-specific change gets its own durability campaign before that airframe's EIS, staffed from the Joint Venture and not from fleet engineering, with partner-shop support in place before EIS. Any change of Joint Venture terms, or any inducement, comes to the Board with McCabe's co-signature, which she has said she would withhold.

other_moves.move: Capital frame and closing account (McCabe; Board recommendation 4)
other_moves.detail: Narrowbody development money is final at $5.71B: the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B fold write-off, $1.71B over the $4B bound, stated openly. No further development spend. The narrowbody value is lifecycle value: $14.9B nominal in 2050 against $6.0B under the status quo, $16.6B at the 2052 peak and $14.2B in 2060, while narrowbody OE falls 43%. It arrives as net LTSA balance growth over flying hours, not straight-line cash. It goes through the capital order: balance sheet first, then the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity, no leverage for distributions. We guide low, and any change to medium-term guidance comes to the Board before release. An in-service finding on P&W's modules is unpriced; McCabe's range is about $0.9-1.1B nominal deferred for each 10% of a peak year's deliveries, with the fix and LTSA cash unpriced.

other_moves.move: Closing objective note to the Board
other_moves.detail: Enter narrowbody: met (25.2% in 2045, 27.2% in 2050). Keep widebody dominance: met (58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050; worst cell 55.2%, 58.0% in S4). Bounded narrowbody risk: NOT met, final at $5.71B, $1.71B over the bound. Widebody never starved: met, strain $0, because every widebody field holds. Closing value: ΔPV +9.98 at the worst column, +10.02 weighted, yield 109.07%.

decision.public_statement: So, our Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and our narrowbody development is complete. Maturity and time on wing come first, on every fleet we power, narrowbody and Trent. We offer the engine on standard terms, jointly with our partner. Widebody is our core, and we defend it through time on wing. Frankly, we don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, the last decision year. These orders fix the end state, and no later round exists in which to cancel anything. I decided on cash and quality of earnings [RX-0054], by the team rule.

1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL: every field at hold. Grid row 'UltraFan NB: hold' is +9.98 / +9.98 / +9.98 / +10.33 (S1-S4). It is the best plan in every column.

2. WEIGHTS. S1 0.75, S2 0.05, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, confirmed by McCabe and the Board.
- S2 0.05: Boeing will not launch 'until [the business case] is', with no date and no maker named. That is a signal against.
- S3 0.10: nothing is on the record, and Boeing calls its 787 line stable.
- S4 0.10: Airbus's 'continue to assess its evolution' is a soft A350 signal, but S4 also needs a 787 Re-engine nobody has signalled. I round it up, which favours the launch rows.
- On these weights the hold row is +10.02. It is +10.00 on McCabe's guide-low set (0.80/0.05/0.10/0.05) and on last round's set, +10.07 on equal weights and +10.05 on a Re-engine stress. No vote turns on the weights.

3. BINDING VETOES.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on `t1000_upgrade: launch` and on `ultrafan_wb: launch` (binding: hurdle and downside). Both orders stay `hold`.
- Watson: no Civil veto on the all-hold package. Maturity: the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 EIS, and no finding is on the record. Early date: none disclosed. Support: in place by 2036.
- Nothing to revise.

4. THE TWO WIDEBODY ITEMS, against hold, column by column.
- T1000 upgrade: -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.63, -6.72 weighted. Its worst column is 3.37 times its $2B bill. Even before the $5B strain it is -1.73: about $0.27B of engine gain for $2B. It counts only from 2053, so it buys no point of 2050 share. My record says regain the 787 share, 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. On this board the answer is the price. It fails the viable-business-model part of the four-part gate [RX-0030].
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32, -8.90 weighted. Its worst column is 2.25 times its $4B bill. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, so airframers-first fails [RX-0058]. It would be ready in 2056, a year after the 2055 EIS of any Re-engine launched this round.
- Either launch fixes the $5B strain (about £3.7bn) for good. It would turn 'widebody never starved' from met to not met and pull engineers off the 2052 peak.
- Both are far beyond the $3B cap and the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap, so no declared premium can carry either.

5. RED-LINE FLAGS.
- Watson flagged B and C: each loses more than its bill, is beyond the caps, fixes the strain, and C has no Re-engine on the record. McCabe flagged C on the same no-programme ground. I confirm every flag; both items were already struck.
- Final check against the company red lines: no UltraFan launch; no early date; no overlap; no cancel; no concession; no disclosure on airframers' dates, the A350 or P&W's modules. Nothing breaches.
- `overrides` is empty.

6. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. My record has no run-down, capacity or closing-account behaviour. On these I follow company doctrine: McCabe's capital order and guide-low frame as my evidence on cash, and Watson on support, capacity and maturity. The P&W module split and measured-rate sizing go to the Board as an open support item. That is advice, not a veto: support was in place before EIS, and no narrowbody order is live.

7. WHAT HOLD COSTS AND WHAT IT KEEPS.
